Feels like a very solid camera in terms of build quality. Nice and hefty. Everybody's networking ability is different. Some may find this very difficult to set up, some may find it a breeze. I hit a snag, and was SMH for awhile, but I figured it out, and I'll share with you my issue, and how I solved it. So if you happen to run into the same issue, these notes may help.

So H.View provides you with an ADMIN IP address which should work once your camera is connected to your home network. In this case, it's 192.168.1.120. You punch this into you browser, and you should be able to get to the ADMIN page to change your password and view your camera. But what happens when this IP address doesn't work for you? You will need to change it accordingly to your IPV4 gateway. I found out the easiest way is to simply let the IPC Manager modify it automatically by DHCP. I posted 3 screenshots to hopefully guide you. Here are some worthy notes...

1. Google "IPC Manager H.View" to find your way to their site to download the software. Top result with the headline DOWNLOAD CENTER should be the correct one. Be sure to download the version for your device, Linux, Mac, or Windows. BTW, they keep this in a Google Drive folder, so don't worry, you're in the right place.

2. Connect your camera to your network via POE switch. This set DOES NOT come with a power adapter, it is meant for POE switch users.

3. Install and launch the software and login in the lower left corner. Default is ADMIN and 12345. You can change this later. The login is strange because it doesn't give any feedback. Usually after logging in to a software, something changes or refreshes, such as a "log out" option, this lets you know you're logged in. But there seems to be no reaction in this software. After you hit enter, nothing changes. So don't fret, you're really logged in.

4. If you don't see any cameras, right click and hit refresh. Once you see your camera, check the box to SELECT your camera. Now, if you right click on your camera, there is a menu with a "OPEN HOME" option. If you click this, it "should" launch you to the admin page at 192.168.1.120, where you can change your password and view the camera. You can also manually punch the ip address in your browser.

5. This is where I ran into a snag. The default IP did not work for me. The browser would load an error page, "This site could not be reached." Proceed to #6 if you encounter this issue...

6. Go back into the IPC software. Make sure the default login credentials are still present, make sure your Camera is still Selected. Now, SELECT the DHCP box, and hit MODIFICATION. There should be a pop-up indicating the modification was successful. The IP address should now have changed from 192.168.1.120 to whatever new address that your router assigned. If it's still the same, try hitting refresh.

7. So now, you right click on your camera and hit OPEN HOME again, and you should be able to get to the admin page now. Or as mentioned before, just manually punch in the new IP address into your browser. When you successfully reach the admin page for the first time, you will be prompted to change your password. Now you can view your camera. Next time you go back tin the IPC software, make sure to use your new password.

I included 3 screenshots to supplement these notes. Hope that helps! This is a 5-Star product!

-This camera is definitely for beginners and I am an amateur at photography so this is perfect for me
-Portrait shots are beautiful on this camera and I find they provide the best quality of them all
-Other images seem to be closer to the quality of a newer smartphone

I have two desks in my den. One has my 3D printer and other electronics. I have a similar (though more expensive) power tower on that desk. My other desk is for my laptop and random crafting. I had been using an old extension cord that lacked three prong plugs. When this tower became available I was happy to be able to replace the old extension cord and be able to charge my numerous USB devices. Then it arrived. . .
It's lightweight. Too light, cords drag it across the desk, you have to watch how you plug things in or it topples over. Overall the plastic feels like a toy not a serious device. A weighted base would seriously improve the unit.
There are no instructions. You have to figure out which set of outlets are controlled by which top switch. The switches feel cheap and engage/disengage roughly. There is no separate power button for the USB plugs (my other tower has one) and the red system power light is blindingly bright. I'm going to see if I have any black electrical tape to partially cover it. It's truly annoying.
The plugs don't want to hold two prong cords, grounded cords hold a little better (not much) but my devices that use just two prong cords barely stay plugged in! Tap it, move something that brushes the cord, the slightest pressure and the plug pops out.
It works and the ten foot cord is nice. I was able to plug this in half way across the room and get it onto my desk but. . . I don't like it. Thin cheap plastic. Klunky switches. Tips over too easily. It doesn't instill confidence in the product. I like the idea of a desktop power tower and have one I rely on. I don't recommend this one.

I got mine for $248 plus sales tax with the immediate $50 reduction in price if one has Amazon Prime. I think that is a fair price for this Soundbar.

There is a lot to like about this Soundbar. You will love its easy ability to program in your TV's remote control, or any IR remote, to control the volume and mute. Very convenient.

The volume on the Soundbar can get plenty loud. The sound is quite clear.

Vizio includes all possible cables you might need.

The Soundbar is heavy and appears solidly built.

Programming features via the Vizio remote are very nice and easy to understand and figure out.

The negative: I applaud Vizio for trying to include bass speakers into the Soundbar so you won't need a separate bass speaker, but sadly they have failed. I did lots of testing on various TV feeds, from Music Choice stations to movies to local newscasts to regular network TV shows. I did adjustments to the bass via the remote on all TV feeds. The bass level is not there yet to satisfy.

I plugged in an 8" Energy brand powered bass speaker (this is not a large bass speaker), and let me tell you the difference is remarkable with all the TV feeds.

I will strongly suggest that if you consider buying this Soundbar you accept that for the most satisfying sound you really need and should have an external bass speaker. You will not be sorry at all.

One day a company might be able to invent a Soundbar with built-in bass speakers that truly deliver. Vizio has not succeeded with this model. But again, excluding the bass aspect, the rest of the Soundbar does deliver the quality.

Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is one of the better computer accessories I have used and it offers a noticeable improvement compared to traditional computer mice. Its unique shape makes it much more comfortable and a no- sliding- necessary design eliminates the need to drag your mouse across a flat surface to move the computer pointer on your screen. To move the pointer, all you do is move the large, red marble trackball. There is less strain on the fingers and wrist, making for a more comfortable experience.

Besides the added comfort, another advantage of the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is that it requires less space than a traditional mouse. Because this mouse is stationary and doesn't need to be dragged across a desk or other surface, it can fit into many small spaces. You don't need to make room to drag it, so it can be placed in tight quarters. This is great for those who work in offices with limited desk space.

The Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse offers four buttons to use for clicking. The large tabs on each side of the mouse are used for the usual right and left click functions and then there are two smaller tabs right above each of the larger tabs that are used for various functions. These two small tabs can be programmed to perform several things, and many will likely program them to scroll since this Logitech mouse doesn't have a scroll wheel. But the tabs can be programmed for other things, too. Since I don't necessarily need to scroll, my small tabs have been programmed as browser back and forward buttons. This makes life a little easier because I no longer need to move my mouse to the top of my screen and click the forward and backward arrows in the upper left corner. I just click my small left tab to go back and my small right tab to go forward.

The Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse is a marked improvement compared to the standard mouse, but I admit that it does take some getting used to. Having used a traditional mouse for most of my computer- using years, I had grown accustomed to sliding my mouse across the desk surface. Thus, when I started to use the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse, I kept sliding it around on my desk also, even though I knew this mouse didn't need to be dragged. It took some time to break this habit. It also took time to get used to the sensitivity of the trackball. The slightest movement sends your pointer flying and when I first started to use this mouse, I would continually underestimate the precision of the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse. My movements of the trackball were far too extreme. The pointer would soar across my computer screen, even though I would swear I wasn't moving the trackball very much. It is a very sensitive device that almost seems too loose at first because it moves so freely and with such little effort.

Compared to a traditional mouse, the Logitech Trackball Marble Mouse has many great things to offer and it is a mouse I am happy I took the time to try. It is superior to the traditional model in most areas, reducing pain and strain and offering greater accuracy and an easy grip. It does take time to get used to, but it is worth it in the long run and even those who initially resist the change will be happy, in due time, that they made the switch to Logitech.

I was looking for a sling camera bag for ease of use when I am in action mode, e.g., hanging off the side of a jeep during safari, hanging over the railing of a boat while photographing breaching whales. I did not want the typical backpack or the shoulder bag (both of which I own) that would impede me from such movements and/or would need to be set down while I was shooting.

I like to leave my zoom lens on my camera. I attach a lens in the open as few times as possible for the obvious reasons, e.g., salt air, dust. I have a Nikon 200-500 lens attached to a D4 body. With that configuration, the camera/lens is 14.25" long, D4 body is 6" wide and lens at its widest is 5" and it fills this bag's length (including the unzipped 30% extra). That set up is also about 10-11 pounds of weight. However, in order to fit it . . . I had to remove the square cushioned "cube" that is affixed by velcro into one side of the bag. Once my cameras/lens was in the bag, there was about 3" of horizontal (lengthwise space) left and 3" of vertical space as well as small pockets of space around the camera/lens itself. I would not be able to fit my IPad. I could probably tuck my IPhone in somewhere. Extra batteries, battery charger and cords would be doubtful. One extra battery perhaps.

The zipper on the top can be zipped either way (which I like). There are cords on the zippers as well for easy grabbing. The "open" pockets on the outside are nice, and while they are 6" deep, there isn't much that has any value that I would store there . . . because the risk of it falling out would be too great. (At least for me . . . because I plan to sling the sling quite a bit). It is difficult to believe that the inside of this bag only has 2 very small pockets. Both pockets have flaps that velcro. One pocket is 4"d x 3"w and the other is 4"d x 2"w. While that seems like a lot . . . the pockets are sewn into the bag and some of that width is lost to the stitching. They are immediately adjacent to each other and immediately under the top zipper (not the most optimum place to be IMHO).

The strap is nice and sturdy and reminds me of my Nikon strap. What I also like is that instead of having the typical strap tightener (don't recall the technical term, but like a buckle), this strap has a cam lock buckle. It is a buckle clip that clips down with pressure on the strap. It will take you less time to adjust your strap, which might not be a big deal to some . . . if you don't adjust your strap very often. Loaded it down with approximately 12 pounds of equipment, slung it on my back and tested it by moving around for a while today . . . and it stayed put. Hopefully, it will do the same when in the field. Strap has 6" wide removable cushion that velcros into place. I will probably double that with another one to make it super comfy. I am 6'0" tall. With the strap over my left shoulder (and the bag sitting on my right hip) and the strap completely extended . . . the top of the bag (where it zips open), is approximately 25" vertically from my right shoulder.

Canvas feels heavyweight. It feels like it might be waxed (and therefore water resistant), but after a bit of due diligence, I cannot find anything that would confirm same. But, you could sling this over your shoulder under a rain jacket or poncho if necessary.

The color is just right for safari (bright colors, whites, greys and/or blacks are frowned upon). This is the main reason why I did not purchase the Passport II or III . . . no natural color choices.

I would describe myself as an intermediate amateur photographer and it has become my hobby in retirement. I live for nature action shots.

I am keeping this bag. I am going to cut off one side of the cushioned "cube" to make a cushioned "U". The open end of the "U" will face up. I will place the camera in the bag so that the cushioned U will cradle my large lens with my camera attached. While it doesn't hold as much as I would like . . . I liken it to a wristlet wallet. It holds exactly what I need at the time I need it. I will still have my camera backpack with me (to hold extra batteries, lenses and the like) and my hubby usually volunteers for carry duty - lucky me! I would like to have given it 5 stars . . . but I feel as though the design needs improvement (the II and III are about the same in size etc.). Unfortunately, this also seems to be the only true sling bag on the market. (My definition of sling is worn like a crossbody with the bag on your back instead of in front).

Look forward to breaking it in very soon.

This is one of the modems that's on Comcast's recommended list for my cable system here in California. When the cable guy showed up to install my Internet service, he checked it out and said "It will work fine." After about an hour of pulling wires around my house, he hooked things up to the modem and I had very high speed Internet service. Pretty sweet.

I chose this model because its upload and download specs are well above what my cable Internet service needs, and because it has advanced features like IPv6. So I'm assuming they got the basic stuff right as well. Other reviewers have said this model runs hot, but I haven't observed that. I have it in my utility room which is in the basement where it's pretty cool to start with.

The lights on the front of the unit show what's going on, which is mostly useful as it boots up. They work well, and are also attractive to look at -- they had a good designer for that. The unit has only 3 connection ports on the back, one for power, one for the incoming cable, and one Ethernet RJ-45 out. If you want to hook up more than a single computer, you'll need to connect this single Ethernet port to a router, or wireless router. I have the cable modem connected into a 5-port NetGear switch downstairs, which is connected to an 8-port NetGear switch upstairs, which is then connected to my Linksys wireless router. My computers then use the IP addresses that the wireless router provides. (It won't work to plug additional computers into the switch that I connected directly to the cable modem because the cable company provides only one IP address. It's the wireless router that hands out additional IP addresses. Each computer that you're using requires its own IP address.) The wireless connection works well for my 2 computers and my Roku box for Netflix. (And the bandwidth available to Netflix is amazing. It spends virtually no time at all buffering before it starts streaming HD video.)

Oh, and of course I had to reboot everything (including the modem and the wireless router) for the new modem to be recognized. For now, I'm keeping my old DSL service as a backup Internet service. Not sure when I might decide to give that up.

This is a very cool digital art tool. It's a combination of wacom-style drawing surface and external monitor, so you can draw directly on the screen like paper instead of looking at the computer screen while you sketch.
Ideally, you can use a USB-C port on a device that supports it so that you can combine displayport and USB input device into one cable. However, it seems like you'd need an additional USB for power in many cases, and in my case I needed to use the three-wire solution: One HDMI out from the computer, one USB for the pen input signal, and the 3rd USB for power. Kind of a rats nest of wire and not very portable. It really makes me wish I had bought a Surface or Lenovo Yoga with the active Wacom pen built in so that I get this functionality in a much cleaner setup, but at least with this it is a pretty cool addition to my desktop without buying a separate computer. And now I can have something else on my PC screen while this operates as a drawing canvas screen #2. Cool for a desktop, not so much for a laptop, since there are 3 wires to connect at a minimum.
I've noticed that the driver is a little bit difficult to use sometimes- I've had to set up the drawing area in settings only to have it default when I reboot to the original drawing area and need to be set again. I'm still getting used to it. But when it works, it IS really cool. You need to find software that can support it properly, like Krita for example, if you want to get the full effect out of the pressure sensitive drawing. That being said, it feels kind of expensive and I wish it were a more straight forward and seamless experience for the money, but I don't think there's really a better way to do this with an existing PC.
If you want to add drawing capability to an existing computer instead of buying a Surface/Yoga/iPad Pro/etc, this is the way.

I wanted a set of speakers to use mainly for my Kindle Fire and MP3 player, but also as my computer speakers. Due to space constraints, a 2.0 system was my only option, since a subwoofer (regardless of the size) would be problematic.

So the search began. There were several speakers that sounded great, including the Creative Gigaworks, M Audio and Audioengine. However, they lacked the convenience features I wanted such as ease of connecting/disconnecting a tablet and volume control without having to reach out and touch the speaker.

The Bose Companion 20 initially caught my eye because of the control pod. That was a great solution to my problems since I could control the volume right on my desk plus have the ability to plug in/unplug a tablet very easily. The sound quality sealed the deal - everyone who hears these speakers think they are a 2.1 set due to the ample bass. But, the bass is not at the expense of clear mid and upper ranges.

I use these 60% for music and 40% for video, and for both applications, the sound quality has been just wonderful. I'm also impressed that they sound just as good with the volume dialed way down as they do at moderate or blast-out-the-walls loud.

The control pod is very well made. It has a nice weight to it and a non-skid backing so it stays put. The volume control works very smoothly with a solid feel. I'm especially fond of being able to turn the speakers on and off by just touching the control pod.

You can connect it to the PC and to an aux device (such as a tablet) and use both at the same time. That's important since I want to listen to music or a video from my Fire, but still want to hear a chime when an email arrives.

My complaints are that the control pod cable is a bit too short for my needs. It's about 5 foot long, which is ample if you have the speakers next to your PC, but I have my speakers on a shelf above my desk. I was able to arrange things to make it work, but another foot or two of cable (or the ability to purchase an extension) would have been nice. It's a custom cable, so an off-the-shelf extension is not possible.

My other complaint is the price. I was able to get a used pair for half of the regular price. I think these are a bit overpriced at the regular price. But, Bose hit a really unique niche - the ability to have great sound without any compromise in convenience. If you want both, there's a high cost for admission.

If the price is not an issue, these very much deserve a hard look if you're in the market for a great sounding pair of 2.0 speakers. Highly recommend.

This case is exactly what I wanted: extremely durable shock-absorbing (read: drop-proof) protection without screen protection. Let me qualify that statement: I did *not* want screen protection. I love the pearl eink display on my graphite Kindle Keyboard, and it now has a big brother. I do not want a screen cover, as this would greatly reduce the screen's otherwise remarkable clarity, adding unwanted elements such as bubbles, surface scratches, and glare to the mix--no thank you. There is a reason I disliked reading on the iPad so much I gave it back (very reflective!). In fact, this OtterBox defender case came with a stick-on screen protector--no way. It would ruin that big, glorious pearl eink display.

A screen cover serves no purpose once you remove the device from your backpack/messenger/tote/briefcase for use. Assuming you transport your Kindle device safely in an appropriate sleeve (you put your other expensive electronic equipment--your laptop/tablet in one; your Kindle deserves the same amount of respect), the screen protector is completely unnecessary--the sleeve protects the screen during travel. THAT is when the screen needs protecting--when you are not using it, from the other goodies in your messenger bag/backpack (keys, pens, earbuds, and anything else rattling around in there). Yes, that's right--I'm talking about a Kindle in an Otterbox Inside a sleeve inside your briefcase. ...Inception-level protection. You got it. Better safe than sorry, right? What if they once again stop producing our beloved Kindle DX and something happens to yours? I do not want to have to replace my DX--especially if it has to be with a Fire device (5% the battery life, reflective, heavy, expensive--no thanks!). When you are holding your Kindle in your hand, reading, a screen cover only detracts from the experience.

What you see in my pictures is exactly what you get: a beefy, black rubber (not silicone--too easily torn; rubber is much stronger) form-fitting sleeve with an equally form-fitting outer plastic shell. Science geeks like me understand how this works, and just in case you are not one, here is the idea: if you drop your device onto the floor, the outer shell absorbs some of the impact energy generated by the device hitting the floor. It then disburses the remaining energy of the impact broadly into the rubber inner lining. The rubber lining then in turn disburses the now greatly-reduced impact energy into the device. In other words, by the time the force of the impact is filtered through two layers of protection, the second of which is very absorbent and resilient (rubber) the device inside absorbs little if anything of the original impact.

I feel very good about having my Kindle DX in an Otterbox Commuter. If I ever had one of those incredibly poorly-designed (read: seriously fragile) apple devices, such as an iPad or iPhone (which I do not, and am not ever likely to), it too would live in an OtterBox Commuter case. OtterBox = the best protection a device can get. I paid $18 including shipping for this. A great price, and worth much more in terms of peace of mind.

After reading reviews in Cnet and Consumer Reports, and feedback from owners on the AVS board, I knew I wanted to get a Samsung LCD. But which one? The 550, 630 and 650 are all highly rated, and all fell within my price range.

I first looked at the 550. Great TV and the lowest price. The picture quality was top-notch, but it did not have the 120hz technology and Samsung's smoothing system (called AMP) to reduce motion judder. In side-by-side viewing, I could see a difference in the picture with those features, and, since the price difference was not much, decided to move up to the 6-series.

Keep in mind that 120hz and AMP are two different things. You can turn AMP off (or set it to low, medium or high); you can't turn off 120hz unless you are in game mode. I like AMP set at low -- to my eye, that improves the picture without making it too smooth and video-like.

Both the 650 and 630 are fantastic TVs, and either one would be a great choice. The major difference between the two is the glassiness of the screen - the 650 has a high gloss screen; the 630 has a matte screen (basically the same as the 550, but with a tiny bit more gloss). I have a very bright living room with lots of windows. The 650 acted like a mirror, reflecting everything to the point of being seriously distracting -- you can see yourself in the screen in dark scenes. The 630 was the perfect compromise -- better quality picture than the 550, but far less gloss than the 650.

The advantage of the glossy screen is that it give more "pop" and saturation to the picture. Colors are deeper, blacks are richer, and the overall picture quality is a bit better. If I was using the TV in a darker environment (such as a basement), I'd go for the 650. But given the brightness of the room, the 630 was (for me) the better choice.

I've been told the sound quality in the 6-series is a bit better than the 5-series. That was not an issue for me since I turn off the TV speakers and run the sound through a receiver. If you plan on using the TV speakers you may want to listen to both sets to see if you hear a difference.

Very pleased with the set so far. You need to do a bit of tweaking to get the picture perfect, but the menus make it easy to do so. You can find configuration setups on several boards that will help point you in the right direction.

Other pluses of the 630 are the more muted Touch of Red in the bezel. I'm not a big fan of the red color, so having it less visible is a plus. Very nice remote with easy to find buttons.

I'm using the set with a Denon 1909 receiver, an Oppo 983H DVD player, and KEF 3000 series speakers. Everything works great together and I'm continually wowed by how great it looks and sounds.

First let me tell you what I like about this keyboard: I like the key action. Keys have a decently long stroke and are easy to press and don't feel spongy. I like the split layout, which makes for a much more natural position for the arms. I like the split spacebar. To me, these are advantages over the Logitech K350 I've been using, which has a curved, not split, key layout and a spongy feel when typing.

What I don't like, and what was pretty much a dealbreaker to me (I thought about returning it almost immediately) is the "wrist rest." It is short and rolls off steeply and provides no wrist support at all, unless you like typing with your wrist positioned lower than your knuckles and your hands bent upwards from the wrist. The recommended position is wrist level with the knuckles, which is called the "neutral" position. I personally prefer typing with my wrists positioned slightly higher than my knuckles.

Look at the product photos and notice that the typist doesn't even have his wrist on the wrist rest. He or she is using a hover hand technique, I guess to make things look more ergonomic or something, because if their wrists were actually on the wrist rest, their hands would be obviously bent upwards at the wrists to reach the keys.

I'm at a loss as to why many keyboard manufacturers (including Logitech with the K350) provide legs to raise the back of the keyboard and don't provide anything to raise the front. That just makes the "backwards" bend at the wrist even more pronounced.

This Periboard keyboard is no exception to that. It has foldaway legs at the back and none in the front. But even if it had legs to raise the front, it wouldn't provide much improvement. I raised the front a couple of inches with a foam wedge I use for keyboard support, and the wrist rest was still so low I pressed the spacebar when reaching for the F2 key.

I even tried adding foam wrist rests but the built-in rest is so steep and short it actually interferes with using a really functional rest. I even tried using wearable wrist rests---which are kind of annoying on their own since they aren't all that stable---and the steep slope and short length of the built-in wrist rest made that a less than effective solution. This keyboard might have been a lot better if it had no built-in wrist rest at all. That way you could use your own and set it up just like you like it.

It's disappointing, actually. I like the key action and layout, but the wrist rest pretty much nerfs the whole thing. I may keep it and experiment with solutions from time to time. I might even see if I can cut off the built-in rest and replace it with something made of wood or something, or just get it out of the way so I can use some other effective wrist rest.

In the meantime, I'm probably going to stick with the spongy-action, non-split Logitech K350. In fact I'm typing this review on it, though I would have liked to use the Periboard 512. But until I come up with a better wrist rest solution it's just easier to use the K350.

And a couple more quick points, comparing this keyboard to the K350, this keyboard is wired while the K350 is wireless. The overall footprint of both (length and width) is almost the same. I personally don't use or need the multimedia keys on either.

Because of the better key action and, to me, better key layout, if it had a better wrist rest, or none at all, this Periboard 512 might have become my go-to keyboard.

So I gave up and used the 4K HDMI connection and the colors look perfect.
When you use the 4K HDMI connection, you can customize all of the picture adjustments the way you want them.
I was able to adjust the colors and whitepoint to look the same as my iMac screen.
And it looks just as sharp with HDMI as it does with USB-C or Displayport.

So I am happy with this monitor. It looks just as good as my Retina iMac display.
I also like the adjustable stand which moves up and down and tilts.

The Zen Xtra (any capacity) appears to be the only portable MP3 player on the marker that features Time Scaling. Time Scaling is Creative's term for the ability to play a file back faster but without distortion. Voices don't sound like the Chipmonks, they just talk faster. For music buffs, that's useless--who wants to hear a song faster? But for podcast listeners, it's quite helpful. A two hour podcast that consists of talking can be sped up significantly.

It's amazing how the human brain adjusts to the faster talk rate, too. I've read that some studies claim we retain more by listening to a faster rate of speech.

Time scaling means more information in less time. If you have many podcasts you'd like to hear but only so much drive time to hear them in, this feature is great.

I don't know why Creative doesn't include Time Scaling on more of their products. It's a firmware feature. They make a ton of devices, but only the Zen Xtra has Time Scaling. I don't know of any other device out there that has it, including iPods.

To experience how Time Scaling works, try it on Windows Media Player 10. Open an MP3 voice recording and go to "Play Speed Settings" and move the slider to 1.3 or 1.4. At 1.4 a 60 minute show plays back in 42 minutes.

The product specs and RatherLiveInKeyWest's excellent November 23, 2014 review cover all of the highlights of this box. I'll confine my review to a few details that I love about this and why this one is yet another milestone in the evolution of these boxes.

First I'll share my opinion about the lack of bluetooth. Frankly I do not feel that it's needed since this box is designed to integrate with a TV and usually that means a home audio system as well. If bluetooth is truly important to you there are two USB ports on this box, so you can purchase a blutetooth dongle and add that capability.

One of the features that I love is you can not only control this with the remote that comes with it, but also wired or wireless keyboards and mice, and a Miracast-enabled phone. The instructions cover all of these options, including the Miracast one. I do recommend using a keyboard and mouse for the initial set up because the remote is tedious. The instructions are terse, but sufficient to get this box up and running. If you own an Android phone or tablet you will have an easier time than if you are more in the Windows or IOS camp. But even then it's not a steep learning curve.

Like the control options you have an array of connetions options as well. They are covered in the product specs so I am not going to repeat them here. Suffice to say, this box is flexible and will connect to legacy TVs as well as the latest and greatest.

Another feature I like is this will recognize SD cards up to 64GB, which provides more than ample space for media files. Plus this box is both stable and blazing fast compared to the previous generation.

Bottom line: the boxes I have used in the past were better suited for geeks who loved tinkering. This one is a major step towards a friendly addition to your home entertainment system that an average, quasi-technical consumer can effectively use. It is also a key building block to seamless integration of home computing and entertainment system. For all of the above reasons I rated it five stars.

The first night I opened it, I was not at all impressed, I wish I had just kept my SD4000 IS PowerShot and asked for something else for Christmas. I took pictures side by side and it wasn't that impressed. Not sure what the problem was then (condensation? The box sat outside for hours before I brought it in and opened it) but it has gotten better.

1) There are lots of improvements over my older Canons but this is definitely bulkier and bigger
2) The wireless feature works great with my home wifi and my Android. Took no time at all to setup either.
3) Low light pictures do seem a lot more bright, as if there is a hidden flash, but are grainy.
4) Camera is solid, feels great in your hand
5) The "ring" isn't a smooth turning one, it "clicks" quite awkwardly between each setting, so you go clicking through options and not in a way you can run through them, one at a time, and not smooth at all, I find myself using the menu items instead.
6) The touchscreen is awesome!
7) Touchscreen picture taking is useless, you'd be taking pictures all the time, there is no way to hold the camera really without touching the screen

In the end, I was quite happy to get a new and fairly cheap camera, but it simply isn't THAT much better than my SD4000, except in low light, and then not super low light, just low light.

I have since ordered and received the Sony RX100. Which is why I waited to return this camera, wanted to compare them side by side. After a couple of days of "playing" (yes I'm clearly not a professional, but I'd guess nor are most consumers), here are my thoughts:

1) The picture quality of the RX100 is better, but not always, and not that much more, sure it has a lot more pixels, but over all, not a huge difference. For just pictures, for ordinary consumer, I'd say get the S110, for being almost half the price, the pictures aren't THAT much different.

2) The RX100's menus are awesome for those who aren't well versed in photography, it actually explains what each setting does and is for, even with a sample picture, and then within each has sub menus explaining what they do, with yet more pictures, and finally has a help button. FANTASTIC!

3) S110's wifi is great, RX100 has none. Sending pictures to your phone and then posting or emailing them on the fly is really great.

4) As great as the S110's low light "brightness" is, the RX100 is a good 10 times better on really low lights. When there is enough light for you to see fairly clearly, they seem close, but when it's dark enough where you can't make out too clearly what you are looking at, and you can no longer see the colors, the RX100 can still take pictures that look like a cheap camera WITH a flash took (with a flash of course they both look great), where as the S110 takes pictures similar to what your eyes see when it's that dark. The RX100 really shines with no flash in pretty darn dark settings.

5) There are lots of other things the RX100 does, but might not be of interest to you, but they are there, like take pictures while recording video (but only in interlaced video, when I put it on p it doesn't let me take pictures), but those pictures aren't as great as doing so without video recording in room conditions. The function ring is much better as well.

6) S110's touchscreen awesomeness is missing

7) You can still put an S110 in your back pocket, though it would be like a thick heavy wallet. The RX100 however is almost a centimeter thicker and most of that is the lens sticking out further so I wouldn't call it a pocket camera. The S110 feels better (grainy, square metal feel, but the Sony has a smooth more rounded metal finish) and looks better.

This is a fantastic tool for people who need to work in remote locations with multiple kinds of computer. Not only does it work in the car for road warriors that need to meet a deadline or watch a lot of videos, but it makes it easy to power up off other DC sources without an additional inverter.
In my case, I do a lot of live streaming events and need to power a laptop for hours, usually too far away from a plug to be charged. So I carry around a portable power bank that offers 12v DC car outlets, and this is PERFECT for use with that!

Something to note: While my Lenovo and HP laptops were easy to identify the correct plug right away (yellow square and blue tip), my Acer was a little bit more difficult. I own numerous tripods of different types, and I have to say that I really like this one as a simple, small tabletop tripod. It appears to be very well-made, and is of substantial heft and construction for such a small device (closed, it is approximately 6 inches long). To me, this is an imperative in order to support my rather hefty digital SLR. Thus far, it has been able to support several somewhat lengthy (and obviously heavy) telephoto lenses--though the max I've tried it with is about 8" long. Incidentally, that is something that I have found quite problematic with some of the adjustable wire-legged tabletop tripods (although they obviously offer more flexibility in range). I'm not sure how it is supposed to reach a maximum height of almost 9" as stated in the item description, since the whole unit is only 6" long, approximately. Perhaps they mean after your camera has been mounted?

I also love that it is very easy to mount your camera. It's a very user-friendly device. I love that I can also mount it to my camera or digital video cam and, when closed, it becomes a sort of hand-held monopod. Although there is no telescopic feature on this device, I'm not sure it would be necessary for a table-top tripod; just get yourself a box or some books and elevate it, right?

At the risk of being verbose, I need to reiterate (for the discriminating buyer): the entire structure is one of quality. The metal swivel compartment and hefty legs are all powder-coated, and they are very well-finished. The only plastic on this tripod (and it is not the cheap plastic that brittles easily) is the actual fob to tighten the swivel-head (which appears to be stainless steel, but I could be wrong) and the anti-scratch feet (which I cannot discern, but may actually be of high-density rubber). The fob is one that, in the unforeseeable event it breaks or falls off, appears to be easily replaceable with a myriad of improvised materials, as it is attached to a metal tightening head and secured to it with a metal pin. The legs are attached via tiny phillips-head screws and onto a metal base with fused bolt-backing, which allows for easy tightening and loosening with a miniature screwdriver.

The long and short of it is: I can't find anything wrong with this tripod! Definitely worth having. And no, I don't work for the company--I'm just an average Joe-Blow consumer like most of you who is tired of purchasing substandard items and feels compelled to share when I find something well worth the cost.

I've been using a Linksys router for years and it never missed a beat (their wireless G model with the two antennas). But, after upgrading my Internet from DSL to cable, I thought a new router would be in order.

Before buying one I searched for reviews from computer and tech magazines/sites. Talk about confusing! I'd read one review that gave a sterling endorsement for a particular router; then another review from another site that gave the same router a horrible review.

Since my router needs are pretty basic (just use it to share Internet access) I concentrated on ease of install issues. In that regard there was consensus about how easy Linksys is to install. Considering that my Linksys G is still cranking along after several years, I'm reasonably confident (or at least hopeful) that this will last me an equal length of time.

First, let me say I own the 47" LG 47LE8500 for my living room with its stunning high def picture and extremely poor speakers. I was looking for a slightly smaller (and less expensive) TV for my bedroom and chose this 42" Vizio. Vizio has a similar 47" model under this newly released line. (So far, I am mostly happy with my purchase.)

Both the LG and Vizio have LED LCD with Local Dimming. I have to say that the high def picture on the Vizio is not as stunning as on the LG 47LE8500, but it is close, and still satisfying.

The black levels are better on the LG, but pretty close on the Vizio.

The Vizio arrived with one of the round rubber "feet" missing under the base. (Better quality control and inspection please?)

The WiFi on the Vizio is fabulous. The remote having a qwerty keyboard is fabulous.

First thing I had to do (for personal preference) is turn off the room light sensor. The picture was way too dark for me when the light sensor was on.

Also, the default screen brightness setting with the light sensor off is too bright, in my opinion. The brightness level is at 50 by default on the standard pic setting, and it looks brighter than the 50 setting on other sets. (But it is very easy to adjust, of course.)

The speakers on the Vizio are much better than on the LG.

I dislike that the Vizio does not have a swivel base.

Standard def is quite acceptable (and better than on the LG).

So, bottom line: If you want to save some money, this new Vizio line is a very good choice (and recommended). Once you customize the pic settings, I think you will be happy with the high def picture. If you have extra money to burn, the LG will give you a more stunning high def picture with better black levels, but you probably will dislike the LG's speakers, especially if you listen to a lot of music with the volume raised.

Adding to my review, August 28:

When the TV is off, the Vizio logo at the front is lit up in orange. I have found no way to turn this off. I hope that if enough people complain, perhaps Vizio will release a software update that will allow the turn off of this orange Vizio light.

I have encountered bad lip sync issues. But luckily, Vizio has included in the Audio settings a Lip Sync adjustment setting. I had to enable this setting, as the lip sync mismatch problem was really bad. The adjustment has helped.

This LEATHER LAPTOP MESSENGER BAG FOR MEN (by Leather Centric) is made of real leather--animal hide, NOT the man-made “pleather” stuff that’s often marketed on Amazon as “real leather” or “genuine leather”. That’s a big plus, but the bag itself has a lot of minuses.

First, the bag’s styling is so old-fashioned, it makes the bag look cheap. You have to really love the 1950s “retro” look, to like the overall appearance. The bag definitely looks handmade, but it also looks crudely rustic.

Second, although the bag has lots of zippered compartments (inside and outside), it is only 3” deep. It has no expansion gussets, so the total capacity is one laptop or one very thick sheaf of documents. Internal zipper compartments are relatively useless if a bag can’t expand to hold the things added to the compartments.

Third, the bag is difficult to open. It opens with two metal clasps--these are hidden beneath the purely decorative buckled front straps. You have to pull up on both clasps at once to lift the flap, and you can’t do this easily without laying the bag flat on one side, or holding it on your lap. The leather flap itself is very stiff (at least when the bag is new), and this adds to the opening difficulty.

Fourth, the bag has no locking mechanism. Not that it is easy to open (see previous paragraph).

Fifth, the brass fittings must tarnish very easily, because the bag arrives with every single exposed brass piece wrapped tightly in thin plastic wrap. It takes something very sharp to cut the plastic, and you must be careful not to scratch the fittings. (I succeeded in removing the wrappings without damaging the bag, but I punctured my left wrist with an Olfa knife in the process.)

The bag is reasonably priced (about $90 on Amazon). It comes with a snap-on shoulder carrying strap, and has a sturdy, permanently attached satchel handle. The handle is very comfortable. The bag leather is already distressed, so you needn’t worry about scratches. This is a truly rugged laptop bag.

The Apple Watch is slowly gaining functionality and popularity, but it does not work with non-Apple smartphones. If you have an Android phone, your choices are Google Wear OS watches like this one, Samsung Tizen watches, and smart fitness watches like Garmin and Fitbit.

Samsung watches work best with Samsung phones since both devices require you to buy into the Samsung ecosystem, which has diverged quite a bit from the Google Android ecosystem. For example, you have to run Tizen apps on the Samsung watch and you have to use the Bixby assistant instead of the Google Assistant. Those requirements are going to be too much for many people using Android phones other than Samsung.

Garmin and Fitbit make some pretty good sports or activity tracking watches that also have some smartwatch features, like playing music or displaying notifications so you don't have to pull the phone out of your pocket everytime it beeps. Garmin and Fitbit also have much better battery life than any of the Apple, Google, or Samsung watches. The GPS and activity tracking features on Garmin watches are noticeably more accurate than the general purpose smartwatches. Garmin and Fitbit watches are more sporty than stylish, but some of the recent models try harder to be at least presentable in a casual workplace. These are definitely a good choice for some types of users, especially very athletic people.

Google does not make its own watches (yet); they release the watch software and allow companies like Skagen to use it in watches like this one. Google Wear OS phones mostly work the same, though they may have different hardware capabilities. This Skagen watch has GPS and heart rate monitor hardware, while others may not. The Skagen watch is definitely the best looking Google Wear OS watch that I have seen so far, perhaps the most stylish of all the most recent smartwatches that I have seen (better looking than the Apple watch as well). From the front, it looks like a regular Skagen watch, though from the side it is much thicker; maybe twice as thick as a regular Skagen watch, since this brand is usually known for very thin watches. The 40mm case size is about the same as a medium-sized men's regular watch or a large women's watch (many smartwatches are huge and out-of-place on medium-sized wrists). In my testing, the Google Wear OS features all work great on the watch. It synchronizes and interacts easily with the phone. Activity/fitness tracking is fine for casual use, but not accurate enough for serious athletes who want detailed measurements of their performance.

Battery life is the shortfall of most of these smartwatches. I get less than a full day of battery life if I do any GPS sports tracking and use the always-on-display, but I will get a full day if I only do one of those. Then I have to charge it every night (and cannot use it for sleep tracking). I've heard that Samsung and Apple get slightly better battery life. Garmin gets several days of battery life, so that is the way to go if you don't want to keep worrying about battery.

In summary, there is no single best smartwatch on the market right now. If you're looking for the most Google experience, this is probably the most stylish choice right now. A new smartwatch CPU that supposedly has better battery life was recently announced, but I don't expect any products to use that until mid-2019 at the earliest, if you want to wait until then.

Connect RCA cables and turn on unit. Do not put a disc into it, or leave the unit open with no disc.
Type 5168. This brings up a menu that includes the choice "Region"
Go to "Region" and press Enter.
Choose "Test 0." Press enter.
Press setup button to exit, or get back to the left menu if enter has not already taken you there and go up or down to Exit Setup and then hit Enter.

I've used glass screen protectors on several smartphones and digital cameras. This is my first time trying a large glass screen protector on a tablet. The kit contains everything you need, including a alcohol towel for cleaning your tablet (and your fingers), a sticker that tries to pick up all the lint on the tablet and the screen protector, and various other things that are less necessary. The glass is fine. It is slightly smaller than the Fire 8's screen (so you have some leeway if you don't install it perfectly). There is a little hole at the top so it doesn't cover the selfie camera. Honestly, I haven't noticed much difference between different brands of screen protectors.

If you've never installed a glass screen protector before, look on YouTube for tutorials. All of the similar products are installed the same way. You need to be really careful when installing this thing since it is large and difficult to align with your tablet's screen. I suggest that you try to align one edge of the protector as well as the camera hole and then hope for the best with the other edges. Make sure you pick up all the lint on both the tablet screen and the back of the screen protector, since any stray dust or lint is going to be noticeably ugly for as long as you have the screen protector installed. If you try to remove the screen protector to wipe off some lint that you missed, I guarantee that more lint will sucked in and make the problem worse, so you're best off doing a very thorough cleaning job the first time.

Whether or not you actually need a screen protector is a good question. If you use a case with a cover, then your chance of scratching the screen is small. I guess that depends on how rough you are with your tablet. You can go by your experience with other devices. A tablet is not like a smartphone that is sitting in your pocket with loose change and keys.

3. MEMORY IS VERY EXPENSIVE. This camera uses Fuji (and Olympus) new "XD" memory. It's smaller and not particularly fast. It also costs three times what regular digital camera memory (FLASH) costs. So tack that [X] premium back on the price.

I'm a die hard 3D fanatic. I've been through it all ( started with 13 Ghosts in a movie theater as a child). Through the years, I've experimented with 3D tech as it progressed. From flickering active glasses to the passive, movie theater style approach . I still have a 3D computer monitor and TV, though they're not set up at the moment. I even have 2 Nintendo 3DS units which was quite an accomplishment being the first, truly mainstream product that did not require glasses to view 3D, and finally, the ultimate 3D experience was/is VR using the Oculus Rift/Quest systems. Yes, it is quite the tech, but wearing the headset is not something you'd want to do for long periods, as it can become uncomfortable , and I don't always like the feeling of cutting off my real world surroundings.

Fast forward to 2021. I had my eye on the Lume tablet, but not at the original price. I already had an iPad Pro which is pretty unbeatable. When I saw the $299.00 price tag (April 2022), it was a no brainer. I always wanted an android tablet as an alternative anyway. The flexibility of the Android OS goes beyond IOS, making it a helluva lot more interesting for tinkerers and people who love to customize!

Well, I'm happy to say, this tablet is beyond my expectations.. Look, if you didn't grow up with 3D tech, and expect Jason Vorhees to jump out of the screen and slice you, then you're not meant for this. Go play in VR insead. When you understand going in, the limitations of 3D, then you'll love this. The 3D is gorgeous, but the tablet's native resolution (2D), will drop dramatically to accommodate the 3D mode (just like it does with passive glasses displays on TVs ). The display will sometimes be dimmer in 3D, but it varies with each app and its contents. 3D Photos look amazing and you hardly hardly notice the dimming, where as some games it's quite obvious, but again, depends on the app. Speaking of which, the game library is not large yet (I think they're around 100 titles at the time of this review). Some games utilize the 3D intelligently and will leave you impressed, while others are too basic or simply not good. Gameloft's Asphalt racing & Architect are both samples of top quality on all levels, and there are few other 3D gaming gems hidden among the crop; I'm still going through them.

Now for some REAL hotness: I just installed Citra, which is a 3DS emulator with an option for Lume 3D. It's still an early version, but quite a number of games already work excellently! Having 3D on a sharper, larger screen with 3DS gaming - are you kidding me? This is amazing.

What I find most impressive are the videos and photographs. It's like, some objects look almost as if they're protruding 4" off the screen. This baby can convert 8K 2D youtube videos to 3D in seconds , or at most, a minute. There's so much to try out on youtube and other social media platforms , that you'll realize, there just isn't enough time in a day. The app is called LeiaTube, which is part of a suite of Leia 3D apps including one where you can even take your own impressive 3D photos and videos with the dual lens camera.

Some of the other pre-loaded Leia apps for the Lume include a viewer for manipulating thousands of 3D objects, mind-blowing community photos and dozens of well-done educational videos covering a wide range of topics, each pretty lengthy! Explore everything from the human body, to heading back in time to ancient Egypt, all in 3D of course.

Want to watch blockbuster 3D Movies? You can head to Leiaflix and for $1.99, you'll have a mini 3D theater right on your lap, and the results are impressive and even more exciting is an app on Google Play called Jellyfin. You also have to download the server software for PC or Mac as well as a custom video player made by a talented individual (check the Leia forums). Now you're able to REMOTELY watch your own 3D videos (and 2D) from your Lume tablet from anywhere in your home over wifi. It's Amazeballs!

The tablet uses a USB type C connector. If you purchase one of those multi inputs to C adapters, you can add a hard drive, USB flash or SD cards so you'll be able to transfer items from your expansion storage to the Lume, or you can download Total Commander, and remotely transfer PC/Mac files to the Lume and the reverse. All from your bed.

And finally - two things that are MAJOR surprises -- beyond the 3D itself are the sound and picture quality. When using the tablet in normal 2D (like any Samsung tab), the picture quality is unreal - it actually gives the iPad screen a run for its money. I mean, this display almost approaches OLED - with crisp, bright and bold colors, and a rich black level. As far sound, we're talking Dolby Atmos. It's the richest sound I've ever heard on any mobile device, and the build quality is solid, like a tank.

So, take away the 3D, and you have one killer tablet on its own. Head to the Google Play Store and go crazy! I hope enough units sell so this unique tablet gets the support it deserves.

I have a strong interest in photography and I always keep an eye open for lights and equipment that will help me take more creative or impactful pictures. I selected this light with the intent of using it for creative photography and so far I am pleased with it. I have other LED lights that have similar functions, but this one is different in a few ways that set it apart.

This is a wand light as opposed to a square LED bank. As such, the light distribution is a bit different. It can directly cover a longer (wider) area which is handy when putting together a mock-up with miniatures. It has a couple of mounting options too, utilizing either a miniature tripod (included) or magnetically attaching to a metal surface. I do wish a clamp was included such that it could attach to the tripod horizontally, but such clamps are available if they're needed.

This light is VERY bright and can easily light a small room when at full brightness. It can be dimmed to cast a soft light too which is good. It's not exactly the most ideal light source but it will work for general lighting in a pinch.

The temperature range goes from 2500k (very warm and orange-y) to 9900k (blistering cold white) and everywhere in between. Getting the color just right is relatively easy though it does take a little patience and experimentation to get it right. Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. In addition to "natural lighting" modes it can be set for specific colors too such as purple, red, blue and so on.

Charging is done via a USB-C port, and the charging cable is included. I have not tried using this as a power source to charge my phone though the documentation doesn't say much about that. A full charge on this light lasts a while, though I have not drained it all the way down to find out how long it will last. Obviously the runtime is variable based on mode and brightness, and what is interesting about this light in particular is that it displays the estimated runtime on the screen based on current settings - this is a nice feature that I have not seen on a lot of these lights.

There are some creative modes for use with video or for special effects in a live setting, though the usefulness of these modes is dependent on the user. I personally will never use them. However, in the right hands these might be very useful for a project. There are several effects available, including police flashers, tube TV glow simulation, flickering candle and more.

The light comes with a nice canvas carrying pouch that provides basic storage and protection.

I really like this light and will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. It has some nice features and it has good color and brightness ranges. It's not terribly expensive either.

This is the first Sony TV that I've owned, and I'm extremely impressed. My primary use for this TV would be gaming through a PS3, watching BD/DVD movies and streaming Netflix. I only have a PS3 (no other game systems at the moment, and I don't ever plan to have cable or satellite) so the "lack of" HDMI ports that some people complain about isn't an issue for me at all, though if you have multiple devices, I can understand how you'd feel about this!

Here are some of my observations/opinions:

*Final Fantasy XIII looks amazing in 1080p! The game really shows off what this TV (and the PS3) are capable of.
*My Battlestar Galactica BD's, which tends to have pretty dark pictures look great! The black-levels are very sharp, especially for a LCD screen!
*I find that many TV's have menus that are annoying to navigate. This one has a very friendly menu system.
*Some people complain that the remote buttons don't glow. I don't see this as a problem... The paint used to label the buttons is very reflective, and I have little or no problem reading them in low-light settings.

Ultimately, if you don't have a lot of space, and want a nice HDTV as a main TV, or one for your gaming systems, I highly recommend this one!

Bear in mind that as gaming headphones, the sound quality is not as suited for other applications like listening to music. Having said that, here's how the experience went:

Appearance: maybe this is some macho thing, but they are enormous and intense-looking in an almost exaggerated way. So if you're one of those people that likes huge flashy stuff or ostentatiously masculine-looking things, this is perfect? They're huge.

Comfort: Very comfy! The cup part is large and fits great, and the headband adjusts nicely to most average head sizes. The microphone is fully adjustable, making it work for anyone.

Sound blocking: pretty good! While it does not use noise-cancelling technology, the sheer size and generous build of the headphones allows for Very effective sound cancellation. I had my partner listen to something with her back to me so she could not see me, and with the volume turned up, I had to full on Scream for her to hear me.

Sound quality: Better for spoken word and voices, honestly. The sound is crisp and detailed, but it's also a little canned-sounding, with somewhat sharp, tinny trebles and less-than-intense bass. This does best in mid-range and capturing voices and sounds, and less so for actual music. Having said that, it is certainly better than cheap headphones for music, so it does have some versatility if you're not too picky.

Overall: These are pretty great! They even have an adapter that can be used by other devices that unites the audio input and output, which comes split for certain applications like computers or other gaming. (Meaning, theres a separate cable for the microphone and audio input, and they come with an adapter to have a single "female" connection that can work on phones or other single-plug devices using audio in/out.)

Just a phenomenal cpu. This is probably the best upgrade Ive done, coming from an i7 7700k. I had 30 days to use and figure out if I wanted to stay with this or go with the latest AMD cpu.

Work- I used to have trouble running programs that were either too complex or inefficiently coded that it led to stutters, hitches, delays or freezes. One program that always caused massive trouble for me over the years was the Think or Swim trading platform. I originally upgraded to the i7 7700k and it could not handle more than 2-3 chart at a time running the time and sales and L2. Run some side charts and you could forget about trading, especially at the open when calculations need to be run at an extremely rapid pace. I even added a total of 32gb ddr4 3400 ram and it still wouldnt run properly. Arguably, the program is encoded really inefficiently requiring much more from the CPU than necessary. Ive tried many different trading programs and this one caused the most trouble. After stepping up to the i9 9900k I can now run this inefficiently encoded program on my main chart screen, with two different tickers having 4 different time frames each with its own L2 and time and sales, PLUS 15 side charts without a hitch! Also im running my browser with at least 5 tabs open and video/audio running. Absolutely amazing. I never thought I could get it to work like this.

Gaming- even if the cpu doesnt run at 100 pct it affects the quality of the experience of the gameplay, especially for demanding games, or just poorly coded, inefficient ones. RPGs fall into these categories. I.e., Kingdom Come Deliverance. Video and streaming is flawless as well.

Vs AMD- Performance isnt always about raw numbers, if there are too many peaks and valleys, it affects the quality of the experience. I havent personally compared it directly to the newest AMD cpu, but having looked at the side by side comparisons, AMD cpu seems to put out better numbers for work-related applications, but clearly on the gaming side, intel is superior. From my observation, the quality of the experience with Intel was greater because the frame rate was consistent with much less, if any micro stuttering, which you can see with the AMD chips. As a result, Intel's presentation was more effortless and smooth. With the AMD setup, you can see some graying/discoloring/hazy effects in demanding scenes. It seems like AMD is an overcharged chip that experiences these dips because of that, causing a deterioration in the experience. AMD is perfectly fine for work I presume, but not for me when it comes to gaming. Intel performs like a more refined, polished product. This is just based on my personal observation of their performance in these two different areas.

Overclocking- its perfectly fine using it the way it is. No need to overclock, but of course you can overclock it. I run mine 16 hours a day without any problems. Top recommendation at the asking price these days.

I have other Brainwavz earbuds and they have never failed to provide me with great sound. These are no exception. While there is some crispness missing from the sound that you get with their more advanced (and more expensive) offerings, these hit the mark far better than the price would suggest. The bass is rich sounding without being boomy. It’s not way dialed up on the bass end like other models, but strikes a good balance.

The comfort is excellent. The Comply foam tips are delightful to use – they mold themselves to your ear rather than the other way around. Excellent sound isolation as well due to the tight, but comfortable fit.

The build quality is nice considering the price. The cords are on the thin side, but are well-anchored. The cord is not, however, something that will take a lot of abuse (such as the flat cable on the S1 model, which is far more durable). The earbuds are plasticy but again, given the price, I’ll rate the build quality as above average. However, I do wish they would have made the R/L markings more legible (which is an issue with all their earbuds). A small spot of white paint on the R solves that problem.

All in all, these are excellent earbuds. Hits the mark on sound quality, build quality and comfort, and does it at a very nice price point. Highly recommend.

A couple of weeks ago I got a monitor stand to use on my desk. It had a large circular hole on the back of the monitor shelf along with a plastic cover for the hole. Apparently the idea was to give a discreet place to run the monitor's plug through. That seemed like a silly waste to me as you could just run the plug off the back of the stand with much less hassle. So the idea of this product, using that hole for a charger with some extra USB connections, seemed like a good idea to me. A real caveat though is that there are several essential details to pay attention to in using this item.

The first essential detail is to pay attention to the size of the hole you are going to use this on and the size of this product. Apparently those holes are not a standard size and some folks have had issues using this item because of that. Handyman types who have the tools to enlarge a grommet hole have an advantage here but it would behoove everyone to make sure this product will fit what they need.

The second detail to notice is that this device only works with USB 3.0 devices. The 2.0 ones won't work. My desktop computer has both 2.0 and 3.0 USB plugs. You can plug any device into any of those slots and it will work although the speed may vary. A 2.0 device plugged into a 3.0 slot will run but at 2.0 speeds. With this product, the 2.0 devices won't work at all.

The final detail to watch out for may be the most important one. Several people who have plugged the charger into their computer have reported difficulties it's created with their machines. So if you want to do that, pay very close attention the first time you try it to avoid any problems.

The prices on big-screen smart tvs are in free-fall these days; projectors are always a bit of a project. But you're sure you want a projector, right? If so this is a great choice. Easy set up, great image, amazing keystoning (more on THAT in a moment), powerful internal speakers, and a decent price point (under $900 currently.)

Setup could scarcely be easier - provided you have your screen and the (not included) input cables/stick - or a wireless dongle. As I already had a projection screen and an HDMI cable for my laptop, all I had to do was switch on the projector, adjust the lens, run the start utility to keystone for the projector being offset from the center of the screen, connect the cable from laptop to projector, then allow the device to find the video source - the device finds the input in a few seconds and is soon streaming video and audio.

The projector's own audio is surprisingly good - and loud. Response to the remote is... a little slow, depending how close you are to the projector. The projector's own audio is great, and as we have it closer to the screen than we sit, I haven't felt the need to connect speakers. Persons with more demanding tastes in audio will of course differ, but the device's own speakers do a solid job.

Video quality is OUTSTANDING. Colors are vibrant and although a light source placed near the screen washes them out, the image is still clearly visible. With a light source more than 10 feet away and even with natural light through windows (at the opposite end of a 25-foot room) the image is perfectly clear; even though as I'm using a white screen the blacks are clear and dark. There was one strange exception to this with a streaming video (Extant) where the darks were warmer in the projection than on the laptop, but we have run other video and also had a DVR player (hooked up via the triple cables), and run DVRS with perfect light levels. I recently got an Amazon Fire Stick, and actually set it up on the projector - setup was easy and there have been no adjustments needed for the streaming video.

The keystoning is an amazing, but somewhat tedious, feature; you can offset the device and still get an excellent image. Using the keystoning feature on the remote, some tweaking gives you a near-perfect image. I say near perfect because when we had the projector placed eight feet back and some feet down to the left of the screen, the upper right-hand corner of the image frame bent inwards - although the cast image itself was clear and undistorted. This was apparently because the projector was not on a perfectly horizontal surface. The real issue was that when the projector was moved back in front of the screen, I had to redo the keystoning manually; holding down the OK key was supposed to reset it, but this didn't work for me.

The projector is relatively light and easy to move around. The feet are easy to unscrew to manipulate the image, but for the afore-mentioned keystoning issue, it was necessary to adjust the surface the projector was resting on; this would obviously be a whole different matter if ceiling-mounted.

I think it's a great projector. So really it all boils down to whether you WANT a projector - the VERY big picture and/or the portability, eh? You don't care about having to control light levels, positioning the device itself (and the associated transmitting device,) maintaining a screen, dealing with multiple interfaces... You're not the complete couch potato, surfing the channels via remote... Not to go on and on - this is a projector, not a tv. You can hook it up to a tv, or a laptop, streaming stick, etc, but - a projector is always going to be more complicated. This, however, is an amazingly uncomplicated projector!

I started reading reviews then first then I stopped by the store with my kids and tried them out. My son was across the store and I could hear him talking to his sister. I could also hear every word of the conversation of people not far away. I removed the Hearphones and could not hear my kids or the people talking. I did this a few times... tuning in on people, music, etc then removing the buds. Tried the noise canceling and the rumbling in my ears was almost gone. Needless to say, I was impressed. I discussed the warranty with the salesman...30 day return, 90 exchange for something else, & 1 year free replacement(btw the 1 yr starts replacement over every time you replace them). I was sold. I purchased them with the intention of using for 30 days and returning if I could do without them.

I have now had them for 1 month. Here is my experience... at first I hated the neckband and was considering returning, but I got used to it and now don’t notice it. I use them for 1 hour workouts every morning, driving in the car for phone calls, music, podcasts, noise canceling at work, so pretty much all day. The neckband twists a little while working out or running and you need to shift it back in place, but it’s not a big deal for me. I would prefer the Soundsport Frees for working out, but I can’t bring myself to spend another $200 for headphones when these are $500. The noise canceling is fantastic for the gym & office and allows me to listen to music at a much lower level, which saves what I have left of my hearing in the long run. I used the soundsport wireless for 1 year before getting these and the sound quality of the hearphones is better, plus the noise canceling, and it has the music boost/phone call boost. I gave my soundsports to my wife and now use these exclusively.

Hearing:
When there is a lot of noise I can put them on and hear every word of a conversation that I would normally not hear or tune all the noise out via the noise cancellation. I recently went to a concert and was shocked at how much I enjoyed the concert more while wearing them. I could hear the guitar strings, vocals, and so much more while having a conversation with my wife. Amazing! I even use them while listening to the stereo in my car because it sounds so much better. I am always surprised at the sounds that I miss while not wearing them.

Sound: Classic Bose sound. The best headphones I’ve owned and I’ve had a few nice sets including the Bose soundsports & Bowers & Wilkins. I enjoy music much more since having them.

Phone calls: Phone calls are so much better, I talk on the phone more now because I’m not struggling to hear the other person and I hear them in both ears.

Overall: They simply work great. One of the best features is the directivity. When you set it to front or focused it ignores the rear microphones. While at the same time merging the left & right sound together. You hear a little of the left in the right ear and vice verse which helps with conversations. If Bose can ever put this technology in earbuds like the Frees they probably could not keep them on the shelf. If you have hearing loss or tinnitus and love music buy the Hearphones. If you love music and have no hearing loss buy the QC30 or QC35 for the noise canceling feature.

There are other fun Easter eggs that I didn’t expect...Wearing these while listening to music creates a “karaoke” effect and you can adjust the world volume so that it increases your voice to blend with the music coming through the headphones. I also played my guitar and found that more enjoyable. I could hear the notes in more detail as well as hear my voice in more detail while playing. These are also great if you like to people watch. When you are in a mall or restaurant you can hear random people’s conversations from across the room in detail, while they think you are wearing headphones and not listening at all. If you have hearing loss and/or enjoy a premium set of headphones these are for you. I have not used any other hearing devices to compare, but there are plenty of other reviews that will provide that information.

My rating is 5 stars from my perspective, but here is the breakdown of positives and negatives as I see them:

Positives:
- The sound is amazing for music, podcasts, phone calls, everything. Probably the best sounding headphones next to the QC35
- Adjustable balance. I set the balance to about 20 toward my right ear and both ears feel equal again.
- The adjustable world volume is awesome. I constantly adjust when my surrounding are too loud or not loud enough.
- Treble/bass adjustment. I set the treble around 30 and my world comes to life.
- Noise canceling is superb. It has almost stopped my tinnitus altogether. Especially good in situations like moving the yard. Before the noise of the mower was exhausting , but now it does not bother me.
- Adjustable presets are nice
- The front, focus, & everywhere settings work great. I use the front 180 setting the most. The focus setting really boost voice in front of you which is very nice too.
- Hearing the outside world while listening to music is amazing. Especially when you want to hear music, but want to hear when someone talks to you.
- “Karaoke effect” is pretty cool and makes singing/playing more enjoyable.
Negatives:
- The neckband was annoying at first, but now I barely notice it.
- Sometimes the app does not connect right away, but it connects after a few seconds.
- You will get weird looks from people, but the look is them wandering if you are listening to them since you are wearing headphones. It disappears after you start taking to people.
- I worry about the durability of them sometimes, but with a free replacement of 1 year I feel better about that. Remember that if you swap them with the year the warranty starts over. I am considering the extended warranty they lasts 3 years.
- I don’t like the charge port, but the only thing to improve it would be wireless charging.
- You’ll get wind noise outside. Use the noise canceling.

Btw I bought these in the Bose store and wrote this review to help others with similar issues. The headphones have improved my life and I love using them for just about everything.
