I received this hub as a review sample and just had to test it on a [[ASIN:B00KCG95M6 Keedox® M8 TV Box With Remote Control]]. It was immediately recognized and worked perfectly. I also use it to extend my USB ports in my [[ASIN:B00C7SK2J2 Micro USB OTG Host Cable to USB 2.0]] with the same results. That one was connected to a Samsung Tab 3 10.1, then a Galaxy Note 3. All of those tests was using the hub unpowered.

For connecting high power devices like external hard drives and DVD ROMs, I powered this hub using a [[ASIN:B00MRGKPH8 Sabrent 5V 4A 100V-240V to DC Power Adapter]]. I only tested a single external hard drive and a DVD player with this test and then only using the USB 2.0 speed since it was connected to a ThinkPad T61 running Windows XP. The arrangement worked and I was able to get expected USB 2.0 performance - not blazing, but not molasses slow either. The only USB 3.0 device I currently own is my Note 3 phone and I could not adequately test this hub using that.

I do love the looks of the hub, but the important thing for me is I was able to use it on some legacy devices as well as three Android devices with no problems whatsoever. I also like the fact that you can transform it into a powered hub with an optional power supply, or just use it out of the box for low power devices. Just be aware that if you opt to use it as a powered hub using the Sabrent power supply make sure that the devices that you intend to plug into it do not exceed 4 Amps total. Some of the larger external hard drives can easily eat into the power budget. Also note that of you attempt to use this as a charger (which you can do standalone with the optional power supply) you are only going to get 1 Amp per port and no over charging protection. I recommend not using it for that unless you are in a pinch.

Bottom like: this is a versatile hub that has worked with every device I tested, and it looks good as well.

The Portal is sort of like an Echo Show but with different strengths and weaknesses. There is SO MUCH I could say about this device, some good and some bad, but I'll try to stick to the more important points here.
The killer feature, as you may know from their ads, as the way it can automatically zoom in/out and follow faces in a video call. So essentially, you can move around a room hands-free and it will find you and make sure you're in the shot. It's like having your own personal camera man on call.
In my experience with it so far, this worked fairly well. Moving left or right, the camera followed me. If more people enter the shot, it will zoom out to get them all in. It isn't without limitations however, and sometimes you'll move too far and it can't see you. Other times it got confused and lost me (if I move out of the frame and back in, that usually fixed it). For the most part, it worked as expected.
The sound is actually EXCELLENT considering this is the Mini edition. I was expecting the sound to be more like the Echo Dot, but this has a very large speaker on the rear which is able to drive very impressively deep bass without even approaching max volume. So that was a pleasant surprise.
While it has its own "Hey Portal" voice commands, it ALSO comes with Amazon Alexa built in. That's where it sort of starts acting like a Facebook-branded Echo Show, playing music, announcements, showing you answers to questions, turning on/off digital things, etc. All the things you want Alexa to do. However, I was sad to find that it isn't considered an Echo device for certain Alexa features, such as multi-room music groups, the Ring doorbell, and probably other Alexa Skills that aren't supported on non-Amazon hardware. So you can't really replace an Alexa Show with this if you need those features.
Now, some things that are better than the Echo Show: PRIVACY. I know, this is Facebook we're talking about, but I really like that they included a tab to disable the camera (by covering it up, not just turning it off), microphone, or both. It's like they realized that someone was going to complain they don't want Facebook recording them in their living room and thought ahead to add that. The Amazon devices with cameras don't have a dedicated cover built in. Then there's video calling to people OTHER THAN OWNERS OF ANOTHER DEVICE. The latest Show devices from Amazon have cameras too, but you can only call other Echo Shows or phones with the Alexa app running. The Portal can call Facebook and Whatsapp users, which means I can actually reach other people I'd want to chat with. This isn't a perfect implementation either, however... For Whatsapp, it essentially uses Whatsapp's web functionality behind the scenes to connect to your account. If you use Whatsapp web on your computer, it will log you out of the Portal and you'll need to log back in again after using it. This is an unnecessarily silly extra step. I use Whatsapp web a lot, so we ended up using my wife's Whatsapp account on the Portal to call our family and friends so we wouldn't have to keep logging out and in.
Then there's media like Youtube- much like the Amazon Echo devices, Google has decided not to allow an official Youtube app for the Portal either. However, there IS a browser, and you can go to Youtube on it. This makes for an awkward user interface (and not just because you can't control it with your voice), but once the video is up it works fine. It not only plays beautifully full screen, but you can even go back to the home screen and it will continue playing as a picture-in-picture overlay which can be moved around the screen by dragging. That's pretty neat. It's almost like they tried to support Youtube as much as possible without actually having an official interface to abide by Google's rules.
Other fun features include Facebook games like Draw Something, Chess, Super Baseball Batting Derby, etc, which you can play against other friends on Facebook or Portal devices. Then there's a bunch of photo effects which are really fun Snapchat-style filters that follow your face in augmented reality-style real time. These features can be used not only in the Photobooth app, but also on ANY call with the device. Then there's my favorite fun feature: Story Time! This feature is sort of like the snapchat photobooth AR-style effects mentioned above, however you read a story and it will animate effects over your face to illustrate as you go. This can be done on the Story Time app on the device locally or in a call to another person. My kids actually really LOVE that feature, and my 2 year old likes to read along with me when we do it. I'll admit they are very cute and sometimes I've laughed out loud when I didn't expect what happens next in the animation being done to me.

Honestly, as an Alexa alternative to an Echo Show, it is close but not quite a replacement. As a video chat device, it is better but only if your contacts are on Facebook or Whatsapp. And even then, Whatsapp is only good if you don't use Whatsapp Web. I'd consider it a 3 star device for those caveats, however the Story Time feature as well as the camera that follows you is really quite cool. Add that they considered your privacy with the flap cover and I have to give this at least 4 stars. It really has so much going for it, and I'm hoping they can iron out some of the software kinks to make it even better in the future.

First of all, the D-Link camera is relatively easy to set up - always the one to play with techie stuff first, my husband had it up and running in a flash (well almost a flash). Just attach the supplied cable to your computer, run the CD and follow the simple instructions and you're good to go. According to the instructions, you have two options to set up the camera: wirelessly or wired. Naturally, my husband tried the wireless option first, which didn't work because it claimed (spuriously, we believe) that it couldn't find the network, so he had to resort to the other method, which worked right away. We're using a Linksys wireless router.

The camera works quite well indoors where the intensity of the ambient light is generally much lower than outdoors. However, in the brighter outdoor light it is difficult to discern what you're looking at (is it a bird, is it a plane?). The colour is not the best, but then again, it ain't a Nikon 7000. There is some amount of adjustment that can be done online to change the settings, but you'll need to create an online account/register your camera first with D-Link at [...] This is also necessary if you want to view your camera remotely. Strange enough, whenever I try to access the camera online, I get a message telling me that the application needs an earlier version of Java. However, after hitting <Run> for the next three dialogue boxes or so that pop up, it will display the picture. I tried accessing the camera from outside my home network but was unable to do so. Maybe firewall issues?? (Too much effort required to check this). There is also an iPod app that is quite good, minus sound.

Night vision was surprisingly good too. In the dark, the images were shades of grey, but in brighter conditions, the colour returned. Four LED lights lit up whenever the night vision was activated (could be an issue if you wanted to place it somewhere discrete).

On the down side, the camera has to be plugged into an electrical socket to work, and the cord it came with is very short. This means you have to either place it near an electrical outlet or use an extension cord. This would obviously have limitations on where you can place it. It also has to be connected to your home network whether wired or wireless.

While in theory it could be used as a security camera, it has to be powered 24/7, so if you live in a country or area prone to an uneven power supply which could damage sensitive equipment, then you may want to consider that before getting it or you may need to install additional equipment such as line conditioners/UPS to protect your equipment.

The sound is not very good. In fact, after a few hours use it started to make a clicking sound in an endless loop.

Recommended for limited applications such as keeping an eye on kids (or pets, or pesky guests), or when you're avoiding (hiding from) certain people who come calling at your gate, but not as a dedicated security system.

Looking at all of those cameras, out of the box, is a little bit intimidating and it leads one to believe that setup will take days and even weeks to complete. But it is actually much simpler than it looks and there is no need to install all 12. Just use the number of cameras you feel is necessary and store the rest for later use.

With this security system in place, you can access the live feed through the internet and even on your mobile phone via the Q- See applications. This is great for convenience and its one of the security systems best features. Other security systems have this feature as well, so it’s nothing unique. But it is very easy to use and it lets you monitor specific places on a property, for maximum security. Wherever you might be, home or away, you can take a look at what’s going on by pulling the mobile phone from your pocket. It doesn’t get much easier than that.

The one issue I have with this system is the same one others have complained about, and that is the wires. In the modern world in which we live, we expect wireless technology more and more. This system is wired and it could present some problems as you try to tape wires and otherwise conceal them from view. If this was a wireless system and I could place the cameras anyplace I like, then I would be hard pressed to find much wrong with this product. But I know many people who would likely reject this product immediately for this reason alone.

Security is important, especially for those who live in less safe areas or who operate a small business in a vulnerable area. With Q- See watching the home or business, you can feel a little more at ease. The cameras detect motion and can quickly help you catch a person in the act of theft, trespassing, or vandalism, providing proof positive of what happened and where. Like I said, the lack of wireless technology is a problem but if you can get past that issue, you will find that this is a very good security system for home or business needs.

I ordered the 'Malektronic Interstellar Premium Wireless Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones' for review and would like to share my thoughts.

So I am no audiophile, but I do love a good quality headphone that is built well and sound good. Sounding good or even great is really subjective depending on personal preference. For the going retail price of these Malektronic Interstellar Premium Wireless Noise Cancelling Over-Ear Headphones, I really expected much more than what I personally find these to be. I'll break my experience and thoughts into a few main points that stood out to me.

Comfort - These are comfortable but they don't fit as snug as I would have liked. I have a small head for a 54yro male, and even on the smallest adjustment setting, they just don't hug my ears like I would have hoped for such an expensive set of headphones.

Noise Cancelling - yea this is a big one for me right hear (see what I did there). I am not at all impressed with the Noise Cancelling in these headphones for the price. I mean it's OK, but I have ANC wireless earbuds that do a much better job for about the same price. There are only two settings. ANC On and ANC Off. For me, It's really hard to tell whether I've turned it on or off. There is no indicator like others I have that would either beep or greet you with some kind of prompt letting you know which mode you are in (there are voice prompts when you turn them on or off so why not anything for ANC modes). In fact the only way I can truly tell that it's on or off, is to pause the song and push the ANC button at which point it's pretty clear. However, and with that said, I do notice that when it's on, the music almost sounds more heavy on the Bass. It's almost like the Bass is supposed to give that "ANC" feel. Remember, I am no audiophile but this is just my observation.

Sound - Now I can say this, and that is that these do sound good until you get close to max volume. At which point they just don't hold up to the volume. Not that they get really loud but if you have the ANC on and you are listening to a heavy Bass song, they tend to bottom out just a tad. It's not bad but again for this price point, I would have expected better. The highs are nice but even better when ANC is off. Mids are there and probably sound good in either mode really. Another thing I noticed is that if you take these off while the music is still playing at full volume, they sound like they are rattling and sound a bit distorted. However when you put them back on, there is no distortion like I noticed with them off. That was kind of strange.

Micro USB charging - I always have to point this out. It's 2020 companies and USB C should be the standard any more in my opinion. Just saying.

Build Quality - They aren't the worst I have seen or tried but at this price point they are not the best either. They are pretty much plastic although fairly solid.

Buttons - The buttons are hidden/covered near the edge of the ear pads and they took me a while to figure out where they are, but after using them for a while, I actually like the fact that they look to be buttonless.

Looks/design - These really do look nice both on and off. They don't look cheap which is nice, as I have some others that just look ugly and I refuse to wear haha. The design is well thought out and I do love how they fold flat and compact into the very nice hard case.

So with all that said, I do like these headphones. They sound pretty good. The ANC is meh but they are comfortable besides not fitting as snug as I would prefer. Build quality is decent and I do love they way they fold up and store nicely into the included hard case. Thank you for including this Maletronics! Micro USB charging is a bummer but they also can be used wired with the included cable if you forget to get them charged up. Battery life is not bad. 30hrs might be pushing it if you like to listen to them loud and are always using the ANC. I have yet to test that fully as the longest I generally go is maybe an hour at a time. So for me the battery life is fine.

Overall, I really want to love these, and I actually do like them a lot, but I am just not that "Wowed" at this price point. I have other brands at or around this price point that I like better. Now maybe I got a dud pair and that very well could be, but I don't dislike them. They are nice and I plan to keep them around as a back-up pair. I hope that this was helpful.

This is one of those products where I have to struggle to come up with a single negative. It’s well-designed, well-made and has many thoughtful touches that tells me some real thought went into the design. The only real negative is the price.

The materials used throughout are all high quality. The body is made of heavy-duty nylon that feels like it can withstand even the roughest treatment without failing. The zippers – which are usually the first item to go on my backpacks – are excellent, with all-metal teeth that zip/unzip smoothly. Even the zipper pull tabs are well-made, composed of leather (or what certainly feels like leather) with a rivet on the end to make it easy to grab. I’m especially impressed with the zipper on the laptop compartment since it has a rubbery “gasket” around it that helps keep it watertight but doesn’t interfere with zipper operation.

The back straps are well-padded with dense foam that feels wonderful. The same foam is used on the back plate, which has a sculpted rim of padding to minimize back sweat when wearing this on your back. Even though the back plate has rigid support to protect the laptop/tablet compartments it feels very comfortable when worn.

All the nylon straps to cinch the pack are thick nylon with an ultra smooth surface so there’s zero struggle to get them through the buckles. There’s a padded top grab handle for when you want to one-hand carry this rather than have it on your back.

I could go on and on about the build quality but to keep this review at a reasonable length I’ll just say that every part and piece is some of the best quality work I’ve seen on a backpack.

The benefits continue on the inside with many thoughtful design touches. The main compartment has both open and zippered compartments. Since the bag has a flat bottom, it can stand up when the main compartment is opened, which I find makes this so very easy to use even with my fumbly hands. The inside also has a very attractive rusty-orange colored liner that color-coordinates nicely plus brightens up the interior to make it easier to find small items.

The exterior design maximizes utility. There is an outside zippered vertical pocket on the front that can be accessed without disturbing anything inside the pack. This “quick access” pocket also has a small interior pouch to hold loose items securely. There are two side pouches (one per side) that can hold a water bottle (and a large one at that) or a collapsible umbrella. Each shoulder strap has a phone pocket. The phone pockets are the only area that may fall a bit short depending on the type of phone you use. An iPhone 6 without a case fits fine; a 6 with a slim-style case fits snugly; a 6Plus without a case fits very snugly; a 6Plus with a case probably would not fit (I don’t have a case for the 6Plus to test it to be sure, but since the 6Plus sans case is so tight, I can’t imagine one with a case would fit).

The main laptop compartment is lined with better quality foam than I’ve found in many camera bags, and has a slidy lining so laptops slip in and out easily. It’s sized for up to a 17 inch laptop, according to the manufacturer. I’m able to put in my 15 inch laptop with room to spare, so the sizing seems very accurate for a 17 inch laptop. There’s also a tablet “cubby” behind the laptop compartment with a separate zipper so you can take your tablet out without disturbing the laptop.

The only potential negative with regard to the design is the size of this pack. It’s not designed for those who want the slimmest profile pack out there – this is designed for people, such as myself, who never learned the meaning of the term “travel light.” I can fit all the electronic detritus I seem to be unable to live without, plus files, papers, food, water, etc. While you don’t have to load it down for it to be useful, I can pack this puppy to the hilt and it still remains comfortable on my less than limber back.

All this good news, and then we come to the price. Ouch! This is clearly a product for those who do not want to compromise comfort, build quality, utility or looks. [[VIDEOID:2b8bb26ef242fcb874bd3c461ac0e558]] For the price, this is a decent circular polarizing filter for amateurs who want to get into using a polarizing filter. It includes a UV filter that I consider just an extra.

I personally don't recommend the use of UV filters unless you are shooting film, as they generally don't improve image quality on modern digital cameras and, if anything, can only degrade it. I know that a lot of people consider them a layer of protection for their expensive lenses, but I am of the opinion that having a cheap UV filter on your expensive lens is actually more likely to damage it. Case in point, the threads on this filter are very sharply cut. You can feel and hear them grinding when you screw it into place, and when it is tightened down snug, the sharp threads want to lock it into place. If the lens was knocked hard on the corner with the filter in this position, the UV filter might actually become stuck in place and damage the threads of the lens, requiring expert repairs to remove the filter and repair the lens. In my experience, just keeping the lens hood in place offers far more protection than a UV filter possibly could.

With that out of the way, let's get to the meat of this review, which is the CPL filter. For the price, this will perform perfectly well. It will darken the sky when used properly in the right conditions, and can help reduce glare and reflections. It seems to have no discernible color cast which would be a problem. In fact the only real issue I have with this filter is related to the mechanical function.

First of all, the threads are very sharply cut, as mentioned previously with the UV filter. This isn't the end of the world, but it is coupled by the fact that the rotating ring on the CPL filter is also very, very stiff and resists turning quite a lot. In order to turn it, as is necessary for adjusting it to the present conditions, you will need to tighten the filter down onto your lens more than I would like, and with such sharp threads, this increases the risk of the threads locking firmly onto your lens. It is possible for them to lock so firmly that it could be quite difficult to remove it from your lens. While $30 is a pretty good bargain for what is otherwise a pretty decent filter, it's not such a bargain if it runs the risk of costing you a lot of money in repairs to your expensive gear. If you are using a cheap lens, then this cheap filter should be just fine. If you have shelled out lots of money for an expensive lens, I would not recommend cheaping out on the filters.

In the end I settled on 4 stars because the glass is pretty decent quality, and if you are aware of the limitations you can safely use it so long as you avoid tightening it down too much. It's just a little less convenient. But it otherwise works well.

Arlo is not perfect, but it is wicked close.

What's Great: You can put it anywhere within range of the link/router. The alerts are reliable, if a little slow on the uptake. The picture is good. Set up was simple and worked the first time. What's Okay: A person who walks fast can get through a room almost faster than Arlo can start recording. Now, it's still much faster than an old Belkin Netcam HD, which sends pictures of where the motion WAS. Before the picture. And the D-Link 930L, which is a fine monitor cam, but has never been able to send a snap or a clip, no matter how many times it has been set up to do that. However, both of those cameras have audio and stream reasonably good images via their apps (the Belkin video resolution is way better than the Dlink). That makes them okay monitors next to smart security sensors - if the sensor alerts, you can look to see what tripped it and listen to see what's going on. Arlo will - most of the time - catch whatever set it off and let you know within seconds. And it's free, not an extra $$$ feature.

What Could Be Better: The link thing is enormous. It could be a little less expensive. And it would be WONDERFUL if it integrated with Z-Wave or Smart Things. The plan here is to station the Arlo cams near other devices that send push notifications - Nest Alarms, Smanos smart sensors, etc.

UPDATE (2/21/19): So far, my clock is working well. I did buy a second clock, and succeeded in pairing it with my 1st Gen Echo Show. If you make a pairing mistake, you can press the clock's pairing button 5 times to unpair the clock and start over. Oddly, when the Show was correctly paired, the light turned solid orange. The Echo Show is hard to pair because it isn't completely integrated with the Alexa app when it comes to setting up a wall clock. However, for me, having two clocks, with visual timer displays paired to different Echo devices, was worth all the Setup hassles.

This ECHO WALL CLOCK does two things that I really want. First, it keeps accurate time by using an Internet connection (through an Echo device) instead of a radio signal (which can malfunction in bad weather or at Daylight Savings Time changes). Second, it gives a bright visual display of the time remaining on all the timers currently set with my first-generation Echo. (Yes, it simultaneously displays the time left on multiple timers.)

If my clock continues to work without requiring frequent Bluetooth re-pairing (as other reviewers have reported), I will order a second clock to pair with my Echo Show. The visual time-left display is very useful when I’m timing exercises or post-exercise ice treatments.

The instructions warn you NOT to try to move the clock hands. (Other reviewers warn that touching the hands will break the clock, or cause it to tell slightly inaccurate time forever if you succeed in replacing the hands.) It’s too bad that the clock does NOT have a plastic cover over the face--dusting it is going to be a problem. I put mine on a wall, to protect it as much as possible from dust, and from accidentally being knocked over.

SETUP PROBLEMS: Out of the box, the clock paired effortlessly with my Echo Show (using the option of asking the Show to set up the clock). However, I ran into a lot of difficulty when I tried to pair it with a second device (a first-generation Echo). The instructions do NOT make it clear that the clock PAIRS WITH ONLY ONE ECHO DEVICE.

Probably because I failed to start the second Setup attempt by using the Alexa app to un-pair the clock from the Show, the second attempt failed. It ended with a green light that has no defined meaning in the paper or online setup instructions. Worse, the clock no longer worked with the Show. Still worse, the clock did NOT appear as a device in the Alexa app; and the app did NOT display the clock as a Connected or Bluetooth device under the Show settings.

Eventually I found the clock under the settings for the Echo (subject of my second, failed Setup attempt). I was able to unpair it, delete it, and start Setup again. At long last, the clock paired with the Echo, and began working again (with the first-generation Echo).

However, I failed in all attempts to use the Show to set up the clock again. Those attempts always concluded with a red error light or with that mysterious green light. At some point, I had to remove the batteries and replace them so that the pairing button on the clock would work. Naturally I now dread having to pair the clock again with any Echo device, should the Bluetooth connection malfunction.

SUMMARY: The concept of the Wall Clock is great. I love my clock now, and really do intend to buy a second one, if the clock that I now have continues to work normally. However, I hope that later generations of the Echo Wall Clock will have a covered clock face, and that later versions of the Setup software will have much better integration with the Alexa app.

The HP MediaSmart server (EX487) is a pretty complex device but, once you get through the installation and learning process, you're rewarded with many benefits -- one of those "didn't think I needed it, but now can't live without it" type of products.

The unit itself is quite compact. I was surprised when I unpacked it - was expecting something a lot larger. Not that I'm complaining -- it fits in very well in the LR with the other electronics. Very attractive design if you're partial to electronics, and certainly unobtrusive/benign if you're the type that likes to keep the "hardware look" muted.

Installation is not what I'd call simple, but it's something anyone who is comfortable setting up a home network can tackle. The server needs to be hardwired into your router, so you'll have to locate it close to where you keep your router. It comes with a cable for hookup but you may want to have a longer one handy if you don't want the server immediately adjacent to the router. After hooking it to the router and powering up, you need to install software on each PC on your network.

The PC installs went fairly smoothly -- just follow the prompts. I'm using Dell PCs (various models) plus a Toshiba laptop. All are running XP Professional (SP2 or SP3). The router is a Linksys. The only glitch I ran into was with (I think) Avast, which is what I use on some of the PCs for virus/spam protection. One PC hung up during the install. After powering down and starting up again with Avast turned off, everything ran smoothly.

The user interface is very nicely done. I was concerned about the interface being too complex, but had no difficulties navigating through tabs and icons to set up folders for backup and sharing. The summary page gives you all the operational stats, again in a "don't need to be an engineer" format. Lots of info, but presented in a way that is useful. I do have some IT background, but certainly don't consider myself to be an expert when it comes to technology. While the setup and operation of the MediaSmart is not something a casual user would want to tackle by him/herself, you also don't need to be an IT professional. Just take it step-by-step and be willing to put in some time reading manuals and coming to grips with some key concepts regarding networks. It took me a bit over four hours to get everything up and running on a five PC network. I expect to put in many more hours tweaking and playing with features (but that's also due to the fact that I find the tweaking/experimenting fun - you don't have to put in too much time if you just want to have a functioning system).

My initial and main use for the server is for backup. I have external USB drives for some of the PCs. They make for decent backup devices, but I wanted something central and automatic -- if you have to remember to run a backup, chances are it will not be done as regularly as it should. The MediaSmart excels at that -- just tell it what folders to monitor, and forget about it. You can backup just files/folders, or do a full image.

This model comes with 1.5TB of storage that, at the moment, will take care of my storage needs very well. But, hard drive space always seems to get chewed up at a prodigious rate, and I'm happy that the server is expandable. I've not installed an additional drive yet, but looked through the procedure to do so and it seems very easy - just plug and play. You can also backup the server itself either online (not explored that, but I expect there's a cost involved) or by an attached drive (which is the route I plan to take).

Power usage is a concern of mine, and I'm pleased to see that HP has power management tools built in. According to the specs, the server uses only 1 watt when in sleep mode. I haven't seen, however, what the power consumption is when powered up. Hooking it up to a Kill-a-watt meter is on the to-do list to see what run-time use is, plus verify the 1 watt sleep mode.

The media collection feature is wonderful -- basically, it will collect specific file types, such as MP3, photos, etc. -- automatically from connected PCs and store them on the server. So far it has worked very well, and has already proven to be great way to avoid the "which PC has that playlist?" search. Everything is in a central location, and is maintained there automatically.

There are several other features of the server that I'm only starting to dabble with, such as photo sharing and streaming. Don't have enough hands-on experience with those to report on yet, but haven't run into any roadblocks either. I'll update the review as needed.

Bottom line - if you're an avid user with basic IT knowledge who is looking for more convenience and utility out of your home network, this is a great purchase. Provided you put some time into learning how to use it, you'll reap several key benefits (plus have a cool new toy!).

OK, it's pricey.  OK, it's a fixed lens.  I shot about 200 pictures around a golf course and duplicated every shot with my Nikon P7100.  The P7100 is an awesome camera and the 28-120 effective zoom range is handy, but for this outing I set the Nikon to the same focal length of the Fuji, about 35 mm.  I shot landscapes with sky dominate, with land dominate, water scenes, close ups of flowers, I shot using both standard and vibrant settings, I used the flash fill for portraits of my wife in full sun, half shadowed face, and full shadow.  Result:  I like the Fuji color and details in the shadowy areas better.  I like the controls better on the Fuji.  I like the old time move-yourself-to-get-the-right-composition mode of the Fuji fixed lens rather than the just zoom in or out of the Nikon.  You can set it to aperture preferred, shutter preferred, or programmed -- nothing different than on the Nikon, EXCEPT if you go aperture preferred (my preference in order to control depth of field) you move the aperture ring on the lens mount and you set the shutter speed dial to "A" (for Automatic); or if you prefer shutter preferred you set the aperture ring to "A" and rotate the shutter speed dial. On the Nikon, if you go manual or semi manual, the control rings are in places that don't make sense -- in the traditional old style sense.  OK, I'm an old guy and have been doing landscape photography since the early 70's, originally with a hand held light meter.  Now my main landscape camera is a Nikon D700 and 11 lenses and all the "modern stuff."  Still, the Fuji is a neat camera and I felt "closer" to photography by using it.

Having recently dug my music collection (odd how we go back into hobbies after years of stagnation), I took time to curate my setup (and by setup I mean my Note8 with a USB DAC) for optimal listening. Until recently, but "best" headphones were my Shure Aonic 4, which are excellent for the price range. The cable it comes with is okay, but preferably replaceable. It comes with an inline mic and makes a lot of feedback-noise when moved. I know cables are a mixed bag when it comes to audio equipment, so I shied away for years. But rather than place the emphasis on audio-quality improvement when looking at cables, I realized I'd rather get a cable if it looks and feels good. This one fit the ticket.

This is the only cable I have that's meant to be swapped with MMCX in-ear headphones. They pair well with the Aonic 4. First, I'll get the problems I have out of the way.

Since this cable is meant to connect with around-the-ear IEMs, there's a plastic wrap near each MMCX adapter. It makes wearing around the ears easier, but putting them on initially takes a few tries. They are easy to tangle, even if I use the "roadie wrap." Putting them on while on the go proved to be suboptimal; I have to be sitting or standing to put them on.

Sometimes I get some feedback noise, but rarely. Definitely not the same as the stock cable that comes with the Aonic 4.

The biggest problem I have is that the end connection disconnects nearly every time I use the cable. Having a modular cable is awesome, but the connection from the cable to the audio jack doesn't lock. I expected there to be a click, indicating it's on and snug, but no such thing. Since I use this cable while on the go, it's connected to my phone, which rests in my pocket. At least once the cable end will come loose. It's easy to press back in (just a little nudge will do), but it is rather annoying.

Now for the good.

The cable feels awesome. I get now why people prefer to upgrade certain cables. I care very little for how much the audio quality is "improved" (there's too much immeasurable subjectivity in that area), but having a cable that doesn't tangle easily and is very light makes enough of a difference to justify the upgrade. The cable is soft to the touch, though I don't doubt its ruggedness in the long term. The MMCX connectors snap satisfactorily into the Shure IEMs; at least those haven't come loose. The metal ends and Y-splitter are very nice and definitely attribute the cable with a premium look.

This cable has sold me on the reasons to upgrade headphone cables.

I came to this tracker cold. The Housemate has a Fitbit, but I never used it, and really haven't paid a lot of attention to what it did so I had no expectations of what the Pivotal Living tracker might do. However before I tell you what I discovered, let me explain some things about myself. I'm in my sixties, and have a sedentary job. I would like to be more active, I would like to compare my actual sleep habits against what I perceive them to be, I would like to keep an eye on hydration. I have some other goals, but these are the main ones that apply to my use of the tracker.

So how does the Pivotal Living tracker stand up to these goals? First off, because so much of my everyday movement is not easily measurable by the tracker, I'm not really getting an accurate step count. (Moving around the house holding things doesn't always register. Sitting and doing something like folding laundry sometimes does.) This is a bit of a problem because it makes it difficult to estimate how I'm doing on my step goal. So, accuracy in step count? Not so much. Going to stick to a pedometer or pedometer app. C, maybe C+ because I can set my own goals based on my health and how my day is going. (Right now I have a torn meniscus, and all my steps are limping or cane-assisted. Not fun, and not conducive to accurate step counts.)

Hydration? Great, unless you forget to enter an amount until after midnight. Whoops, sorry, can't add anything to your daily total. This is a huge oversight IMO. I sometimes finish my daily amount late in the evening when I'm not thinking about using the mobile app. However, the process of tracking it on your own is a good one. They simply need to fix the access problem. B+

Daily activity. Honestly I have NO clue how this is tracked. I'd have thought it was step-based, but I've never yet had daily activity show up on my dashboard, so there has to be some other way this band tracks activity. However, having an activity alarm that reminds me to stop what I'm doing, get up and walk around for a few minutes... that's immensely valuable to me. Without it, I'd simply forget and keep on writing or editing. I'm going to give it an A because I love the alarm which can be set for 20/40/or 60 minutes.

The rest? Sleep alarm... I've been wakened by this exactly once, when I was very nearly awake anyway. Every other morning it's done zip. I'll wake up an hour later and think, "Wha?" It's back to my clock radio. C, at best. However the sleep tracker seems surprisingly accurate based on what I remember of my nights. It fairly accurately charts how many times I've woken up, and how much good sleep I've gotten. I find this quite reassuring. A, even A+.

Calories burned: Since this is both step and activity based, it's pretty useless for me. Anyway, my goal isn't about calories, it's about activity, so I'm not going to grade this part of the app. Also, weight: Clearly this is another sub-app like hydration, which requires you to input your numbers. It keeps my weight in front of me which is a good thing, but it's not really something I feel I can adequately grade.

Problem: If you take it off it will turn itself off. I tried to put it on my desk when I was typing since it interfered with the position of my wrist. I could hear the activity alert when the band buzzed against the desk, but then it stopped because the tracker had shut down. I thought it was out of juice and couldn't figure out why I was getting less than 24 hours on the battery. When I finally figured it out, I had to start wearing it up high on my arm. Fortunately the band is big enough to allow it to sit several inches above my wrist.

Price: Very, very good. I recognize that the modest cost of the tracker is intended to get you to buy the yearly subscription, but I don't mind that. If the service works, I'm happy to pay $1 a month for it. That's still minor league stuff. However I get frequent errors saying that the goal information can't be updated from the site, and I get odd readings on my dashboard. However, by the end of the day it's usually sorted itself out, so I don't have a lot of quibbles so far.

Overall, and taking price into account I think I'd give this a B, at least for my needs. It reminds me of the things I need to remember to do, and it gives me a place where I can keep track of those goals. The cost to do this is, as I indicated, quite modest. If you're not ready to drop a lot of money on a more sophisticated tracker, give the Pivotal Living tracker a try.

Note: I'm using this on a Fire phone, which means I had to side-load the app. The instructions on how to install Google Play and everything else you need to side load Google Play apps are available on You Tube, and it's dead easy. Once you've done that, just go to the Play Store and download the Pivotal Living app, and have at it.

I have worked with quite a few car kits and some work better than others. Most of them are rechargeable Bluetooth receivers that allow you to turn your car’s stereo system into a hands-free system for talking on the phone while driving, though some plug into the 12V power outlet for power. All of the others I have used have connected to the car stereo by way of the AUX jack. But, not all systems have an AUX input which makes those solutions useless in those situations. I had an FM transmitter solution years ago that allowed me to connect a CD player to my basic AM/FM radio and it worked but I had forgotten about that type of solution until now. This kit works with Bluetooth and FM to connect phones to cars and it works very well. It also has some nice features I wish other kits had.

This is a basic kit that works by allowing the phone to pair with it via Bluetooth and then uses a small, low-power FM transmitter to connect to the car’s audio system on any FM channel desired (I suggest using an unused frequency). Music can be streamed from the phone to the transmitter and from there it goes to the radio frequency in the car. It’s simple in concept and it works. No more AUX jack.

For power the transmitter plugs into a USB port, and the kit includes a 2-port 12V plug. This allows for powering the transmitter and still having enough power for another device like the phone or a GPS navigator. One port on the adapter is a 1.0A and the other is a 2.1A so if you have a high-speed cable and your device can accept a high-speed charge it will work with the adapter. Because the adapter has two ports and it allows for completely disconnecting the transmitter it can be used for charging two devices at once.

Regardless of where in the vehicle the 12V adapter lives, the kit comes with a magnetic pad for attaching the receiver so that the receiver can be mounted almost anywhere. This is important - it means that it can be put in an optimal spot so that when speaking it has the best chance for picking up the voice clearly which is a very good thing. In my car, the 12V outlet lives under the center console so other kits sometimes do not get the best reception for my voice.

Sound quality is clear for both caller and receiver, particularly because the transmitter can be placed anywhere. When there is no competition for the channel the sound is as good as an AUX-connected sound source.

This hands-free kit for the car is better than most others I have used as it is easier to place the transmitter to get clear voice transmission and it does not require an AUX port on the care stereo system to work. I am pleased with it and am happy to recommend it.

Most tripods in this price range are poor quality, with unstable or flexy legs, heads that don't lock securely, and lots of plastic parts that don't last very long. This tripod is mostly metal for stability and durability. My postal scale says it weighs only 58 ounces, which agrees with the advertised weight.

When folded (with the head attached), the tripod is 21 inches long, which fits in many carry-on suitcases. With the legs fully extended, but the center column in the lowest position, the tripod is 50 inches tall, so average sized men will have to stoop a little to use this tripod. I try to avoid extending the center column on any tripod for stability reasons, but especially on lighter weight tripods like this one. Because of the height, this is going to be mostly a travel tripod for most people, since constantly hunching over to take photos gets old real fast. Tripod that are a foot taller are widely available, though they will of course be heavier and harder to pack in a suitcase.

Note that the 62-inch advertised height is with the center column in the tallest position, which no serious photographer would ever do. Quality tripods are usually advertised with the column in the lowest position, so advertising the highest position is misleading.

An unexpected extra is that a nice nylon carrying case is included.

My biggest complaint is that only one quick-release mounting plate is included, so using this tripod with more than one camera is difficult. The plate appears to be a proprietary design and I don't see anyway to get extras or replacements.

I’ve used the Sudio N2 Pro Earbuds for about a month, and I like them. I typically wear them for about 2-3 hours a day while working at my desk, and I have two major pros and three major cons I’ve noticed during the last month.

PROS:
🎵 The earbuds are super comfortable! I have multiple inner ear piercings in both ears (rook, daith, tragus) and a LOT of earbuds hurt after about thirty minutes. I can wear the Sudio N2s for several hours at a time. Small, medium, and large silicone tips are included so you can get a good fit depending on your ears. Sometimes I walk around my house and do chores with these in, they haven’t fallen out once.

🎵 For earbuds, the ANC is good! I can actually notice a difference with the ANC on and off; with some earbuds that claim to have noise cancelling, there’s really no difference. The ANC on the Sudio N2s blocks out when the television is playing in the next room, and even muffles the sound of the heater right under my desk.

CONS:
🎵 Battery life is not great. With ANC on, I get 4 hours, maaaaybe 4.5 if I’m lucky. I put the case on my charging pad every other day, it seems. The case supports wireless charging, which is a positive, or via USB-C. I’ve noticed the earbuds don’t always turn off when put in the case and the lid is closed, which undoubtedly contributes to the faster battery drain.

🎵 The earbuds support Multipoint connection, or connecting to multiple devices, but I can only get them to connect to my Mac. No matter what I try, they will not connect to my phone (Samsung Note 20 Ultra). I tried every suggestion in the online manual, but I can’t even get the earbuds to factory reset.

🎵 The touch controls are VERY sensitive. I have to make sure I don’t have any video tabs open when I put them in, or the video starts blasting in my ear. The only audible cue I noticed was to turn ANC on, and that is “Noise Cancelling.” A beep indicates turning it off, and beeps are used for all other cues. I don’t know what does what, I just wish I could turn them off.

Although the cons slightly outweigh the pros, I still use the Sudio N2s every day. The comfort is a huge factor for me. I’ve tried probably 8 pairs of earbuds in the last year, and this is the only pair I can wear for more than an hour at a time.

Not a huge deal, but I'd like more output options. More on this below:

Here are a few details that a pretty important about these two alternatives to the Nikon SB series:

a) The 568 light is much higher quality - and I really mean the LIGHT quality. It is even, consistent, and clear. On the other hand, the SN600N is very scattered - what I mean by this is there are lines of brightness and darkness from the flash burst. This must be an internal flash "lens" issue - whatever the light is bouncing around and through within the flash is creating texture and light inconsistencies. This is not the case with the 568.

b) Yes, the SN600N is a more powerful flash, but in my opinion, it needs to have more levels of output on the lower end (1/256) because it's TOO bright for some situations. I use grids and modifiers during wedding receptions, and I like balancing the natural light with the flash output. 1/128 with the SN600N is equal to about 1/64 on the 568. I use the 568 at 1/128 quite a bit for details - so this was kinda a bummer to me.

c) The AF beam on the SN600N is better and more centered than the 568 - but they both need to improve designs. The ONLY reason I'm holding onto my Nikon SB900 at this point is the AF beam - which makes accurate AF possible in pitch black - no joke. The AF beam on the Yongnuo is a joke - they need to fix it on the 622 triggers too - it's basically worthless and too bright/annoying to the subject.

d) In my experience using the 568EX, the batteries get warm and stay warm, whether you're using the flash or not. If the flash is on, the batteries will get warm. It also EATS through batteries. I used to be able to photograph 2 weddings without recharging my Nikon SB setup (using SB600 previously) - now I have to recharge between weddings. I've upgraded to 2800mah EBL AA rechargeable (previously using Amazon 2000mah) and it has helped quite a bit.

So this is my current setup: SB900 on camera, 2x 568EX off camera group A+B for reception lighting, and then SN600N as group C for periodic fill. Rather than commit to a single brand, I'm using them all as tools for different situations, because they all work differently. I also am really enjoying the SN600N as on-camera if I don't need the AF beam - the quality of light is bright, crisp and rich - and the SN600N "brain" (basically how it works using iTTL mode) just works really well with Nikon - it's a very consistent flash, sometimes even better than my SB900. I like that it can zoom all the way to 200mm, too. If the SN600N had a better AF beam and better quality of light, I would ditch my SB900 and use it all the time. But I switch between the SB900 and the SN600N for different effects. I actually like the previously mentioned internal lens flash inconsistencies at times - it creates a grittiness that I like.

These glasses are the perfect gift for the minecrafters in your family. We've only been playing mine craft since the summer and already it's become a favorite. When my hubby and son figured out they could play a 3-D version, we pulled out the paper 3-D glasses that came in a box of cereal. Quickly it became evident that if we were going to use the 3-D function, we'd have to get better glasses.

First off, I didn't realize there were so many different kids of 3-D glasses, some are red and blue, like these, and some are red and green, which means there are two images, a red image for one eye and a blue image for the other eye. When Jaws 3-D came out there was an urban legend that if you didn't have the 3-D glasses, the movie would be invisible. Crazy and completely untrue.

But the newer kind of 3-D, like what you see if you watch a newer 3-D movie (like the upcoming Star Wars) uses a new system, called polarization (two projections of the movie are shown and your eyes are fed both images simultaneously, creating a 3-D effect), for a polarized movie you get those black glasses they give you when you buy a movie ticket.

Those black glasses will not work on an old style red/blue or red/green 3-D game or movie (we checked, just to make sure!).

My only complaint with these glass are the fit, they slide around a bit and on my son, they slide down a lot. But other than that, they are great.

I really like the "ZeroTouch" voice-command app that comes with this ZEROTOUCH DASHBOARD CELL PHONE HOLDER (With Voice-Command App for Android Phones). It was easy to set up on my Galaxy S7 Edge, and it seems to work very well "on the road".

I haven't tested it a whole lot (because of physical installation issues, more on that later), but it seems to have an excellent, up-to-date GPS Navigator, and a terrific Text Message Handler. To send or reply to a text, you wave a hand to wake the app, tell it to "Send a message to (name a contact)", dictate the message, listen to the readback, and answer "yes" to the query "Should I send it". If you have the Samsung "S Voice", it's quite similar, except that "ZeroTouch" notifies you of incoming text messages, and lets you reply to them strictly with voice commands.

The "ZeroTouch" app only works when your cellphone is docked with the cellphone car mount base. Docking and mounting are where I ran into problems. First, there aren't many places in a Honda Civic that are suitable for a suction-cup-base cellphone holder--at least not if you worry about the suction cup losing its grip and dumping your expensive smartphone on the car floor.

Second, the cellphone docks with the car mount base via a thin, adhesive-backed magnetic plate that you're supposed to attach directly to your cellphone or cellphone case. (Tip: If you're having trouble pairing during setup, place the thin metal plate that attaches to your phone directly atop the round part of the base until the magnet grips.) Attaching the plate was an issue, because I didn't want to apply it directly to my new phone (and maybe mar the finish). Applying the plate to my cellphone case worked for a short time, but the adhesive wasn't strong enough to hold the cellphone case through repeated dockings and undockings. Now the adhesive is worn out and won't adhere to anything.

However, there is a workaround. If only the magnetic plate is docked on the base, the "Zero Touch" app will work whenever your cellphone is NEAR the base--within Bluetooth range, I guess. So my hands-free calling/messaging arrangement uses the Honda Civic's two cupholders. The base with the docking strip goes in one cupholder, and the cellphone with the "Zero Touch" app goes in the other.

With this setup, I can use all of the "Zero Touch" features. Of course, if I want to use the handy "parking location finder" feature, I need to undock the magnetic strip from the base when I leave the car, just as I would if the strip were still attached to my cellphone.

The magnetic plate did NOT interfere with my S7 Edge's wireless charging feature, when I had the plate attached to the lower quarter of the cellphone case. (The "ZeroTouch" app setup has a diagram showing you where to attach the plate, if you use wireless charging.)

Because I love the easy-to-use "ZeroTouch" app, but am dissatisfied with the holder mounting arrangement (suction cup and adhesive may not adequately secure the cellphone), I rate this product at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I bought an Atoto F7 standard last summer, and while I loved the features for the price, there were some shortcomings that made me want to try their higher end S8 editions instead. I got a chance to swap it out for an S8 Ultra, and I'm very impressed so far.
Let me tell you, I had my reservations about a phone/tablet OS running as a car stereo, but Atoto has done an incredible job making this as smooth and user friendly and FEATURE PACKED as you could ever imagine. Android Auto works of course, if you want to use your phone connected to the display. Even better, WIRELESS Android Auto works as well! They don't advertise this since it is in beta as of the time I'm writing this, but after asking Atoto customer support about it I was given access to the new test firmware and it works surprisingly well with my Galaxy S10 phone. All I have to do is press the Carlink button on the screen, my phone can stay in my pocket, and within 10-15 seconds the Android Auto connection is displayed on the car screen as if I had plugged it in. It also has an excellent Bluetooth audio input for the microphone, which is something I struggled with on the F7 I purchased previously. My car has a convertible roof that creates extra wind noise on the highway even closed, and callers can hear me just fine! But of course, the biggest pro is the ability to run Android apps directly on the head unit without needing to connect my phone.
I preloaded offline maps for most of NY/NJ in Google Maps, so wherever I end up I can navigate home (even if I don't have reception up in the mountains), all without needing my phone connected. I can also stream youtube and other apps (for the passengers, obviously!) as well as install all kinds of cool automation tools and car diagnostics thanks to a bluetooth OBDii plug I already owned.

It's not without a few caveats, however. Some things to be aware of:
1) The unit has a 5 minute delay when shutting off. This is apparently to avoid data corruption in case of a power cycle (key removed and restarted, such as for example if restarting the car). If you plug anything into the USB ports, you'll see them still on and drawing power for a solid 5 minutes after you've left the car. My wireless charger, for example, continues to be lit up and charging if I use the head unit's QuickCharge port built in. Any other peripherals such as remotes or volume knobs, etc, will remain illuminated for those few minutes. While most apps (built in music player, youtube, etc) are able to receive the signal to stop playing when the power is shut off right away, third party apps (such as some podcast or other streaming music players) actually CONTINUE TO PLAY during this 5 minute delay unless you paused/stopped them before removing the key. It's only a few minutes, and the truth is I usually play podcasts from my phone streaming, which DOES shut off right away since the Bluetooth connection is severed immediately when the key is removed. However I was surprised to find out it didn't stop everything immediately and they don't tell you this in the instructions at all.
2) If you are using Wireless Android Auto / Carplay, it creates a wifi ad-hoc connection that your phone connects to. With Android Auto, this can take a pretty big hit off your battery, but it is worth it to not pull your phone out on a small drive. However, due to the 5 minute delay I mentioned earlier, you might find that your phone is still connected to the car for a few minutes after you've left if you are in proximity of it. My car is parked just outside my office window, so I was surprised my phone wasn't connecting to my office wifi at first, then a few minutes later the car finally shut off the wifi and my phone was able to connect to the local network as expected. That delay, once again, was a little bit unexpected since at first I did not understand what was wrong.
3) Bluetooth and Android Auto volume are not consistent. For some reason, when connected with Android Auto, the volume is louder. So if you switch between them you'll have to adjust. Again, none of these are deal breakers, but things I found odd.
4) Bluetooth streaming has limited control over track. This is the one that surprised me the most since the less expensive F7 is superior in this regard. For those who know about Bluetooth profiles, there's the streaming stereo profile which gives you some ID tag metadata, and then there's AVRCP, which is the part used for remote controlling the playback. It seems that if you're playing audio from a phone, you are only getting the first profile, and not the AVRCP one. I've included a picture to illustrate the difference. With track control like you get on a dedicated bluetooth headunits, it shows the duration of the file being played, and you can even scrub through it by holding the forward and reverse buttons (like you would on an old school CD player). I listen to a lot of audiobooks so I like seeing how far into the file I am. But on the S8, it just shows the name of the file and artist/title, and then dancing lines to the audio levels. To be honest, the dancing lines are kind of distracting as well, but I can just hit home to go back to the main screen and not look at them. There's not much point in staying on that screen if I don't get track duration info anyway.

All in all, I think these setbacks are largely due to the way Android works and was designed as an OS. Atoto has had to customize a lot of things to make it work as a head unit, since things like receiving a Bluetooth stream (remember, phones and tablets running Android transmit to OTHER speaker systems, the system itself wasn't designed to be a receiver!) and going into a specialized "sleep" that shuts off all critical functions when you leave (all radios and apps running shut off) yet starts back up within 2 seconds when you turn it back on, etc (this is not regular sleep which still runs background operations- you don't want to come back to a dead battery! but powering off completely means you have to wait longer for bootup)... I think these limitations are reasonable. Atoto support has been amazing and incredibly responsive, whenever I had a question or concern, they got back to me within 24 hours which is more than I can say about radios I've owned from Pioneer and Sony in the past.
I think with time and software updates, they can eventually find clever ways around most of those caveats mentioned above, in which case I'd update this review to 5 stars. For now, I'd say this is a solid buy for what you get, I don't think a better iteration of this product with these features exists yet today. Frankly, I've tried a few different totally wireless earbuds and been less than impressed by all of them. Bluetooth headphones that have a wire connecting the two pieces can be had for much lower prices and have much better sound quality and much better battery life. These are the first security cameras we've ever used, and I was able to install them myself in about a half hour. While they do a good job recording video and saving it so I can view it on my phone, the app is lacking and there are a couple of things that I find frustrating. I'll break my review into pros and cons.

Pros:
1. Fast install
2. Rechargeable (but only one base station)
3. Can view what is going on in my house when I am not there, can talk to the dog if I see him getting into the trash
4. Backs up my videos so I can look at them later if I am not home but cannot check the notification
5. I like the option to have a light come on at night, sound a siren, or call emergency services.
6. Decent video, I don't think it's 4k HD though, and wonderful audio.

Cons
1. The battery life. It lasts about 5 days, but one of mine is mounted outside so I have to stand on a chair or ladder to disconnect it and reconnect it.
2. Only one charing base is included for two cameras. They usually die around the same time and I can only charge one, the extra chargers are pricey and it seems to be a proprietary wire.
3. It came with one magnetic mount, which I love, and another mount that is a screw and ball. This mount doesn't feel as secure and I don't get why it just didn't have two of the same ones. It looks weird having the same camera with different mounts.
3. They are 4k, IF you pay. If you don't then they record in a lower quality. I don't mind, but it's misleading how it's phrased.
4. The app is clunky. I found it hard to block out areas where I didn't need notifications (like, every car that drives by on the road). I also was overwhelmed with notifications every time someone walks through my living room. I figured out how to set the cameras to a schedule/geo-fence, but WATCH OUT! The geo-fence doesn't work if you disconnect your phone from Wifi when you leave.
5. Notifications: When I'm not home I get an alert every time my cats walk through the room, so I had to shut off notifications all together. A little frustrating, but understandable.
6. Timers. If you want the camera to run from 10pm to 5am, you have to set it for the current day 10pm-11:59 pm, then the next day from 12:01am to 5:00am. It's kind of difficult and it kept not saving it when I set it up that way so I gave up and just set it from 12:01am-5:00am.

This is a review of the new Beo Soundstage soundbar.

The instrumentals are amazing. Listening to the London Symphony, or Boston Pops, I can differentiate different string instruments.
Vocals are excellent.
I listened to podcasts and didn't find much difference in the speaking voices.
However, this replaced my Sonos Playbar which has fine audio.

This is an outstanding speaker with a poor app and virtually nonexistent instructions.
This would not be a problem if professional installation is used.
Because I have not used HDMI ARC previously, and I expect that most buyers will either use professional installation, or have experience with B&O or similar high end products, I did not deduct a star. My rating is based on the audio quality.

My current audio equipment includes a SONOS Playbar, a SONOS Beam, a SONOS one, and the Sony HT-X9000F.

I found this Beo Soundstage soundbar the most frustrating to set up.

Setup.

I did not get anywhere trying to get the unit set up using the app.
I have all Apple equipment, plus the Google mini, and the Google Home App.
I have a paid subscription to Google Play and You Tube Music.
Apparently, Beo and LG have a relationship, and the instructions for setting up the TV gave the setup instructions for the LG OLED TV. I have a Samsung TV.
The Beo app stated I could use the Google Home to set up the speaker. I have a Samsung TV. I followed the instructions in the app. That didn't help at all either. Not for WiFI, not for bluetooth.

I finally got bluetooth connected with no help from the app. My IPhone eventually connected to the Beo, via blue tooth. I never connected via WiFi. After connecting via blue tooth, and while listening to music via bluetooth, I again tried using the app to get WIFI. I received the message, error cannot connect to bluetooth. Sure, I was already using bluetooth.

I then moved the Beo to the room with the ethernet cable. I had never used an HDMI ARC connection. I made the connections.

I then turned my Samsung TV on, and the soundbar worked perfectly. My Direct TV remote worked perfectly without any pairing.
I then changed the source to my Apple TV. Everything worked perfectly. I used the Direct TV remote for that also. So, yes, your TV remote will control the sound.
I use bluetooth to play music from my IPhone.

Beo says the speaker can be wall mounted, or used on a tabletop.
My wife doesn't want it wall mounted.
My TV is wall mounted, and I wanted to place the Beo, vertical side up, on our entertainment center, directly under the TV. However, if used in the vertical or tall position without wall mounting, it will fall over. It is not balanced. I was very disappointed.
If used in the horizontal, or flat position, resting on a shelf, one of two soft pullout tabs must be removed. The power cord and HDMI cables can then go through the bottom of the speaker, to the back.

Beo needs to provide or sell, a small stand for table mounting. They do sell a large entertainment type piece of furniture, apparently adapted and with screws to hold the speaker in the vertical position. I'm not interested in another piece of furniture. A separate company sells three different accessories for the mounting. The one for tabletop mounting consists of a few pieces of soft feet. It sells for 100 pounds plus 20 pounds shipping from England. Probably weighs 5 ounces at most. I'll pass. Beo could have included that with the Soundstage. Probably costs under $ 1 to produce.

The speaker looks much more impressive in the vertical position, than it does laying flat on a table. For those that prefer a non intrusive look, the horizontal position would be fine. I tested it in both positions. In the vertical position, speakers aimed directly at my seating position sounded much better than in the horizontal position. However, when in another part of the room, as you may be when entertaining, the sound was better in the horizontal position. In the horizontal position, the speakers face my 12 foot ceilings

I did contact B&0 and asked if horizontal placement degraded performance. A simple question.
They e-mailed back. Contact a dealer and have an installation technician help me. More $$$$.

The speaker is just under 44 inches long, and weighs about 20 pounds.
There is no remote.
The wall mount is part of the speaker, and it just drops onto two small round holders put in the wall with screws. Screws are not provided.

The small box provided was missing the fabric puller, which would allow the speaker direction to be changed for tabletop placement.

Update.

I finally connected through the B&O app.
There are a number of optiuons.
One of features allows me to tell the speaker whether it is in a horizontal or vertical position.
On my failure to get a Wi Fi connection, I didn’t notice that the speaker has icons that can be pressed for pairing.
The icon, and others such as sound and the on/off icon are deliberately made hard to see in order to present a more streamlined appearance. In my initial setup, I set it up in the vertical position, propped up to keep it from falling over. I just didn’t see the icons.

There are 2 ways to hook up the TV to the speaker.
1. Plug the HDMI cable from the satellite or other type of receiver directly to the TV. Works great. An initial 20 second delay in sound when the TV is turned on.
2. Plug the HDMI cable from the receiver directly into the soundbar. This reduces your cable use by one. In both cases, the ARC connection remains the same. The sound was instant.

With option 2, on my Samsung TV, the "Anytime NET, " appears to cause compatibility problems.
The soundbar went on immediately, but after about 30 seconds, the video disappeared, and the message appeared, "check your connection." My Apple TV was not affected, neither was the OTA connection. The soundbar was working fine for both of those.

Troubleshooting.
On my Samsung TV, I went into menu. Nothing notable there.
I went into tools.
It showed the Anytime Net setting.
I clicked refresh, for the Samsung Genie, the Apple TV, and the B&O.
Each time I clicked refresh on the B&O, the video shut off, along with the sound.
I tried everything a number of times.
I went into every setting.,
I disconnected the Anytime Net. Nothing helped.
I have read that some older satellite receivers can cause problems with HDMI ARC.

I finally decided to go with my original connection, the receiver to the TV, and then the ARC connection for the robust sound. That did give me one extra cable, but is problem free.

Dec19th update.
Things coming together. I finally connected my google nest mini to my Soundbar. Went through the google home icon.
I selected my premium YouTube Music as my default service.
Now every time I want to listen to music on the Soundbar. I just say, Hey Google, Play Dean Martin in the family room. Works great.
I also noticed that when I request music, the Soundbar automatically turns my TV off.

I’m very pleased with the features. Just wish B&O had a 30 minute You Tube video walking buyers through the features.
Would have avoided a lot of frustration. I really love the features and the sound quality.

I wanted a wired connection in a far room out of reach of my router. This works perfectly for that by allowing me to use any power outlet in my condo as a way to extend my wired network.

I tested my upload and download speeds with a network cable plugged from my laptop directly into my router and compared it to a wired connection with the Netgear Powerline Outlet. There was no discernible difference either positive or negative. I even ran video under both scenarios and I detected no difference in performance.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the router, my ping was 12 ms, download was 17.08 Mbps, upload was 5.17 Mbps.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the Powerline using my electrical house wiring, my ping was 12 ms, download was 16.63 Mbps, upload was 5.20 Mbps.

Although these speeds are not great, that is the performance I usually get with the router and service provider I have. Based on my results, this works as designed. Below is a list of what comes in the package and the PROS and CONS.

The package includes two Netgear Powerline 1200 Outlets each with an extra outlet and one Gigabit Ethernet port, two 6.5 foot Ethernet cables, and a quick start guide. For the initial installation of these units, both outlets have to be used because one Powerline must be plugged into an outlet near the router so that the Ethernet cable from the Powerline can plug into the router. The other Powerline can be plugged into an outlet anywhere else in the home. The other Ethernet cable is then plugged into this unit on one end and an Ethernet-enabled device such as a laptop, SmartTV, etc. on the other. If additional Powerlines are purchased then both units can be used for two additional wired connections.

PROS
- The LEDs on the Powerline enable the user to diagnose if there's power, Ethernet connectivity, or the ability to "Pick A Plug" (a.k.a. electrical outlet) with the strongest performance.

- There's an extra outlet on each Powerline. This unit covers the second outlet if it's plugged into the top outlet of a two-outlet receptacle. However, I do not see that as a problem for two reasons. First, there's an extra outlet on the unit. Therefore, I am still getting the ability to plug in two items like I would have had I not been using the Powerline. (In this case the Powerline is one item and a light is another.) If I want to turn my outlet into a three outlet receptacle, then all I have to do is plug it into the lower outlet. This would allow me, for instance, to plug in a lamp in the top receptacle, the Powerline in the bottom receptacle, and another item into the extra outlet on the Powerline.

- According to the manual, the network can be secured by pressing the security button for two seconds and then pressing the security button on one of the other adapters in the existing network. If additional adapters are added throughout the house when security is already enabled, then ALL the adapters should be factory reset. To re-enable security, all that has to be done is press the security button for two seconds on one adapter and then select any ONE other adapter (it's not necessary to do all adapters) and press that security button for two seconds. Both security buttons have to be pressed within two minutes time.

- There's a 1 year warranty plus 90 days basic customer support.

CONS

- I see none at this time.

I will write Netgear to find out what is meant by security with these security buttons. Up to 16 adapters can be installed in a home. I know if I were to install another set of these, I would actually be able to use both Powerlines for extra wired connections, thereby increasing my wired connections to three from one. It's only for the first installation that the extra Powerline is lost because that is used to connect to the router.

In summary, I feel this Netgear works as designed with no discernible difference in speed over a wired connection whether I was plugged directly into the router or the Powerline. Installation was simple and turning any one of my electrical outlets into a wired connection was practically instantaneous.

UPDATE April 27, 2015 - I contacted Netgear for an explanation of why there's a security feature on these adapters and exactly what that means to me. Below is Oleg Fishel's (of customer support) response which I slightly paraphrased.

The security refers to encryption between each of the Powerline adapters on my network. A random key is generated and shared among the adapters when the security setup button is used. All traffic is then encrypted using the highly secure 128 bit AES encryption protocol that prevents any unauthorized person from accessing the communication on my network. The reason enabling this security is recommended is to prevent someone from coming into my home with another Powerline adapter and connecting directly into my network to get information or for free Internet access. Although this scenario might be rare, this may be a concern with apartment buildings and offices where electrical circuits might be shared and in the case of homes that have outdoor electrical sockets. In summary, it is best to enable security. It is especially important when the Powerline is on a shared electrical circuit where someone can come along and plug one of these adapters in and piggyback off the network.

In regard to another question I had regarding the use and installation of 16 adapters all at once, he said "The HomePlug standard (HPAV2) used by the PL1200 supports up to 16 adapters on the network working together simultaneously. So if you purchased 7 kits (14 units) in addition to the original kit, you could have a 16 node network."
