I have worked with numerous pairs of active noise canceling (ANC phones) and I’ve seen a wide variation in sound profiles, features, and the quality of the ANC function. Some are better than others. I was a bit skeptical of these because of the price; most of the ANC phones I have used that were worth anything have a higher price tag. These are better than the price suggests.

Right out of the box, these headphones do not draw much attention to themselves. They’re not flashy and do not have any noticeable markings on them unless you’re looking for them. They are over-the-ear headphones which tend to be more comfortable than on-ear phones, and these have a snug fit without clamping down tightly. They adjust easily to fit almost any size head too. The padding on the cans is soft enough to not pinch, though after extended wear they do start to get a little warm.

Pairing and connection with my computer was a painless affair and these were ready very quickly after they were powered on.

The ANC function is far and away better than any other headphones I have worked with in this price range. They’re almost as aggressive as that of the Bose QC-15’s that I own, without that weird faux pressure sensation when the ANC is turned on. Even with the volume down low, these cancel out enough background noise to make them a serious contender. I have no complaints with the ANC.

The sound quality is very good, though not quite to my tastes. The bass is very strong – much stronger than I like personally, but not out of line with what has been trending in the last decade. Where Skullcandy got it right, though, is in how well they’ve implemented the bass enhancement. Even though the bass is very strong (enough to give me a headache at higher volumes), it does not distort or turn into just low-frequency noise. More importantly, the bass enhancement does not stomp on the midrange which is the usual casualty. The midrange is warm and fairly balanced. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. The end result is a sound profile that sounds full and rich. So many headphones with enhanced bass I have used have killed the midrange which makes music sound hollow, or distort the bass so much as to make music sound like a low-fidelity render. These are refreshing in that regard.

Some headphones detect when you take them off and pause music or playback when you take them off. These do not.

These come in a carry pouch that offers little in the way of drop and crush protection but it does keep them clean and free of scuffs and scratches. Also included is an audio cable for wired use as well as a USB Type C cable for charging.

Overall, these are far and away better than the price would suggest. They are very comfortable to wear, they have a good sound profile (particularly if you like heavy bass) and the ANC function is better than average and competitive with much more expensive headphones. These are budget-friendly ANC headphones with higher-end performance.

This is my first ergonomic mouse. Wish I had tried one way before now. I dont know what my hold up was, maybe because they looked weird and uncomfortable, haha. Well I know what prompted me to try one: my wrist has been bothering me, and it seemed to be made worse with mouse use. I guess all my gaming years have added up.

I didnt know which to try. So many! I didnt know what would fit. There are some really small looking ones and some that look bulky, some that are nearly same in appearance as a standard mouse, and some that have a deeper cut out where hand rests. Very confusing. So I just spent some time reading through various reviews of a wide assortment of ergonomical mice.

While I think some of it is trial and error for getting the right fit, I think I happened upon a really good fit and feel with my first try. I really have nothing to compare it to, but so far I am really quite pleased.

--I dont have small hands, but they aren't exactly big either. Size can be in length and width. I have quite small fingers, but wide palms (3.75"). So typically a size "large" in gloves, but the ends of the fingers always dangle quite a bit. Hope that gives impression going forward with my review:

--My hand easily grasps the width of this mouse. Feels very comfortable. My pointer finger just reaches the scroll wheel. I dont need to reach for it; my finger pad sits directly on top of apex of the wheel.

--Press of left or right side is easy and comfortable. Plenty of length to accommodate even the smallest of fingers. Yet plenty of spare room for fingers longer than mine.

-- Not a loud click, but I can feel the click. I personally find that satisfying. Gentle yet makes me feel my action.

--Scrolling is smooth.
--No stuttering or jerkiness
--Instant connect when I first got this, and no problems since

--Impressed with how natural it feels. Didnt realize how much the wrist and forearm twist to use a standard mouse. With this, the mouse and arm are in a natural alignment

--Charging is quick and easy. Comes with cord for charging. I charge it directly through use of my laptop. It can be used as a corded mouse with ease. Can store dongle in the mouse if need be. Has on/off switch. When in the ON position, it will go to sleep when computer shuts down (or after x amount of time when not used), and wake up along with computer. Typical for rechargeable mouse. If this is anything like any other rechargeable mouse I have had, it should hold a charge for a very long time.

--Haven't used this for gaming yet as I have it for use on my laptop, but may try it out on my gaming PC. If I like it, I will just buy another. I think it will work out. This is just so comfortable and easy to use.

Take a little getting used to, yet at same time feels really natural. Good grip, good responsiveness, all around good experience in the short time I have had it. Your experience may vary in terms of fit, but I think the quality is evident. I will update if I have anything else worth sharing :)

EDIT/UPDATE: Seriously love this mouse, and this company is great. They are VERY RESPONSIVE and helpful when I inquired about an issue I had. WOW really good customer service. Rare these days, thank you. Truly, 5 STARS ALL AROUND.

This is my new favorite tripod head. With two controls for setting friction and locking the head in place it's amazingly versatile. The previous ball-head mount I had was either locked or fully loose which made camera control a little scary. With the Vanguard TBH-250 you can have free movement and maintain enough friction to keep your camera from flopping wildly about. You can also lock and unlock the horizontal movement of the head so you can take panoramic shots with ease.

The mount is threaded for 1/4" which is a sleeve that fits inside a 3/8" threaded fitting so the TBH-250 will fit on the majority of tripods on the market. The 3/8" thread fit my Dolica AX620B100 tripod perfectly and even fit, separate from the tripod and with a lot of finagling, in the bag that came with my Dolica tripod. A small tool was included to remove the 1/4" sleeve but a flat head screwdriver would also do the job.

The only thing I'm not crazy about is the camera mount. It's advertized as a 'quick shoe' mount but it's not that quick and if you're not careful it's not that secure. Slightly loosened you can reposition the mount forward and backward about an inch or thereabouts to get better balance. But loosen the camera mount just a slight bit more and the camera will easily pull free of the tripod head. There is a brass pin which keeps the mount from sliding out front to back and that's great but there's no locking or safety latch keeping your camera attached to the tripod.

While we're on the subject of the camera mount the screw holding the mounting plate to the camera requires a screwdriver, coin or in a pinch you can flip the tool for removing the 1/4" thread adapter and tighten the plate to the camera with that. I'm surprised that a tripod head of this quality doesn't include a butterfly nut to hand tighten the plate to the camera.

While I do wish it had a more secure mount and an easier way to attach the shoe to the camera I would still recommend this tripod head. It's very smooth, solidly built and feels like it will last for years.

I thought I used Google and its products a *lot.* I use Gmail and Google Drive and Chrome constantly, and I’ll always have an Android phone. So, I thought it would be easy to adapt to a Chromebook and Chrome OS.

But the adaptation process wasn’t as easy as I thought. It turns out I rely even more on other programs. I also thought Chrome OS would be like Android, which it isn’t. So, while this isn’t a review of Chrome OS, I’d say do a lot of research to see if Chrome OS is all you need. It’s a very odd mental switch to go from a full operating system to something so limited.

I’ve been using the Acer Chromebook R11 for about a month. Size wise, it’s comparable to my 11” Mac Book Air. The R11 is just a touch heavier, 2.76 pounds versus 2.38 pounds.

I like the feel of the keyboard, it’s soft and felt nice to type on. There’s no Caps lock key, which I thought was an odd omission; it’s replaced with a Search key that opens the Google launcher. I did miss my Mac’s illuminated keyboard, but the R11 is a much more inexpensive machine.

The touchscreen was my favorite part of the R11. I didn’t think I’d use it much at first, but now I find myself touching my Mac’s screen! And it’s good that I liked the touchscreen, because the trackpad was my least favorite part of the R11. It’s very cheap and plasticky feeling. It was much faster to just touch where I wanted my pointer to be.

The convertible nature of the R11 is cool, too. Another one of those features I used more than I expected I would, since I could read long articles in bed or watch a movie with the R11 tented on my stomach. There’s an option to lock screen orientation, if you flip the screen around.

If you’re considering a Chromebook, I’d do some research on Chrome OS and determine if it will meet your needs. If so, I think the Acer Chromebook R11 is a good value, especially with the touchscreen and convertible nature.

I bought the printer because it was affordable, and had lots of features. I wanted something with a duplex document feeder scanner, full duplex printing, color, and flatbed scanning. This seemed to have it all. As a scanner, it's pretty good if you manage to stay away from the HP software. As a printer, the quality is decent, but the ink situation is enough to make me never buy from HP again.

I'm sure HP read lots and lots of letters from angry customers complaining about their ink prices. Indeed, with other HP printers, it can be frustrating to be charged $35 when you run out of black ink. HP's solution to this can be seen with the 564 ink cartridge - the colors are $10 and the black is $12. Seems cheap!

Here's the awful truth: the black ink lasts about 30 - 50 pages. This is not an exaggeration. You need to replace the ink ALL THE TIME. The printer also has a bizarre habit of using ALL of the colors even when you're printing things that look black and white. So even if you're not printing very much in color at all, the printer will inexplicably run out of colors. Since the ink cartridges are so small, it seems like the printer CONSTANTLY has a low ink warning, and is CONSTANTLY stopping with out of ink errors. So even though you're only spending $10 - $12 on each cartridge, you're buying tons of them, and you need a huge stock for replenishment. This is HP's marketing department guiding the hand of their engineering department and delivering a crippled product. You will learn to hate this printer. It will constantly need your care and feeding, and you won't save any money on ink.

Here's a tip: in the print settings on your computer, you can tell it to use black ink only. That's a lifesafer.

Side note: the wi-fi on my unit has gone out twice. Out of warranty though, but the range on the Bluetooth is excellent, so not that big a problem for me. Don't know if it's endemic, or isolated.

This is a fine wireless router, well above average. It has a few shortcomings that I'll get to in a moment.

The good stuff: It's got lots of features -- wired ports, WiFi, VPN. It's pretty easy to configure, especially if you're familiar with networking.
The not-so-good stuff: The Web-based configuration utility is fine, but somewhat strangely laid out, especially for content filtering. The screens all work, but they are somewhat confusing. The content filtering works well, but it's not as flexible as I had hoped.

I bought this to keep the kids away from video games. The content filtering is sort of ok for that, but it's inflexible. You can permit access by time of day, and you can deny access to certain Web sites, but you can't deny access to certain sites at specific times of day. It's all or nothing. The content filtering works well, but if you have more than a few words you're trying to filter out, you'll find that Web pages load more slowly because the router has to scan them for your blocked words.

So in summary, for the price paid I'm happy. I wish it did a bit more for content filtering, but for the price this is a pretty good deal.

In comparison to my Toshiba Satellite 15" with similar specs, this ASUS is about equal - there are definitely some things I like better about the ASUS for everyday use and a couple of small quibbles that bother me. First off the computer itself is about the same weight as my Toshiba so carrying it around is exactly the same and it fits in my existing laptop sleeves and bags. It does have a DVD tray so you can play movies & music and burn discs as needed (as does my Toshiba), but a lot of laptops don't offer this anymore, so this is a definite plus.

I do really like that the ASUS comes a lot cleaner out of the box than my Toshiba - almost no bloatware pre-installed. The basic Windows 10 and you can don't have to spend 30 minutes messing around with a bunch of garbage you don't want and won't use anyway. Additionally, the ASUS boots up about 20 seconds faster from off than my Toshiba and again from the sign in screen, the ASUS is still faster. The screen is very pretty and clear with a variety of images and video - keep in mind that it's NOT a touchscreen. I've been averaging about 6 hours of use with the battery before it hits the 30% mark - that is net surfing, watching some random videos, and mostly word processing. Leaving it on in sleep mode with no use - it went almost 4 full days before needing a charge. The wifi connects immediately and I've had zero issues with it dropping out either inside or out on the back deck.

I really like the keyboard and the overall shape of the frame on this particular laptop. My Toshiba has the keyboard just open and exposed and what happens is that the heels of my hands tend to slip upwards as I type or bump the space bar. Or my thumbs slide into the mousepad area and now my cursor has bounced someplace new & I'm typing in the wrong spot. The ASUS keyboard is slightly lowered and has a border around it - for me anyway, this design is MUCH easier to type with. (See the photo.) The shape of the overall frame is better on the ASUS than the Toshiba as well. The rounded corners and edges on the ASUS don't poke into your wrists after an hour of writing or research.

My quibbles seem small on the surface, but after almost three weeks of use, they are aggravating me. First - the ASUS doesn't keep time as well as the Toshiba. It's off by 2 full minutes. (See the photos) I've checked both a couple of times and set them manually at the same moment and within 24 hours, the ASUS has lost 2 minutes - it never loses more than that though. Second - The charger is smaller than every other one I have for the other two laptops and the Chromebook in this house. The other three are standard size, but the one on the ASUS is a tiny bit smaller and thus you can't use another charger for this laptop in an emergency. Third - the speakers on the ASUS don't sound quite as full as the ones on my Toshiba. Of course... no built in speakers on a laptop are really meant for full music enjoyment.

My bottom line is that at this price point, this is a nice machine and will do almost anything you can want with regard to basic internet surfing, movie watching, office work and the like. This is not a gamer's computer and it's not meant to be. But as a regular, go to every day laptop, it's a pretty good one. I want to give it 4 1/2 stars.

My partner has a Surface Pro 3 and I've been very jealous of his ability to do design work (he is a jewelry designer) on his Surface. The sensitivity of the stylus is impressive, and I hoped that this tool might so something similar for my iPad. I'm a landscape designer, and hoped to be able to create vector images to import into my CAD program - plant figures, sketches, etc. Pretty simple stuff really.

Well, this was partly successful, but the stylus isn't as sensitive as I had hoped. It has a chunky tip that wobbles (I think they are calling that "pressure sensitivity") so it can be hard to know exactly where you are setting the tip down. The Surface tracks where the pen is before it touches, so you can easily see what you are doing when drawing delicate lines, and once the pen "tracks", you can rest your wrist or hand on the tablet without messing everything up, not so for the Ink, which needs you to only touch the iPad with the stylus.

There is also no discernible lag on the Surface Stylus. This Ink stylus by contrast has what feels like an excessive lag to me - I'll be a quarter inch away before it starts laying down the line I began drawing. And it does not track, so I just have to put the stylus point down and hope I am connecting my figure ends properly. I was also not very impressed by its pressure sensitivity as compared to the VERY sensitive Surface stylus.

So far I have only figured out how to export png files, so I have to run them through another program to get a vector file for import into my design program.That is fine for me because the data lost is not important for my uses.

The Ink/ Slide only works in Adobe programs like the free Line.

The slide is OK, but doesn't do anything really necessary in my view. I am glad to have it but it probably won't get a ton of use for the freehand type drawings I do as a landscaper.

Overall, this is a stylishly designed and beautiful looking stylus that certainly ups the usefulness of my iPad. But compared to the (admittedly much more expensive and high-end) Surface, it functions like a children's toy. Much clunkier. I don't think the lag time is acceptable given the price point as compared to other stylus products for the iPad.

I was always impressed with the room filling "surround" sound of my boyfriend's two Bose wave units. In my opinion, this system delivers that same quality audio I am used to hearing.

Besides the tabletop unit, a slim remote control, demo CD, power cord, and instructions are included in the box.

PROS

- Setup is exceptionally easy.

- The sleek design has no visible buttons.

- The slim intuitive remote is operable from up to twenty feet away. It worked for me even when the unit was not within sight. The battery is included and installed. Battery replacement requires a CR2032 or DL2032 3-volt lithium button cell battery

- It has a touch top which provides the ability to tap the top center part of the console to turn the unit on or off. Of course, those with animals might find the unit being toggled on and off by their furry companions.

- There is excellent surround sound which comes through crisp and clear. The radio required optimal placement in my house in order to receive the stations without minimal static. I actually have both AM and FM antennas on order.

- It has a sleek design and beautiful espresso black color.

- It has an integrated AM/FM tuner and the front display displays the text of music playing.

- It has a CD player that also plays MP3 music files recorded on a CD-R / CD-RW discs. I played an MP3 CD fine. In my case, only the names of the songs were displayed at the beginning of each song followed by only the track for the remainder of the play. I suspect this has something to do with the way this CD was recorded. There are also different play modes available when playing an audio CD such as normal play, shuffle repeat, repeat track, etc. (NOTE: The CD player is not for use with mini-CDs.)

- There are two alarms available.

- There are 6 presets for AM and 6 presets for FM available and are simple to program.

-There is an auxiliary input to enable playback from an audio device and a headphone jack for private listening. The audio through the headphones is as crisp, clear, and smooth as without headphones.

- A demo CD is included that wonderfully demonstrates the sound range.

- The digital clock and LED display is easily readable.

- Most system settings are permanently maintained even during a power outage or if the system is unplugged with the exception that the clock time is maintained for only 48 hours in backup memory during a power outage.

- It has a sleep timer from 10 to 90 minutes. It remembers the last sleep setting that was set and increments up from that.

- I called Bose twice asking pre-purchase questions about the Bluetooth options and also about an AM antenna recommendation (the Terk AM Advantage). Each time they answered quickly and were very helpful. The number for Bose is in the comments section of this review.

CONS

- An optional $99 Bluetooth adapter needs to be purchased to wirelessly stream music, movie sound, etc. from smartphone, tablet, laptop, or other Bluetooth device. I ordered the [[ASIN:B007ZG03DG Bose Wave Bluetooth Music Adapter]] and plugged it into the Bose Link port to test their optional adapter. Adding the additional Bluetooth adapter takes away from the sleek design and increases the footprint of the unit as a result of have to attach an extra component. Since this external adapter can only pair one Bluetooth device at a time, I had to turn the Bose on, then press AUX to cycle it to Bluetooth. Once there, I pressed the 5 button to make it discoverable. Since it remembers the last device I paired, I did not have to make it discoverable again. However, if I wanted to pair a new device, I had to press the 6 key until the unit beeped (about 10 seconds) and then it would clear the Bluetooth memory and become discoverable again. One negative I did see with the external adapter is that the volume is about half that with Bluetooth enabled. What I mean by this is that a volume of 30 on the radio sounds like 15 when paired with Bluetooth. I found that I had to double the volume when using the Bose Bluetooth adapter I purchased.

- No AM or FM antenna is included. This is not a terrible CON as for most people antennas should not be needed. I live in northwestern NJ and could not receive any AM stations until I moved the unit toward the window. I went to the Bose store and the fellow there said the power cord acts as the AM antenna (the manual did not say this). He suggested I call Bose directly. When I did call, they recommended the [[ASIN:B000069EUW Terk Indoor AM Antenna ADVANTAGE]]. I also ordered a [[ASIN:B00ZXI2MJG FM Antenna Male with 3.5 Jack Adapter]] for the FM radio. I will update this review with the results of both antennas once I receive and test them.

In summary, this tabletop Bose wave music system provides premium, crisp and clear, high-performance surround sound. However, Bluetooth capability should be both integrated into the unit and standard. The absence of integrated Bluetooth with this wave system is like buying a cook pot without an attached handle and having to purchase a "detachable" handle separately. Although most people will not require an antenna for radio reception, that might be a required purchase for some. I actually had to spend $152.10 for the additional Bluetooth and the two antennas. At a minimum, most people will have to shell out $640 (with tax) just to have a Bluetooth enabled system. If antennas are also needed, the full purchase price will be about $687. If this Bose unit had integrated Bluetooth, I would have rated this five stars. Despite the lack of Bluetooth, the incredible Bose sound comes through loud and clear.

UPDATE 9/24/2015 - I received the [[ASIN:B000069EUW Terk Indoor AM Antenna ADVANTAGE]] and tried it "wirelessly" (meaning in proximity of without the wired connection) with this Bose and it did not work to improve AM reception at all when I dialed into the stations on the antenna. I also tried it wirelessly on my [[ASIN:B013G6TMUS ION Block Rocker Bluetooth Portable Speaker System IPA76C]] and on another older system I had and it also did not work. Instead I wound up wiring this to the AM ports on the back of my older system (not a Bose) and only then did this AM antenna work. Unfortunately, I found this use for this Bose because I did not see a way to "wire" it to the music system. (For those who are interested, the link to my review of this antenna is in the comments section of this review.)

UPDATE 9/25/2015 - I received the [[ASIN:B00ZXI2MJG FM Antenna Male with 3.5 Jack Adapter]] for the FM radio today and plugged it into the FM antenna port on the Bose. No matter how I manipulated this FM antenna, it did nothing to increase reception of the FM stations. Unfortunately, this antenna purchase was useless for me as well and very disappointing.

In the lab where I work there are literally hundreds of computers running constantly so there is need for ANC headphones, especially if one wants to listen to music. The gear of choice in said lab is Bose but not everyone is willing to spend $300 for a set of good headphones. Philips offers these headphones which cost a fraction of most other ANC phones and work well enough to make them worthwhile.

Because Bose is considered the standard when it comes to ANC phones, I will use them as a reference point.

These headphones are a bit smaller than the Bose QC15's, and the way they lay on the ear can be mildly uncomfortable over time when one is used to larger headphones that completely cover the ear. Not everyone will have this problem, though. Some people find these phones to be perfectly acceptable and are content with the soft pads.

Sound quality is fine. I have a pair of Sennheisers that have better sound, but Sennheiser is known for their sound quality and are hard to beat. Then again, they tend to be expensive too. When considering the price differential, the quality of sound coming out of the Philips is very satisfying. Unlike Bose, the Philips phones do not overdrive the bass and they provide a more realistic sound.

These are noise canceling phones, and with a battery in them they do indeed actively cancel noise. It is not in the same league as Bose, but that is relative - the Bose cost nearly 10 times as much but the ANC is not 10 times better. Overall, Philips does an adequate job of canceling low-frequency noise, to the point that one can listen to music at lower volumes in a noisy environment like a plane. They don't completely knock out all the sound but they kill enough noise to make an appreciable difference.

I have only one complaint with these headphones - the cord is not detachable. It would be nice to use them strictly as ANC phones in the lab like the Bose, but unfortunately this is not an option.

For those on a more conservative budget or those that refuse to spend a premium for ANC headphones, Philips offers this set for a reasonable price that perform very well for their class. This is one of those weird cases when you actually get more than you pay for.

But let's just jump right into the odd design. Why is there an "external mic" option that is RIGHT NEXT to the internal mic? Usually an external mic is supposed to be mounted somewhere closer to the driver's mouth (up by the visor or mirror, or over the dash by the steering wheel, etc). The purpose is to get better sound, and either having the internal one as a backup if you don't want to mount one, or using it to pick up ambient background noise for NR filtering. Having an external nub right next to the internal one makes ZERO sense at all! Why even have one?! If anything, making it lower than the internal one seems like it would get WORSE sound, and if the position were so good, why not make THAT where the internal one is? Not to mention it looks weird as heck.
The features seem to be functional at least, but it has a pretty noticeable lag to the user interface. If you're expecting an OEM style menu experience, you might be disappointed. This feels like an old-school web browser loading pages when you open up a feature. Compared to modern units like, for example an Atoto F7, this feels like something a generation older at least.
I want to give this at least 3 stars for functional purposes, but the truth is I know that you get a much better unit for not a lot of money more. I can't really recommend it unless it is on an extreme sale.

I'm a burgeoning audiophile and I'm always eager to try new cans to add to my listening experience. A while back, say 2007 or so, I jumped into the deeper waters and decided to upgrade my stock Apple ear buds (why I didn't sooner is beyond me). I haven't looked back since, and continue to look forward this very day.

But do these headphones do my ears and music justice?

Right now my arsenal consists of some Sound Blasters I use for my computer and my trusty ol' Sennheisers which I've had since 2007 (the selfsame headphones with which I used to help me jump from Apple), along with Monoprice ear buds I keep at work. I'm not the most professional audiophile, but I sure as heck can tell some differences in quality, especially if the sound source is in FLAC.
Unfortunately, I'm not the most ecstatic about SMS Audio's STREET by 50, especially at the higher premium for Star Wars branding.

I've always been wary of celebrity-endorsed products; never trying Beats, I've been bombarded by them on the streets of Chicago by the candy-colored headbands on people's heads. I've always wondered about their integrity, until a fellow flesh-and-blood audiophile renounced them after she had used her ATH -M50s for some time. I took her word for it and never considered using Beats.
But me, being the Star Wars fanatic, had to try the SMS Audio. When they arrived I admit I was impressed by the fancy packaging. For $200, the headphones arrived looking like it.
They came in a slipcased box that was a little difficult to remove as the vacuum-sealed enclosure proved a tough fit, but they open up sweetly after that.

There are some nice manuals that come with, along with some neat little Star Wars stickers and papers. There's even a cleaning cloth and nice soft zippered case. The headphones came folded inside the case.
When I opened 'em up and took out the included removable cable and tried them on, I was a bit dumbfounded and how uncomfortable they felt around my head with such soft ear pads. I'm not sure if I need to break them in longer, but I've been using them steadily for a month and so far I haven't noticed a difference. My ears ache after just 20 minutes.

The sound was very disappointing at first, though I admit it did warm up (or down?) after a few weeks. But are they a large improvement over my $30 Sennheisers? A little, but not considerable. I can hear more background noise--that is, in the music--but there's not much balance as I have to turn up the volume to notice any huge improvement. There's a bit more bass than I'd like, but not enough to drown my ears in it.

I like the fact that the cable is detachable, but the ones they included feel a bit cheap and they tangle easily. I HATE the fact that they have the buttons, something which I've always hated since the iPhone came standard with them. But that they are removable altogether makes up for the buttons, as I'm able to change them out with custom, and higher quality, gold-plated cables.

The colors are fantastic; honestly, they were the reason I was drawn to them, but they look metallic in the press shots whereas, when you get them, the material is actually plastic, forcing the colors to be a lot lighter, more matte, and cheaper in feel. I'm all for matte, but I had hoped the headphone band was metallic; alas, it's plastic.

So that's my take on the cans. Take them or leave them. They're nice headphones, and I've gotten plenty of complements on them both from friends and at work, but at the steep price tag I can't recommend them, especially when you can get far superior headphones for much less (like the revered Audio-Technicas).

For the non-professional photographer looking to get high-quality images in a variety of settings, this camera works great. I did a little experiment to see how it performed by taking it with me to Europe along with a much more expensive semi-professional Nikon (D3100). Here are the results:

Advantages:
-With our limited time, my camera was able to take a variety of shots (panoramic, zoom, close-up) quickly and easily while the Nikon could only take limited kinds because of the need to bring several lenses and because of the complexity (sometimes) of setting up a given shot
-Because it was small, I didn't have to lug around a big camera bag, which also had the potential of getting a little too much unwanted attention
-One feature I really enjoyed was the two simultaneous flash/no flash shot which gives you the same picture with and without flash, letting you choose later which you prefer
-Didn't need more than one lens
-With city shots of architecture, my camera fared better with its versatility

Disadvantages:
-In the mountains, the Nikon did better, capturing color and clarity/detail. In my shots, the trees looked less defined from high up. Also, his zoom lens was able to capture much more detail than my camera.
-Nature shots and portraits have slightly duller colors, missing something the other camera was able to capture
-There was slightly more blur in shots with movement with this camera

Conclusion:
For the price, this camera performed much better than I expected and was not as much of a hassle as our semi-professional camera, so for most people, this is not only going to be a better value, but less frustrating and cumbersome. For the professional, this is obviously not the best choice, but this isn't being marketed as a professional camera. This is a great family and vacation camera that everyone can use, and that still yields quality images with plenty of artistic integrity.

According to the MyHarmony app, the 650 can control 8 devices. I only needed to control three for my patio setup, so it was a simple process.

It is located out in the weather and everything has worked great through a year of use in our driveway; very cold winter and very hot summer. I changed batteries recently but did so out of precaution, not because the batteries were weak. We drive in and out at least 4-5 times a day, children ride bikes by it many times a week, along with several trips to the mailbox. About the only thing to watch is when replacing batteries the little screws will fall out if not careful so I placed a white towel underneath since our alarm is mounted on a post with pine straw underneath.
Excellent product and has been great, highly recommend. You can see my full review below.

REVIEW:
After researching several products including much cheaper alternatives, I ultimately decided on this particular brand/model. We use this specifically to alert us of cars coming into our driveway. If you are looking to use this for security reasons, be aware the sensor blinks red when motion is detected which can be seen at night.
Based on two week’s usage, I highly recommend this unit thus far and here is my pros, cons, & discoveries after a few weeks of usage:
Pros/Discoveries:
• Easy to setup and install. Read the manual first!
• Transmitter easily mounts to anything. We used a 4”x4” treated post mounted about 3’6” above the ground. Post is overkill but does look nice.
• Does not seem to have many false alarms but will pick up anything within the range of the sensor which has enough movement to trigger the sensor (as it should). Had one alarm over two weeks that we never saw the reason for the alarm. Perhaps something blew across the sensor. We also have a sprinkler system which sprays water across the sensor and it never alerts, which is good.
• Install the sensor at least 3-4’ above the ground which will avoid most dogs/cats/squirrels, etc., and do not place it on metal. I also would not place it near/within range of bushes/tree limbs or similar items which might move with the wind.
• Adjust the sensitivity distance on the sensor (you must remove the four screws on the sensor to do this). Our driveway is for one car so I decreased the sensitivity level to 23’ (set 39’ from the factory). Options are 13’, 23’, 26’ and 39’.
• You can easily adjust the angle of the sensor once installed.
• Has a sensor low battery indicator which flashes inside on the receiver.
• Easy to add other sensors if needed up to 16 (4 on each zone).
• Uses common batteries. Sensor takes four AA batteries (should last a year); receiver uses four AAA batteries and/or wall outlet power. Receiver can be plugged in with batteries installed acting as a battery backup if power is lost.
• Receiver has plenty of sound melodies to select (~30), and can be very loud if volume is adjusted all the way up.
• No problem with range as our sensor is only about 150’ from the receiver but does go through a couple walls.
• Our sensor is installed in the weather without any other coverings. Based on the instructions it can be mounted anywhere outside and I don’t see the need to put the sensor inside a protective covering.
• I like the removable top of the sensor to keep out weather and sunlight on the sensor.
• The 12 volt relay is a nice option for linking to alarms, gates, or whatever else you might want to do.
• Receiver is easily turned off and on. If leaving home really early on weekends for example, I’ll turn it off to avoid waking my family when I drive out.
• Came with a small screwdriver which fits perfectly to remove tiny screws in the sensor for battery installation and sensitivity setting.

CONS:
• I thought the sensor would have been enclosed in stronger PVC (aka thicker plastic). But it does have a lifetime warranty as long as the company is in business.
• Would have liked more color options for the sensor. For example, black, white and camo.
• Worried about losing the small screws when adjusting sensitivity and/or replacing the batteries in the sensor once installed. Our sensor is installed over a plant bed with pine straw, so I had to put down a white towel under the unit when opening the enclosure to make final sensitivity adjustments. Would have been nice if the sensor came with the type screws that don’t fall out when unscrewed.
• Receiver is not the nicest to look at but we managed to place it where it was centrally located in the house and not so obvious.
• There are over 30 melodies available but we were hoping for more chimes/bells similar to doorbell type options. Many are song type melodies which we didn't like.

Overall very pleased and highly recommend.

This HP Pavilion desktop is a solid, but basic PC that, while it can be considered a gaming PC with its discreet Radeon RX 5500 card, that isn't going to raise too many eyebrows with its specs. What's out of the realm of this machine would be 4K gaming and VR, but it can run most modern games at medium settings at 1080p.

That's not why I needed this machine, though. As a Plex server, this serves well. It is quiet and can transcode videos using hardware transcoding. Unfortunately, it only has a single slot for an additional hdd. As a video editing machine, it can handle 1080p videos, but will struggle with 4K. As a photo editing machine, it can edit pretty much anything from the devices you have, but if you work in print, you'll find this machine lacking. For emulation, this machine will work quite well for all classic systems and even some more modern ones. Of course, for everyday web browsing and watching videos, this thing will be more than enough.

Overall, this is a fairly priced machine that is a step up from the basic computers that one may find and the discreet GPU will help to make this machine last longer than those with embedded graphics.

I work in photo/video for a living, and I can tell you that good LEDs aren't cheap. I have worked with hot tungsten lamps for high output and smaller LEDs for lightweight smaller setups, but LED lights that can compete with the output of Tungstens are pricey.
That being said, this is a FANTASTIC light. It has high output yet has the pros of LED panels such as lower power consumption and heat, as well as being dimmable and color adjustable from the panel or remote control. I had the opportunity to use this for a job yesterday setting up an interview in an office setting. My tungsten bulbs would have been too bright and need gels to match the rest of the office. My other smaller LEDs would have cast smaller spots and we all know a larger light source casts a more pleasing glow. It seemed effortless to get the amount of light we needed in a short time.
HOWEVER, I did find that the mounting point was a little bit difficult to use. There are two bolts to secure it to the stand, and both need to be loosened to mount it properly. It took me a few attempts to get it on the stand, one side felt like I was screwing the bolt the wrong direction most of the time. Meanwhile, the light is large and kept wobbling during this overly complicated procedure. It didn't feel like a premium product during that, which I found odd considering the price point. I have lights that cost about half of this one that felt more premium during mounting. But, that being said, once the lights are up it works a treat!
So, a solid 4 stars from me. Almost 5 if the mounting were easier or the price lower to make up for that. But as a light, it does what it should do and well.

The Philips SQM6415/17 Tilting LCD Wall Mount for 19-Inch to 31-Inch Screens mounts your 19 inch to 31 inch screen weighing less than 44 pounds onto the stud on a wall, attaching the mounted bracket to the VESA holes at the rear of a tv or monitor.  Prior to receiving this wall mount, I downloaded the manual from the Phillips website, and I recommend you do the same.  The manual is far from the best, mainly pictures, and like the one which arrives with the package. I received my headband as a review sample. I want to note that I did not experience any drops in streaming as noted by other reviewers when using this with my Samsung Note 3 phone, but did have some issues with my Samsung Tab 3 10.1. The latter has some bluetooth problems that are well known, so I am attributing my issues with Tab 3 flaws and not this headband. I briefly tested this with an HTC One Remix with no problems either.

This headband is unique in that it was designed with real, strenuous sports in mind - or at least activities that make you work up a sweat. As such I tested my streaming as noted above with my source devices (phones and tablets) at least twenty feet away. That simulates where you would place those devices during a game of tennis.

It does seem impervious to sweat, although I would not call it sweat-proof. If you use it heavily and frequently you'll need to clean it at least weekly - see some of the top rated video reviews on this page for instructions for that because it is a bit tricky disassembling it the first time.

Also note that it's a snug fit on my head, which is size 6 7/8. I am guessing that if you wear a men's hat size above 7 1/4 it will be too snug. Take that into account.

Sound quality is excellent in my opinion. For the past nine months or so (at the time of this review) all brands or phones seem to have taken a major leap in that respect and these are no exception. The high frequency response of the phones is clear at max volume and the bass is deep (but not thumping). The mid range seems to be the sweet spot, and is rich and full. The volume itself is not super loud, and it is not noise-isolating. It does keep out most ambient noise though, and while these are not perfect for critical listening they are excellent for casual listening during sports and other strenuous activities.

If you want phones that stay in place regardless of that you are doing, and also demand respectable sound quality these merit consideration. I have not researched the market, but these are the only headband phones I have come across among the dozens I have tested to date.

I find that the best price to performance is in the $30 range for Bluetooth headphones, and they keep getting better and better. I have several pairs that I use for the gym, general listening to music, watching movies, and playing poker. I like to have other charged ones ready to go if a pair gets low.

These were rated very well, so I decided to give them a shot. They are super comfortable and they stay in place at the gym. I am not an audiophile, but these are well balanced and have better sound quality than my other pairs.

The greatest thing about these is the battery life- I used them for about 11 hours, and there was still 50% battery life left. With all my other pairs the battery life is a real problem, and it does not improve as they age. The charging case is also nice and there is a display for remaining battery life of the case. Remaining battery life of the headphones is displayed on the mobile device.

The BT connection is also super reliable. I have not experienced any disconnects or interference.

There are a couple cons (no product is perfect) and I want to briefly discuss them.

1. The rubber snap-on ear buds are not universal. They have a unique oval shape where they snap on and are secured. I have a bunch of spares, but they will not fit on here. If you lose one or it breaks it is useless. It comes with 3 sizes, but most people are probably like me and can only use the one size that fits.

2. The gain is too high on these. Adjusting the volume from zero, there are not many steps until the volume is too high. This means that micro-adjustment of the volume is not possible. All my other pairs I can use at 100% volume or near this (though I would not recommend it) and there there are maybe 15 or more micro-adjustments all the way back down to zero. Also, the notifications "power on," "power off," and "connected" are too loud. It's possible that with different mobile phones they behave differently, and there may also be an adjustment for this.

In summary, I highly recommend these. They are comfortable, they stay in place, they stay connected to my device, and they sound great. Probably the biggest Pro is the battery life. I purchased these to use as a backup for my other pairs, but it turns out that these will be my main headphones.

For what it’s worth, this product does the anti-glare job. But part of the use of an iPad is writing and getting around easily with the touch of any finger. Frankly, this screen protector makes it harder to do both.

The connection to the stereo can be done via a single cable or using a two cable (L/R) setup. Cables for both options are included. I'm using the L/R option, and plugged the cables into the TAPE input on my stereo receiver.

The sound quality is excellent. It is very hard to tell the difference in quality when streaming audio via this receiver versus playing a CD on the receiver. Movie dialog was outstanding as well.

The fact that it does not require a battery is a plus and a minus. On the plus side, no need to worry about recharging or swapping batteries. On the down side, it was a bit of a problem for me to get the cables routed since the wall outlet near my stereo is not easily accessible. I wound up running a short extension cord so that I could plug in the receiver close enough to the stereo so that the L/R cables would reach.

As a bonus, it includes a USB port so you can use it to recharge your phone/tablet/etc.

That one minor issue aside, I'm very impressed with the performance of this product. Highly recommend.

I ordered the 'Jabra Evolve 65e UC & Link 370 Wireless Professional Earbuds' as I'm a sucker for trying out new wireless earbuds. I've tried various different types. There is really no sound isolation as the buds don't fit snug in the ear, (even trying the included different size tips and wings) but that seems to be on purpose. As from I can tell from reading about these, is that they are meant to allow some outside sound, so that if you are say jogging, you should be able to hear to be safe right? Now with that said, I see the purpose and the market for these earbuds, and there is absolute value to these.
Pairing these to my Android mobile phone was an absolute breeze. Also, using the USB Bluetooth adapter on my Chromebook made pairing these super simple as well.
Call quality is on par with most wireless earbuds. It's good, but not the same as just using your phone obviously but better than some "cheap" buds I've tried. These are definitely built with the Jabra quality you would expect and I'm overall impressed.
They fit comfortably and secure and I've had no issue with them popping out, but then again I'm not a jogger. They are easy to fit into your ears, unlike others that I've had that take a bit of twisting to get the fit just right.
The app is nice and works well but as with most apps like this, it's gimmicky. I mean I've played with it a bit at first but any more, I just pop the buds in and go, and haven't used the app in quite a while.
So to summarize, these are great earbuds if you don't need "truly wireless" and you don't need sound isolation.

----------------------------
-HDMI Splitter that can bypass HDCP (For digital caputuring. What device isn't digital nowadays?)
-Flash drive or Hard Drive: Maximum flash drive space is 256gb. Maximum hard drive is 8tb.

As a kid, I used to love recording tv or cable to VHS. Then in the late 90's and early 2000's, I was into those Hard Drive recorders with built in dvd-r burners by Pioneer and Philips, remember those? But then Tivo and Cable DVR really took off and made recording to actual dvds a thing of the past. So what we have here with the ClearClick is simply a device that brings the "old way" of archiving to 2020, but instead of VHS and DVR-Rs, it will record as MP4 files into your flash drive. I also think the reason these devices are still relevant is due to the phenomenon of gamers who love to record all their game-play. Anyway, I'm happy to report it does exactly what it advertises brilliantly. However, unless you're only capturing analog signals (VHS transers), you will need a HDMI splitter that can bypass HDCP. In my use case scenario... I have a Caavo Universal Remote/HDMI Switcher. The Caavo has four HDMI inputs. I have my Tivo, a Fire TV, a Android TV box, and the Nintendo Switch hooked to it. Then it has one HDMI output. This output normally goes to the TV. So that's my set-up...

Now to hook up this ClearClick, I remove the HDMI that connects to the TV from the Caavo, and instead, I connect it to the Input of the special HDMI Splitter. Then HDMI OUT from this splitter to the input of the ClearClick. Finally, HDMI OUT from the ClearClick to an input on my TV. This way, I can capture from any device I want that's connected to my Caavo. Of course, you can just connect one source at a time too if you don't have a hub like I do. But remember, you need to connect your source to the HDMI splitter first. If you don't, you will just get a black screen that says "unsupported format." One more thing, the HDMI splitter obviously has 2 HDMI outs, one of which is going to the ClearClick. I also use the second HDMI out to connect directly to another input on my TV. The reason is to avoid having to turn on the ClearClick when I'm not recording.

The spliiter I use is called the ViewHD Model: VHD-1X2MN3D. You can find this on Amazon. However, I believe it is still YMMV (your mileage may vary.) I bought that years ago and it still works. But if you search in the reviews for that splliter, some do complain it didn't work for them. Sometimes a different batch has different chipsets, I dunno. So it may take trial and error before you get a splitter that works. I also have a 4tb Western Digital passport connected the ClearClick, and it works perfectly.

Lastly, inside the box, they give you a free license of Videopad software. This is so you can touch up your recordings, add effects, transitions, or even output to DVD. Before I registered my copy, I wanted to see how much this software cost, so I proceeded to purchase as if I didn't have a code. So currently, it's listed as $99, but it is on sale for $35 until August 15. We get it free!

I have a smartwatch that I have worn now for over a year and I have been pleased with it. I was unfamiliar with the idea of a "hybrid smartwatch" and was interested in this one from Skagen. It's an interesting concept and the watch itself seems to work well, but I have some frustrations with the software.

This is basically a traditional analog watch with some smartwatch functions built into it. The smartwatches I have used usually have a full digital face with all manner of things on the display, and depending on the face chosen it may or may not be easy to read. This watch keeps things relatively simple and has the hour and minute displayed with moving hands, and around the center are displays for steps, heart rate and weather-at-a-glance. The whole is clean and easy on the eyes. Now, that said, if you cannot read an analog watch this one might not be the best choice.

Charging requires the special cable that comes with it and it takes a relatively short time to charge. The run time is much longer than most smartwatches I have used, getting well over a week on a single charge where a smartwatch is often 2-3 days or less.

Skagen has a special app for interacting with the watch and it was easy to find in the repository. It installs quickly and guides through the setup without too much issue. It is good for activity tracking and limited health monitoring as well as limited customization of the face. However, I have had some difficulty with connectivity and staying connected through the app, such that it has been an annoyance. This is the biggest complaint I have so far.

So far this watch has managed to keep good time, connected or not.

Overall I am happy with this watch though I am less than thrilled with the app. Hopefully an update will correct the connectivity issue I see with it. Otherwise, this is a good-looking and functional watch.

This digital camcorder has features not found on many camcorders.
First the things I like about this Camcorder:
This camcorder records in high definition (1020 at 30 fps), and two low resolution (720P at both 30 and 60 fps) select-able from the screen.
There is a option for setting the camera up for motion control triggered recording.
The system has a IR based night vision system to record in total blackout conditions.
The remote can be used to control most modes of the camcorder and start/stop recording.
This system comes with a external mic to help in recording the audio component of your filming, you have the option to use this mic or not depending on your circumstances.
You can use the camcorder as a photo camera with resolutions ranging from 5mp to 24mp along with settings for white balance, color, and shutter speeds.
You can turn off the beep sound for camera functions, something you may use if recording wildlife.
This Camcorder comes with a wide view lens, great when recording in a shallow area such as a room to get everyone and everything into one shot.
Extra battery, handy for extended use or areas where you cannot recharge the camera.

Things I would like to see improved:
The zoom is digital only, not an optical zoom. This limits the camcorder to recording only items in a shallow depth, not great for outdoor use unless you are up close to your subject.

All in all, a decent camcorder for use where you are close (physically) to your subject, or as long as you understand its limitations.

At this point, I have had the Sense 2 for 2 days and I know at least some of my issues will likely be fixed with later software updates. First, the good. I like the form factor. The case is thin and the watch, even with the supplied band, is comfortable. Speaking of the band, as a big guy, I was overjoyed to see the inclusion of a second band that actually fit. Also, changing bands is a snap.

Overall, it seems to be relatively high quality. The battery life, so far at least has been fantastic. I am on hour 42 of wearing it after a 99% charge and it is down to 70% battery left. The screen is fairly bright and crisp. An understated advantage of the Sense 2 (and one of the reasons I switched) is that is OS and phone brand agnostic. You can use it with Apple or Android and, unlike the Galaxy Watch, there are no features locked away if you are not using the correct brand of phone.

If you are coming from a Galaxy Watch where you could customize the watch face and all sorts of other things and that is important to you, then move along. This watch will not be for you. For now, at least, there is not really much substantive you can do to individualize your user experience. That's not so great.

Also not so great is the things that are missing. There is no Google Maps at launch. Also, despite being a Google company, no support for the Google Assistant (Alexa only sadly). There is also no interface to control music on your phone if that is important to you. I found it mildly annoying, but not a deal breaker. In addition, some people will be turned off by the fact that there are features that require a Fitbit paid subscription to get, even though you get six months for free.

The real reason I bought this watch was the ECG function. I have had A Fib for a couple of years and used to use (and still do) a Kardia XL to check my rhythm. The Galaxy Watch 4 was nice because it did a reasonable single lead reading and it meant not having to carry another gizmo with me. You simply held still and put a finger on each of the side buttons. Unfortunately, when I switched from a Galaxy phone to a Pixel, I lost the ability to do an ECG.

On the Sense 2, the ECG has not been impressive. First, I have big hands and contorting my right one to get my thumb and forefinger on the corner of the glass has been a challenge at time. It often takes several tries to get it right. Second, despite confirming on both my Kardia and my Galaxy Watch, the Sense 2 will never indicate that I am in A Fib. Apparently, if your pulse goes above 120 (which mine frequently does while in A Fib) then the Sense 2 just gives up and won't really check. Even in instances where it was below 120, the Sense will not confirm. I guess we get to settle for inconclusive results instead. Given this feature was the main reason I bought the watch, it may be a deal breaker for me and I may return it for that reason. If this feature is not that important to you, then it may still be a good option.

Overall though, it may be a good option for the right person. If you care primarily about health and fitness tracking and want a good battery life, then this is a good option. At the current $300 price point, I still feel like Fitbit may be asking a little too much given the features of the other higher end options on the market.

Power isn't everything. My intention was for the A90 to replace an old portable DAC/Amp combo that is only rated at 1.6W total at 75Ω. It's not a horrible amp. It's just not a great amp. Maybe the A90 would sound better when paired with muffled/veiled or extremely warm sounding headphones. For Sennheiser HD800's or HD820's though, which are inherently bright, it's a horrible match. The A90 sucked the soul from the music with those particular headphones.

The chain I tested with the A90 was a Naim ND5 XS2 streamer > Nordost Silver Shadow BNC > Schiit Gungnir Multibit DAC > Cardas Clear XLR > Topping A90. There's usually a Schiit Mjolnir 2 at the end of the chain and it sounds amazing. I didn't expect the A90 to outperform the Mjolnir but I did expect it to outperform my little DAC/Amp combo, especially when being fed such a good source

All I can really take away from my experience with the A90 is DO NOT pair this amp with bright headphones. Can't comment on other headphones but avoid this amp if you've got HD800's or 820's.

I purchased this Panasonic Soundbar in June of 2013. At the time, my requirements were:
- Good sound (can't afford GREAT sound)
- Wireless Subwoofer
- HDMI input and good HDMI-CEC support
- Bluetooth support

In my search, I tested the [[ASIN:B00811NMMI Toshiba SBX4250]] and the [[ASIN:B00BLX9510 Samsung HW-F450]] from my local Costco. My final choice was the Panasonic.

Sound:
- Acceptable sound -- The front speakers are not a big improvement over the built-ins. With the subwoofer turned off, it is easy to mistake the Panasonic sound bar with the speakers from the Television.
- Good subwoofer -- The sub sounds good even at high volumes and fills out the overall sound from the sound bar.
- The Samsung has clearer mid and high ranges so the Panasonic seems slightly muffled in comparison.
- Overall sound better than the Toshiba.
- Wireless range for the subwoofer is short -- especially if placed behind the sofa (interference from people sitting in front of it). Range is about 15 feet with clear line of sight.

Decoders and Passthrough:
- AC3 and DTS Decoder (Toshiba lacks DTS)
- ARC (Audio Return Channel) -- If you use the Netflix app built in to your TV, audio is generated by your TV. Normally, an "optical out" cable from the TV back to the sound bar is necessary. ARC removes that need.

HDMI-CEC (also Aquos Link, Anynet+, Bravia LinkSync, Regza Link, etc):
This is where the Panasonic beats the Samsung. HDMI-CEC allows Televisions to control a connected device -- no matter the brand; The TV remote should be able to turn on a bluray player and send navigation (up/down/etc) and standard playback buttons without the need for a second remote control.

In the case of a sound bar, through HDMI-CEC:
1. The sound bar should turn on when the TV turns on -- Panasonic does this, Samsung does not.
2. The TV should play all sound through the sound bar and volume buttons on the TV remote should control volume on the sound bar -- Panasonic does this.
3. Turning on a bluray player, the sound bar should turn on and switch to the correct input automatically. The TV should also turn on and switch to the correct input -- Panasonic does this. It's then up to your TV do its part.

In conclusion, I chose the Panasonic because it gave me the ability to eliminate a remote control through HDMI-CEC (which Samsung didn't) and it had both AC3 and DTS decoders (which Toshiba didn't). With the added ability to play music from my phone through bluetooth, I'm still happy with my purchase one year later.

Tip: Unlike the Samsung and Toshiba, the Panasonic has a small "receiver" unit that adds another machine to your entertainment center. For me, I use some velcro strips and attach the "receiver" to the back of my TV. It is only 1 ¾" thick which was thinner than my wall mount.

Took delivery of one of these 18" 640 LED ring lights yesterday.

As I shoot through it at test subjects, the overwhelming response is, "Boy is that bright!"

I had my camera down to ISO 200 and working at about f/5.6 or so.

The supplied diffusion sock is not quite enough. LEDs are really annoying to look at.

A lighting manufacturer at NAB 2013 explained to me that LEDs put out most of their energy in the UV spectrum. The way they emit visible light (at least some of them) is to excite tiny amounts of phosphors placed over the LED itself, similar to how a fluorescent lamp excites phosphors deposited on the inner surface of the tube.

It also means that to be safe, manufacturers need to build in a UV filter. I sincerely believe that we instinctively realize such bright LED light is bad for our eyes and react with a squint.

Then again, your poor subject also has 640 very bright point sources searing their eyeballs.

The diffuser helps spread the light a bit, and it works as far as it goes, but my plan is to cut arcs of additional diffusion material and attach them to the light, over the LEDs, under the diffuser sock.

The gooseneck is functional and the 5/8" socket fits a standard lightstand nicely, though I don't know how long the fine threads of the locking knob will last. With care, it'll be fine. Just don't crank the knob down or you may strip the thread out. Won't be an issue unless you are hanging the light from overhead. On a stand, gravity is your friend.

What it really lacks is a way to store and transport. It arrives in a square cardboard box about 1-1/2" thick. After you attach the gooseneck, it can't fit back into the box. I don't want to unscrew the gooseneck every time to put the light away, so I'll have to locate a large, flat case of some sort.

*****
UPDATE:
The http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B002JPKWK2/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s01?ie=UTF8&psc=1 case to carry artwork holds this light, its power supply and even a small light stand very nicely.

*****

You also need to wrangle the power supply, which has a permanently attached 2.5mm x 5.5mm angled coax power plug with its approx. 2-meter cable on the output side and on the input, a two-prong removable AC cable, also about 2 meters long. The light runs on 15 volts. There's a remote control multi-pin socket, for an optional remote.

On the back is an on/off rocker switch and a large dimmer knob that gives smooth control of intensity.

The light is sturdy and, as I said, extremely bright.

Best part: it really flatters the ladies! Every wrinkle disappears. And that circular highlight in the eyeball is really unique.

After a very quick test shot this afternoon of a woman friend, my coworker looked at the results and exclaimed, "It makes her look like a model!"

It's such a different look over "normal" lighting that it's sure to make certain shots really stand out.

And when the ladies ask me to put the "Remove ten years" filter on, I'll actually be able to do it.

I have been learning more about photography and as time has permitted I have been improving my skill as an amateur photographer. I have worked with other types of filters, in particular CPL and FL-D filters, but before now I have never worked with ND filters. I have been able to achieve good results with it and so far I am pleased with this filter though I know I have more to learn about it.

A neutral-density filter is used to reduce light reaching the aperture without fiddling too much with the colors. This allows one to get creative with shutter speeds. This particular filter is adjustable and turns on the lens body face, allowing the photographer to increase or decrease the amount of filtering done. At the lowest setting the filter does very little filtering; when turned up to the maximum filtering level very little light gets through and a moire pattern appears so I do not recommend turning up the filter to this level.

To get a feel for how well this filter works I took my camera outside as a big thunderstorm approached and took some pictures of one of the cloud formations. I selected two pictures from that set, one where I did not use the filter and one where I did use it on about 1/4 strength. Although the filter evenly reduced light levels, the color contrast in the filtered image is much more pronounced and obvious.

The most common use for this kind of filter is to reduce the light levels, then take an extended exposure for a scene with motion, such as a waterfall.

This is a very nice filter and I could not be happier with it. It is very easy to use and it really works well.

I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. It’s not perfect but it’s close.

I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both.

I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable.

I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk.

I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth.

The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. For me that’s a positive; others may dislike the added weight.

One of the things I have missed has been a tilting scroll wheel. This trackball has one and I have been enjoying getting used to that feature again.

One thing I did notice is that there is no CD/DVD in the package for loading drivers. This isn’t a big deal, and it’s easy enough to get the drivers from the net. That said, the trackball just seems to work when you attach it, without any issue. For me it has absolutely been plug-and-play, on every system I have tried.

If I could change one thing - I would have made this trackball a little bigger. I have big hands and I struggle to find a trackball that’s an absolute perfect fit. This one is close. For the large majority of people it’s going to be spot on.

I am very happy with this trackball and have no issue with recommending it. It works great, connects easily, when connected to two different systems it switches at the press of a button, it has a bit of heft to it and the tilt is adjustable for wrist comfort. It’s really all I could ask for.

This is my first IP camera, but I've used many analog cameras and DVRs.

I've hooked this up three ways: By itself, to a switch on the same network as a stand-alone NVR, and to a switch on the same network utilizing my QNAP NAS as the NVR - in each case powered by PoE. Here are some details I've figured out in the process:

---By itself: You can view it quickly and easily without delay with the App, which seems to have all the things you'd expect from a camera viewing app. I assume you can record to or snapshot to an SD card from the description, but I'm going to record to my network, so I didn't try that feature. This was just plug and play, worked super easy.

What I love is that once you figure out the IP address, you can access the camera via a webserver, which pretty much future-proofs the hardware. I despise "smart" devices where you need an app, because then you're at their mercy to run their app on whatever OS they decide to use and they can force you to make accounts, update, etc. Having this open to the user/owner is the way to go. Bravo.

And that web server is full featured. I was able to play around and do everything here before I bothered downloading the app.

Note that - like every camera I've ever used - the viewing software sends a substream which is lower resolution unless you demand the higher resolution. With the app you can see low and medium resolution, but 4k has trouble playing over WiFi (or else it's just smart enough to realize my screen can't support it anyway). Just pointing this out so you realize if you're seeing pixels, that doesn't mean the camera isn't actually recording at 4k.

---With NVR: I recently acquired a cheap 8-channel 4k NVR that I believe to be a Uniview OEM. I added a hard drive and put it on the same network as this camera. The NVR has an 8 port PoE switch built in, but it must also be a router, because it wants to use a different subnet if you put the camera on the NVR's switch. Otherwise, you can easily point the NVR to the camera via IP address.

So...if you point the NVR to the camera via IP address, you can view the camera from its own app or from the NVR app. I assume this still takes one of the NVRs 8 channels. This might be useful if you want to give someone access to just one camera on your network. But it occurred to me that, setup this way, you have constant data streaming over your network, and after you add quite a few cameras in 4k, this is going to start adding up.

If you put the camera directly on the NVR, you'll have to change the IP manually to match the subnet, or maybe you'll somehow get it to work through the NVR or with DHCP. I hadn't bothered spending time figuring this out yet because at the time I thought I'd just use my other switch, but I'm thinking once I get more cameras, it'll probably make more sense to put them directly onto the NVR and ...actually, then I won't have to change my entire IP scheme since I won't have so many new devices to organize.

I'm certain I can get it all working in unison with no problem, but it is more complicated than if you just buy an NVR set with a bunch of cameras already ready to work together. Either way shouldn't be a problem if you have IP knowledge, but I'm guessing a random homeowner might prefer a set.

---Using my NAS as NVR. Hmmm...a little disappointed with QNAP in this regard. I mean, I have three NASs, and I'm assuming they all have 2 licenses included, but to combine them into one program then I believe requires yet another license. I'm not into licenses, even if they're a one time deal, because that means you need accounts and if something happens where they're lost, you can run into all kinds of other issues. I just think consumers need to stand up to this sort of thing. But anyway, I had two included, so I tried it out:

I realized that this is a lot of work for my little consumer grade NAS, and even if I had a more hardcore NAS, I'm not sure I want resources being used all the time. It seems like I couldn't get it to use H.265 compression, nor could I get it to record at the higher resolutions and frame rates. Again, I didn't play with this too awful much once I got it recording and working because I already realized I definitely like the stand alone DVR better. The QNAP even had extra stuff to download and windows to pop up on your PC and all this other stuff. Just not as streamlined as I had hoped.

----Conclusion is that the camera is awesome. I'm not sure many are any better at this point. If you want something that just works easy and you don't know much about networking, you may wish to just buy an NVR set. But if you are IP capable, I think buying components separately could be a great way to go because you can really customize what you want to do. But as always, more options with networking means more potential headaches. But I am pretty certain that once you get it working the way you want it, you should be able to forget all about it and have it work indefinitely.

Oh, and after all that, I shouldn't forget to point out that I'd be thrilled to have this all by itself watching my porch just so I can tell when there's a package out there. My Ring (that came with the house) can't even see that because of the angle it is set at.

IBI - THE SMART PHOTO MANAGER (US Version) makes it super easy to extract, back up, and share photos stored on my mobile devices. Instead of emailing cell phone photos that I want to share among electronic devices (an iPad Air (3rd Gen), a desktop PC, and a Samsung Galaxy cell phone), I can upload the photos to Ibi via a network connection with only a couple of clicks in the Ibi app.

No longer do I have to address an email, select and add the photos, send the email--and then reverse the process on a second device (open the email, download the photos, and save the photos to the device). All that’s necessary is to take the photos, open the Ibi app, choose “import photos”, select the photos, and hit the import button.

The photos are immediately uploaded to Ibi, and I can access them immediately on all of my other devices. There is no need to clutter up email or to consume precious storage space on my mobile devices, when all I want to do is share photos.

Ibi is extremely versatile. It allows you to sort and organize photos, and create Albums. It allows you to authorize certain people to email photos directly to Ibi. It allows you to set up different areas of Ibi for the use of individuals. It allows you to upload its contents to a PC or other even larger storage device by plugging in a USB cable (not included). It even allows you to stream your videos to a television set (using Chromecast or Roku apps).

Ibi is easy to set up, using Bluetooth. My iPad and my Galaxy phone both found the powered on (plugged in) Ibi in less than 30 seconds. Once set up, Ibi communicates via your home network’s Internet access. When your Ibi app is set up, click on Help, and download the complete user manual (a PDF file). The manual is easy to understand, and will enable you to get the most out of your Ibi.

Ibi is a small drive that easily fits on a bookshelf. It uses just one power cord. I really love this Ibi storage drive. It is simplifying my life.

+++++IMPORTANT NOTE: You should NOT choose “automatic backup” in the Ibi app Settings until you understand how the app works. With automatic backup enabled, Ibi will copy all of the photos stored on EACH mobile device, and you will probably get a lot of duplicate photos. For example, if you have been sharing and storing the same photos on an iPad and a cell phone, Ibi will copy the photos from each device. Worse, if you go into Ibi and delete the duplicates, Ibi will keep automatically adding the photos back as long as the photos still exist in storage on the two different devices.

You will probably want to use “automatic backup” when you first set up your Ibi. That way all of your photos will be automatically copied to Ibi to start you off. But you should turn “automatic backup” off before you start deleting duplicate photos. You will never have a problem with duplicate photos if automatic backup is turned off.+++++
