The UV filter is useful as a basic protective cover for a lens, but it also does filter out UV light. This is a lot less of a problem when it comes to digital camera, as UV light was harmful to 35mm film. UV light can make images hazy and this filter can reduce that. In very specific situations, there can be reflections between the lens glass and the filter, so there are occasions when using the UV filter is not advisable.

I had the opportunity to use the CPL filter on a sunny day at a lake and I used the filter to cut through the reflections on the water. It worked well and I was able to get a picture of things on the bottom. That’s all I could really ask.

I have not used the ND4 filter.

This set comes in a nice carrying case that protects the filters when they’re not in use. The case is small enough that it fits inside my camera bag without any issue.

FOSCAM is a well-known name when it comes to security cameras and security equipment and they make a good variety of security solutions for home and business use. The F19803P camera is a wireless IP camera that is weatherproof, has night vision and can be accessed via smartphone. One configured and set up on the network it works great but the setup process can be a very painful one.

In the box is the actual camera, the antenna, power adapter, mounting kit, installation software and an Ethernet cable. The camera housing is roughly the size of a new roll of bathroom tissue - very small, compact and lightweight. The mounting kit is a small but solid painted aluminum bracket plus the screws needed to secure it. When mounted properly, this camera can be very inconspicuous.

Following the included directions, I installed the software first and then hooked up the camera to the router. According to the included documentation the IPCamera application should immediately see the camera and from there one can select the camera, log into it and manipulate it as needed. This did not work for me and the camera never did appear. I tried downing my firewall, I tried connecting to a different router and even tried directly connecting to the camera and still was unable to see it. I finally managed to reach the camera by opening the FOSCAM client software and telling it to search for cameras. When I did this, the camera finally appeared, and the IPCamera application showed it too. This works but runs contrary to the documentation.

I did get into the camera finally and was able to change the username and password. I also set up the wireless network settings and found other settings to adjust like IR timer, time source and more.

I found that the camera’s administration settings can be accessed as needed through the IP address and specifying port 88 (unless the port is deliberately changed). I strongly encourage assigning a fixed IP address to the camera via DHCP through the router; otherwise, the IP address can change and accessing the camera gets more difficult. I learned this the hard way, when I had the Ethernet MAC defined but not the WiFi MAC in my router’s DHCP table. My fault, but this was made more difficult by the IPCamera application still not seeing the camera and I had to let the client software scan again.

I made one more mistake and reset the camera via the reset button and it cleared everything I had set already: user name, password, everything. I was concerned that I would lose everything again with a power failure so as a test I unplugged the camera for a few hours and plugged it in again, and fortunately it retained its configuration.

The camera cannot see my 5G network, only my 2.4G network. However, even though my computer is on the 5G network it still can access the camera. Both networks are handled by my one router so I assume that this is normal. If you have a 5G network, make sure you also have the 2.4G network configured or keep the camera connected via Ethernet. The fact that it does not support 5G networks is not necessarily a problem but is worth knowing beforehand.

Once I made it through the configuration (which was all of two hours, most of it trying to figure out how to talk to the camera), the client software allowed me to add it to the configuration and stream a live video feed from it. The video quality is actually very good and when not in IR mode is in full color. When streaming IR video the image is straight black and white, but the image is very clear. Testing with the camera indoors I killed all the lights in the room and the IR kicked in, my intent being to see how clear the image is. The image is clear enough to read text off a white sheet of paper when angled right. Specifically I held up the instruction manual to the camera at about a 2' distance and was able to read the front page without difficulty. The only complaint I have with the IR is that it does not seem to kick in early enough; when in a dimly lit room the camera still tries to use non-IR and the result is a very dark feed. I have found no way to adjust this in the camera settings other than to set the IR to cut on at a specific time which may or may not be the most useful thing.

I like the fact that this camera does not need a specialized hub to work and can be run from a PC or MAC instead. This makes the system a lot more flexible and easier to manage.

The real power of this camera comes in the client software. It allows for adding additional cameras (the screen settings suggest up to 64 cameras) and monitoring all of them at once on one screen. Some of the camera settings can be manipulated such as setting up recording times, setting alarms and more. Adding a camera is as simple as running a search and then adding the camera to an area. There is even the ability to play back the video that has been recorded built right in.

This is a nice security camera and it works well. It has very good IR capability, it works wirelessly and has full-color video that is clear and workable. Configuring this camera can be very unpleasant, though once configured it’s a great solution. If you need a good outdoor wireless camera and you have some patience for an install that’s not necessarily smooth, consider this one.

I’ve been sold on the 13.3” size by day and switch to my engineering work station by night. If you are looking at a 13.3”, Asus and Dell are the leaders duking it out for market. As I have both, I’ll compare and contrast to answer questions regarding stuff I’ve found important between them

Newest Dell …
- Extraordinarily fast … speed has not been a discriminator for non-game use for some years. I can’t detect one faster than another. It’s just really fast. It behaves like MS and Dell are better integrated behind the scene than Asus.
- Dell is physically smaller and presents a ¼” display bezel to reduce the footprint and shave about ½” off the external X and Y.
- Dell’s LED-backlit display appearance is superb. The 4000:1 contrast is a noticeable attribute. Viewing angles appear to be like >60 degrees all around (outstanding!). It seems unusual that Dell incorporates a UHD graphics card to drive an FHD display ... I suspect a UHD display is coming when competition demands.
- No touch screen. I don’t like the touch screen 95% of the time (thin film over LCD, busy pointy fingers on the screen make stuff happen) … but you pick’um.
- Keyboard illumination has moved into my must-haves. The Dell delivers a different take in light piping. It works OK. In daylight, the Dell keyboard has to be turned off if you want to read the keys. Could be the color or light pipe strategy, the illumination obscures the key characters like an optical illusion. The Asus keyboard lighting is better.
- The keyboard of course feels different. Asus uses membrane switches offering minimal tactile feedback and less noise (I think it’s faster). The Dell is using a spring key switch to provide more tactile feel and audible ‘click’ feedback. User decide. Both work fine for me.
- Integral sound quality is comparatively outstanding from the uber-tiny speakers. Dell has fixed the typical awful anemic 13.3” sound quality.
- The Skype view camera is at the bottom of the Dell display providing crisp up the nose hole vision. Come on Dell! You gotta be kidding! It’s awful. This is not a Skype’r PC.
- Very responsive touchpad. Better than Asus.
- Face recognition is by True Key and works fine. After a couple initial failures, the fingerprint reader works great ... faster than the FRT.
- The 128G SSD might have concerned me a couple years ago. Asus standard is 256G. However, cloud and share applications have become so good and so responsive that I simply don’t store data locally from the start. The paradigm that more SSD is better is obsolete for me. I’m not going to suck up 128G.
- Not initially obvious, the Dell keyboard deck is made from an excellent composite. Water beads up on it, great for sneezes and general hygiene. Easier to keep clean than the anodized metal Asus top deck.

I'd say the chief consideration for the Dell is the USB-C only connectivity that for the moment, must be dongle/hub adapted to your USB A-B, HDMI peripherals. As these 13.3” offerings get faster and lighter, they have to get thinner. This Dell is the thinnest I’ve seen and too thin to even fit a USB-A port in it. USB-C thin is the tech trajectory so get with the program.

So my wireless mouse here is hanging off an adapter dongle. Who among typical users even have a USB-C Thunderbolt device to plug in? The Thunderbolt 3 Type-C ports run at a blazing 40Gb/s transfer rate and support full 4K TV and more … for now, you will need to buy an adapter hub to plug your HDMI, and various collections of USB A and B peripherals. The Dell is significantly ahead of the market here. On the plus side, it’s been a while since I’ve had to do some uncharted pathfinding and the USB-C, Thunderbolt 3 connectivity is going to be interesting for me.

The bottom line … if I need a day with the best display and no mini-mouse, I’ll take this Dell. If I need to be flexibly capable for connecting HDMI and USB A/B on the fly, I’m going to use the Asus. Whether or not you'll like this case depends to a large extent on two things: 1) how much of a klutz you are, and 2) how you use your iPad.

Here's where I fit into that picture: I'm not generally klutzy -- I can count on one hand the number of times I've dropped any of my portable electronics in the past 10 years. I use my iPad mostly when I travel and don't want to bring my laptop, and it stays in my bag unless I'm using it. Otherwise, I bring it out now and again for games or to read (I have the Kindle app installed, and it works great for that). For me, this Otterbox case is probably a case of "overkill": perhaps a little more case than I really need.

The basics:
This is a multi-part case: the two-piece inner plastic "shell" with a clear window over the screen, the outer silicone "slipcover" that hugs the back and sides of the plastic shell, and another hard plastic snap-on outer "cover" that includes a pop-up stand, that snaps onto the back of the silicone cover.

The good:
This will definitely protect your iPad Pro 9.7. The thing is built like body armor -- solid, form-fitting, not too difficult to install. The colors "damson purple" and "hibiscus pink" aren't too garish, either, and match the photos on the page here.

The concern(s): The only screen protection is the thin plastic "screen protector" -- that's all. I'm a little concerned about how protective it would be in an accident. It would have been really nice if they had designed the outer cover/stand to snap onto the FRONT of the case. I've tried it a few times, and it doesn't work. The corner "clips" get caught in the silicone slipcover so that it can't snap securely. It only fits securely onto the BACK of the case. Pity.

Also, it's VERY heavy. I realize that you don't get this level of protection without adding weight, so that's a trade-off that you either choose to live with or not.

Soooo ... bottom line: if you have klutzy tendencies, if you're looking for 5-star protection for your iPad Pro and you're willing to live with added weight, this might be a super option. If you're more like me -- light user, not of the klutzy persuasion -- this might a little more protection than you really need. For me, it rates 3 stars: "It's OK."

NOTEWORTHY FACTS:
--------------------------
* Solid build. The camera is about 1 lb.
* POE, so you only need an ethernet connection. No power adapter necessary. If you do not have a POE ethernet switch, you can use a power adapter (sold separately).
* If you do not have a dedicated NVR, you can simply use H.View's software. You download the smart client app onto your PC. You can get this software from their website.
* You can access via smartphone too via the AVIEW app, which is in the Google Play Store.
* Instructions are very good. They included several mini booklets for how to access via PC, via Smartphone, as well as a quick start.
* Though the instructions are very good. It did not touch upon the issue I had with the IP address. As a matter of fact, no tech product I've ever used have ever discussed this potential issue. As you may know, IP addresses will look something like this... 192.168.1.XXX. That's the pattern that he H.VIEW camera goes by. But my service provider goes by 192.168.254.XXX. So when you plug in the camera to your POE switch, it's never going to connect. The troubleshoot in the manual suggest changing a setting to DHCP. This doesn't solve the problem, the manual is still assuming your IP address follows the 192.168.1.XXX protocol. So if you have this issue, you simply need to login your router admin and find the IP address of the H.View camera. It will be under the name AUDEARA PTY. If the name isn't listed, you can always find the camera by the mac address. This will be on your box, as well as under the camera. Look for the same mac address in the admin, and use the IP address that's associated with that mac address. Go into the Smart Client software and modify the IP address and your camera will show up.

FINAL VERDICT:
-------------------
* This is a solid camera. But I must say the smartphone app is sort of unprofessional because all the different names is puzzling. The camera is H.View, the app for the PC is Smart Client, the app for the smartphone is AVIEW, and the company listed under the app is some dude name Jack Bobo. Does that sound trustworthy? If I want to download Alexa, the company listed will be Amazon. If I want to download Youtube, the company listed will be Google. If you want to be taken seriously, you need some more consistent branding that will inspire trust. It's a solid camera, but the company is a bit green. I'll rate this camera 4-Stars!

I haven't reviewed this sooner because, let's admit it: my rage at the design of the new MacBook Pro, which eliminated USB ports and rendered all my peripheral devices nonfunctional, interferes with thinking clearly about the system at all. But I've now had this hub gadget for about a year, willy nilly. I will say, then: It does what it says it will do.

It has three USB ports, two of Apple's annoying C-style ports, and a slot for my camera's memory card. They all work. Good.

When you plug it in, the thing fills or covers all the connections on that side of the computer. No big deal, I suppose, since it does provide the connections you need. It sticks out about an inch from the side of the computer, which makes it "in the way." Then, when you discover that you hate the accursed MacBook keyboard, whose weirdly sized, weirdly spaced, and weirdly designed keys make it impossible to type more than three words without inserting a slew of crazy typos, you go out and get a wireless keyboard. This device requires you to plug a wireless receiver doodad into your da**ed dongle, and IT now sticks out another inch and a half. So you have gadgetry -- unnecessary gadgetry, in any rational plane of existence -- jutting out from the side of your computer about three inches.

This is not the hub's fault, of course; it's Apple's fault. But the hub does have a little drawback: if you so much as jiggle the laptop or the table it's sitting on, the dongle jiggles loose from its connection. This disconnects the devices you're working with. So that amps up your infuriation at Apple's absurd design flaws, and that leaves you feeling even MORE stupid for having spent all that money on a new Mac when you could have spent three months of your time -- for free -- relearning the PC, purchased a PC for a lot less money, and been only about half as aggravated.

If I were to buy another USB hub, I'd look for one that would connect more firmly. Or at least it could come with a roll of duct tape so you could secure it in place.

After finally needing to retire my last phone with a headphone jack, it was time to try out some of these USBC to 3.5mm adapters. The good news is, it works really well and actually is small enough to leave attached to the end of my favorite set of wired headphones. You're not going to get audiophile quad-dac quality out of it like my old LG phones, but it will drive a normal pair of headphones just fine for music or videos.
HOWEVER, there are a couple of things to note:
1) It seems to support the audio out channels but not the microphone, if your headphones have one. You know how phone earbuds usually have an extra pin for the microphone on the tip (3 rings instead of 2)? I think this doesn't support that. I believe this jack is TRS instead of TRRS. Or even if it IS a TRRS, it's only telling my phone that the left and right audio channels are there. Which leads me to item #2:
2) It tells the phone a headset is connected even if it is not. And I think this also is related to #1, because it doesn't seem to care what's plugged into the other side of it, as soon you plug this adapter into your phone, even empty, the headphones icon shows up and all audio is routed out to the empty 3.5mm jack. Plug something in, you hear the sound. Unplug it, the sound goes nowhere. This is why I'm happy to leave it semi-permanently attached to my earphones, and just considering it an extension of them. You don't want to leave this attached to your phone with nothing plugged in.

In a nutshell, this is great if you want to listen to music. Not if you want to use a wired headset for phone calls.

Because the telescope requires assembly, I pulled out the instructions...and became very confused. While some of the parts looked similar to what was in the box, I quickly realized the instructions were for a completely different model. Even if these were the right instructions, the photographs provided were taken by a camera and not the clearest quality; good assembly instructions usually have computer-generated images or diagrams, not photographs taken by a camera. The rest of the instruction manual was a general guide on using telescopes, though a much better quick-start guide can be found easily online.

So, with some trial and error, and a lot more time than I anticipated building the telescope, I finally got it assembled. And just in time too, because the moon had just crossed the window of the room I build the telescope in, and the moon was in great view. Despite all that, it's super fun to use. It comes with decent eyepieces to play around with; I didn't know how much of a difference eyepieces can make. With this telescope, I was able to view details of the moon for the first time. It really is just a big ball of rock spinning around.

If you are seriously into photography a speedlight is a valuable asset that can help you get the lighting just right, which I have found to be particularly helpful when dealing with portrait shots. I have worked with other K&F Concept products and have had consistently good experiences with them so I expected the same from this speedlight. I have not been disappointed. I encountered a couple of minor speed bumps along the way, based largely on learning curve.

This is a sizeable device, and it has a bit of heft to it when the batteries are installed. Please make sure you have proper support for the camera when you are using this light as it can unbalance the camera and make it awkward to use. This is not specific to this particular speedlight but to speedlights in general.

First things first – this thing takes 4 AA batteries and that adds weight. The battery compartment is easily accessible and it is easy enough to install the batteries.

The controls on this light are very straightforward though knowing what the settings do is a different matter. If you do not know what slave mode is or how the settings relate to the zoom, you are going to find yourself frustrated. It took a little bit of research and some experimentation to get the hang of this light and I have found the best use for me is to use it in slave mode to supplement the lighting my the flash that came with my camera, though through the hot shoe I can install it on my camera.

Read the manual that comes with it. It will help a lot in learning how to use this light properly.

The light comes with a small stand so it can be set up independently from the camera and in that manner it can be used as a standalone flash. Turning on slave mode allows for positioning it so that it can add the right balance of light in reaction to the flash on the camera and as a result you can get very good backlighting.

The mode button on the back of this light allows for switching between modal settings and making adjustments, There are also 4 directional buttons that are used for making individual setting adjustments such as zoom. There is the on/off switch which toggles power but also toggles the backlight on the LCD display. Finally, there is a flash button that allows for activating the flash manually. The flash can be fired repeatedly in manual mode but seems to be on a 3-second recharge when not so.

The light has 90 degrees of freedom of movement so that it can be positioned as desired. I like the fact that the neck has angular measures on it for 45, 60 and 75 degrees,

Be aware that this speedlight is not universal and does not work on all cameras. It works fine with a Canon camera; my Samsung camera does not register the presence of this flash at all so to use it with my Samsung camera I have no choice but to use it in manual or slave mode.

This is a nice speedlight and it works well, It is not the fanciest or most expensive but it gets the basics down very well and it has not let me down. This is an affordable speedlight and it is good for the photographer who wants to learn how to improve their lighting techniques.

Once I signed into the box, I pretty much had to change my password, but then I had a world of options at my fingertips that I could change at my leisure. There were a few things I wanted to configure right away, and plenty of others I realized I wanted after doing some research. I still have plenty to learn and play with when I have time I want to spend on this.

I do believe you can use Cisco command line to configure these, but it also has a very familiar (to other consumer/business equipment) GUI that is intuitive to use. I will say, though, that the GUI it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. This switch can be a little slow to respond and therefore frustrating when changing multiple features in a row. I also have a 350 series 10 port switch that does NOT have that problem. I am not sure if it has more resources available or just has less to keep track of because of having fewer ports., but that might be a consideration if choosing between the 250 and 350 series. And if you use command line, you might not care at all...

Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

I am using this in my telecomm closet, which manages to keep nearly all the ports in my house hot. I'm using ports 25-27 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 350 series switch in my external cabinet, which connects my servers with multi-Gb links. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-The ports are counted strangely. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

There are a ton of features here, and even more on the 350 series. If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on the 350 (yet it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on a 10 port 350).

One thing I don't like is that on some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet (Well, you can also mount the switch backwards, if you consider that helpful). It would be better to have the option of recessing the switch an inch if you needed to. I also wish they could recess the power supply port on these things since - even with the heatsink on the back of this - the power cord is still the thing making this a tight fit in my closet.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Yes, I can absolutely imagine this to be a great line for a company to use, and I think I could even get a robust network up and running without too much stress or trouble. But there are plenty of other real-world applications for a home network as well: setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc. I love having these features at my disposal, even at home!

I'm somewhat particular about my music and my headphones and have specific things I look for. I'll try to touch on those items in this review.

Sound Quality: obviously most important. I look for solid bass (not boomy or hyped). And clear trembles (not sizzling or hyped). These headphones performed admirably on both counts. I have some expensive headphones that these compare favorably to. I also look for general clarity in vocals... nothing nasally or buried in the mix. Vocals are natural and enjoyable.

Comfort: okay, I have a big head (size xxl hat). So comfort is important to me. These headphones are adequate in that regard. I had to extend them fully, but at full extension they fit me properly and comfortably, sealing off around the ear. These headphones are advertised as an over the ear design, but with my big ears, they did not completely surround my ears as some studio monitors do, but they did cover my ears. The padding is decent and I was able to listen for about an hour before they became uncomfortable pressing on the perimeter of my ear.

Noise reduction: I'm not used to using this feature and wasn't sure how to test it, so I simply sat down next to an air cleaner I have in my home and tried turning noise reduction on and off to see what happened. There was definitely a reduction in the noise... mainly in the lower frequencies. It didnt completely eliminate the sound of the blowing air, but what was left was a thinned out version of the original noise. It was definitely an improvement... and with very little impact on the sound of the music I was listening to.

Wireless: pairing was pretty straightforward (I guess that's typical these days) and the wireless aspect suffered no dropouts anywhere in the room. Going up to a different floor in the house did cause dropouts, though. So I guess that's about the limit.

Overall, I was impressed with these headphones. Especially considering the price, they seem to do well. They come with a carry bag and needed cables. I expect I'll get some good use from these.

Long cord. The long cord is very important.

Setup.

I used the long cord to place it on the floor, next to my patio door.
I then set my TV to auto scan.
It gave me many more stations than my non amplified leaf antennae pulled in.
Every station was crystal clear.
However, that was not a convenient permanent location, so I then placed it behind the TV.
It was important to first place it in the best possible area, in my case against the patio door to identify all possible stations.

Issues.

After auto scan identified all possible stations, I moved the antenna to behind my entertainment center. I lost half the stations. But, the TV showed those station numbers, it just couldn't pull them in. I then placed it flat on top of the entertainment center. It improved the reception. I then slid it partially inside my TV wall mount hardware, flat against the wall. It gave me excellent reception on all identified stations.

My advice.

Take advantage of the long cord, move it next to a window even if it won't be left there. You can then place the antenna in more convenient locations, trying to get back to as many identified stations as possible.

Sometimes manufacturers will list these memory cards as having far more memory than they actually do. In this case, these are pretty close to accurate. Even the name brand cards hold a little less than advertised, because some space is wasted in formatting. Often the listed memory will appear to be accurate when you plug it in, and it will even appear to store that amount of information when you write to it, but when you go to access the data, it will be missing, because it actually holds much less!

I tested these by writing 7.5 GB of data to them, and then transferring that data from them to a new folder. The transferred data was complete and uncorrupted, which means that these cards do store what they say that they do.

The write speed is pretty slow, but if you're not using this for a purpose where write speed matters then it's a pretty good deal. I wouldn't recommend it for a video-camera for instance, but for transferring files and the like it will work just fine. The read speed was much faster than the write speed, so you should be able to play videos off of them without any issue.

I have never had an e-reader before. I used to read a TON, but then I grew up and life happened, so wanted to get back in to it.

I purchased both the Paperwhite and the Oasis. The Paperwhite seemed like a great device, but I could tell immediately how much more my eyes liked the larger screen on the Oasis along with the warmth feature. The warmth feature was the biggest factor for me, as it made it look much more like an actual page out of a book. I've included a picture of the Paperwhite (on the right) and Oasis (left), both set at the same brightness, but with the Oasis's warmth setting on. You can also see there is no white Kindle logo on the Oasis, which I found ever so slightly distracting on the Paperwhite. The quality of the screen on the Oasis is also much better than the Paperwhite - text is more clear and crisp. If you commute a lot or size is important to you, Paperwhite is definitely the way to go.

I was really overwhelmed with the Oasis at first, just because it was so new to me. I'm pretty good with new tech, but the whole environment was slightly overwhelming because it's not just as simple as getting a new device on a platform you're already used to (ie, Windows, Android, Apple, etc). Once I got past the learning curve, I started to actually like it a bit. However, the way the Kindle sorts and handles your books could be much better. You can organize things in to 'Collections', but it still doesn't feel like enough. I recommend looking up Calibre and going from there.

My biggest gripe is the ergonomics of the Oasis. Although it's not much heavier than the Paperwhite, it feels like it because of the shape of it. It just feels heavier because of the weight distribution towards the center, and is awkward to hold with that bump/excessive weight distribution that sticks out. I am a 5'9" woman with 'normal' sized hands, so I can't even imagine how this would be for someone with smaller hands. I bought a case immediately because the shell is ridiculously slippery, and in my opinion, a horrible choice of material for something you're going to hold for hours. Looks pretty, but not very functional for an e-reader. I bought the 'Ayotu Skin Touch Feeling Case', and it is awesome. I ordered a couple of others and this one stood out among all of them big time.

Last gripe is that the screen is pretty slow and laggy at times. I know it's an e-reader, but it's a very expensive one that doesn't do anything else (which to clarify I am absolutely fine with BUT, see next point), but at that price, it should really be perfect.

A positive feature of this that is nice is that you can flip the device around and the screen flips with you, so if you are right or left handed or just want to switch sides during reading, that is super helpful.

I do like it, but am considering whether or not I am going to keep it due to the ergonomics alone.

This is very similar to the Spider Monkey stand offered by Octa except that instead of a “tail” to hold the stand it has a rather unique clamp. Like the Spider Monkey it does take a few minutes to figure out how to use it (I would strongly recommend reading the brief, but well-written user guide before using this) but once mastered, you have a stand that can be positioned on pretty much anything.

As with the Spider Monkey version, the look and feel of the stand is excellent. Very solid build quality, and looks nice as well.

There are three parts: the jaws that hold the tablet; the clamp; and a short (about 4 inch) bendable bar that joins the two together.

The jaws are very well padded, which give it a good grip plus ensures the tablet they are gripping doesn’t get scratched. It’s a ratchet design – you press the release button which opens up the jaws, then ratchet them down so they close on to the tablet and hold it tight. It’s a universal design, so you can position the jaws so they don’t interfere with ports/buttons/etc. regardless of the brand of tablet you have.

My favorite feature is the clamp. It is also a ratchet-type design. That has a lot of advantages over the traditional spring clamp, most notably a very secure grasp of whatever you attach it to. I was able to clamp it on a table, a shelf edge, a pole – pretty much anything I tried to attach it to. It holds tight – I couldn’t get it to budge even when pulling on it with a decent amount of force. It only releases when you press the release tab. The grip surfaces have a thick pad to give it lots of grip without damaging the surface to which it is clamped.

The bar that joins the jaws to the clamp is thick, but bendy so you can position the tablet easily. It holds its position when bent without any wobble or drooping.

I tried this with the 7 inch Fire, the 8.9 inch Fire and a Nexus tablet. Each fit very well and secure. The max the jaws will open is about 7.5 inches but, since it rotates, you can grip pretty much any tablet either lengthwise (which is how I held the 7 inch Fire) or width wise (which is how I held the 8.9 inch Fire). There’s a locking ring on the collar so you can lock the tablet from rotating should you want to.

The downsides are the same as with the Spider Monkey. There is a brief learning curve to get the hang of it. The ratchet teeth for the clamp are made of plastic, which give me a bit of concern about longevity. It’s working fine now, but metal teeth would have been nice to have. Lastly, the release button for the jaws can be hard to find since it’s a monochrome black color scheme.

The first board I got was bad. It was plagued with "WHEA uncorrectable error" BSOD's and random restarts from day one. After over 100 hours of troubleshooting the BSOD crashes graduated to a never ending BSOD loop.

I booted into a Windows 10 install USB drive and my C: drive that was in the M.2_3 port on the rear of the motherboard wasn't even being detected. I formatted a different NVMe that I had installed in the DIMM.2 expansion card, installed Windows on that drive, and never had a BSOD since.

The NVMe I had installed in the rear M.2_3 slot would sometimes show up in disk management but would always end up disappearing eventually.

After determining that it was most likely something related to the M.2_3 port on the rear, I ordered a replacement. After installing the new motherboard and updating the bios, everything is running perfect just as it was before. Except now the NVMe drive that I have in the rear M.2_3 port doesn't keep disappearing.

Overall, the board is rock solid now that I've actually got a fully functioning unit. The BSOD error I was getting can be caused by a number of things so finding out what was causing all the crashes was a nightmare. I was having problems with fan control when I first built the PC but soon after ASUS released a Bios update and the problems went away so that's a non issue now.

This board was 2-star rating worthy for the first couple weeks of use. I've only read about boards that are bad right out of the box. Now I can confirm that it happens. Thankfully I've got a seemingly 5-star motherboard. Won't be able to get those 100+ hours of life back that I spent troubleshooting though so I'm docking a star for quality control.

I own two rabbit ear antennas:
- GE Model TV94713 VHF/UHF/FM
- RCA ANT111 Television - Radio - Indoor - FM - VHF - UHF

I had replaced my GE Model on one 19" Vizio HDTV with a Mohu Leaf Ultimate Amplified Indoor HDTV Antenna which turned out to be a superb upgrade. Therefore, when this antenna came up for review, I decided to replace my RCA set-top on my other 19" Vizio HDTV for this non-amplified Amazon Basics HDTV antenna.

I live in northwestern NJ around 30 miles from NYC. In this area, my RCA gave me around 45 channels but in order to get those channels, I had to constantly adjust the antenna to bring in some stations. After running the automatic channel scan, this Amazon Basics Antenna gives me 44 channels. In fact, a few of the channels I now receive appear to be different than the ones I received before because I do not recognize the call letters.

The PROS are:

- Installation was so simple. I attached the coax cable on the antenna to the antenna port on the back of my HDTV. Since the coax cable is very long, I was able to run the cable up the wall and across a shelf and then let it hang on the other side.

- I no longer have to adjust the antenna to bring in the channels.

- The antenna is like a flat piece of cardboard which I can tape up if I want to. Two double-side 3M Command Brand Strips are provided for this purpose. Personally I would not use this because if I want to adjust the reception, I'd have to remove the antenna from its permanent location.

- The instructions are easy to understand.

The CONS are:

- The user pamphlet says to run a channel scan every month after the initial scan; however, the quick start guide says to run a scan every time you re-position the antenna after the initial scan. Let's just say, I won't be doing this unless I have problems with receiving a particular channel.

- The one big negative for me is that the picture quality is not as vibrant as with the RCA rabbit-ear antenna I used previously. I do realize this is not an amplified antenna, but I did expect the picture quality to be equivalent to the RCA rabbit-ear I replaced and it is not. The colors appear to be washed out for most channels and the reception is closer on those channels to a "dot pixel" image rather than a vibrant image. For this reason, I consider this antenna to be just okay. However, I will continue to use this over my RCA because I don't have to adjust this antenna to get all the channels I sometimes view.

Nevertheless, the current low price of $20.24 makes this a respectable choice if money is an issue. However, if a vibrant picture quality is most important, I would recommend looking into a Mohu Leaf Ultimate Amplified Indoor HDTV Antenna (or equivalent) even though the cost is a little over three times the price.

Also, it seems antennas for some are hit or miss depending on the area one lives in. The Amazon Basics user pamphlet recommends you check for a list of channels available in your area. I put the URL in the comments section for those who are interested.

I really like this GPS sports watch so far. Garmin makes a huge range of sports watches. This vivoactive HR is one of their lower priced GPS watches. It doesn't have the more advanced sports training features or build quality of the more expensive Garmin Fenix and Forerunner watches. However, for this price, you do get GPS and smartwatch features in addition to basic fitness tracking.

I tried the GPS mode on a 3-hour bike ride, running my dedicated bicycle computer at the same time. Distance calculations of the 2 units were less than 1 mile different, which I think is very good for small portable units like this. Current speed was always about the same, though looking at the watch to see your speed while riding is kind of difficult, especially compared to the big display on my handlebar-mounted bike computer. You can mount the watch on your bicycle handlebar, but that would of course disable the heart rate tracking feature of the watch. The wrist-based heart rate monitor is not as accurate as a chest-strap heart rate monitor, with a slower response time that is very apparent during interval training (short bursts of high-intensity effort), but you can connect an ANT+ HR monitor to this watch to improve accuracy.

GPS mode has an advertised battery life of 16 hours, which I think is really terrific for a gadget of this size. My 3 hour bike ride burned about 20% of the battery on the vivo, so 16 hours of GPS time is plausible. Garmin also advertises 8 days of battery life with the GPS turned off, but realistically, who buys a $250 GPS watch and never turns on the GPS? Still, I expect to get in at least a couple of long bike rides or several runs before having to recharge this watch. Recharging is very quick using the USB charging cradle included with the watch. Because battery life is so good, you don't need a spare charger for your office like you might need with the Apple smartwatch.

If you have a (free) Garmin account, you can upload your daily activity to the Garmin server so you can review it on their website afterwards. This is useful for tracking your fitness progress (speed, distance, etc) over time.

The smartwatch features are pretty basic (compared to dedicated smartwatches from Apple or Google), showing phone call caller-ID and copying notifications from your smartphone (via Bluetooth) and displaying them on the watch. If you like checking your notifications quickly and don't want to pull your phone out every time it beeps, getting them on your watch is great. If I'm jogging or in a business meeting or at dinner but am expecting an important message, I can just glance at the watch and quickly ignore it if it isn't important. I have my notifications for high-priority emails, SMS, and a couple of messaging apps synced with my phone. This seems to work mostly flawlessly with my Samsung smartphone. Occasionally, the notifications will stop working but restarting my phone fixes that. I don't know if that is a problem with the phone's base software or with the Garmin app that runs on my phone. The Garmin app that runs on your smartphone lets you pick which app's notifications to show on the watch. I do not know how this works with Apple phones. There are some other smartwatch apps like weather forecasts and calendar, but I'm not sure if scrolling through these on your small watch face is really easier than pulling out your phone to view the app on the larger screen there.

If you're comparing this Garmin watch to an Apple smartwatch, yes Apple has a lot more apps, but Garmin has an 8 day battery life compared to less than 1 day for Apple. Personally, battery life is more valuable to me since there are not yet any killer apps for the Apple watch. Having a dead watch because you forgot to charge it the night before is not fun. Also, the Garmin watch has a built-in GPS, while the Apple watch does not. This means you can record a bike ride or run carrying only the watch, not your phone as well.

Garmin also has basic fitness tracking features like resting heart rate, sleep tracking, intensive exercise tracking, step counting, etc. If you're active enough to want to spend money a GPS sports watch (instead of a cheap fitness band), I don't think the step counting is going to be interesting to you. I bike or run at least 10 hours every week of the year and steps have no interest to me. Resting heart rate is an indicator of your health and fitness and I'm looking forward to tracking that. Intensive exercise tracking may also be useful if you tend to slack off during your exercise. Sleep tracking is reportedly not too accurate on this watch (it can't tell if you're really sleeping or reading a book in bed), but that isn't something that greatly interests me.

On the subjective side, this chunky plastic rectangular watch does look like a fitness tracker rather than a real watch. The much better looking Garmin Fenix looks like something you could wear to the office, but this watch maybe not. At least the vivoactive has a very comfortable wristband that should fit well on a range of wrist sizes.

Again, this is one of Garmin's cheaper GPS watches. I think the features and performance are great for this price point, but if you're involved in hard core training program, you should definitely look at the features of some of Garmin's better GPS watches.

I would have given this watch 5 stars for functionality and value for the price if it was better looking, but Garmin seems to have made it intentionally ugly in try to upsell you on their better looking and more expensive Fenix and Forerunner watches.

I want to preface this review with a quick note; I returned mine shortly after receiving. This had everything to do with the feature set that I was looking for and not with the quality or performance of the item.

Within the price range that this dashcam is offered, this is a fully-featured and functional dashcam. I did a considerable amount of research about several of the more affordable offerings and determined that the LEVIN dash cam seemed to satisfy and could be a solid investment.

The product pictures appear to be taken at an angle that make the item appear to be much bigger and bulkier than in hand. In reality, the LEVIN Dash Cam is slender, small, and discrete. The installation is not dissimilar to other models and is very quick and easy.

I don't want to comment on the actual performance because I had a very limited experience with the item. But according to the research I did while shopping for a dashcam, the image quality and video performance was satisfactory if not very good. Nevertheless, consider this just a vicarious assessment.

The physical buttons and layout are good. The button click action is substantial and assured and the buttons themselves are easy to find and depress. Unlike the dashcam I upgraded to, finding a button doesn't necessarily require direct sight as the button layout allows for easy tactile navigation of the control panel. My upgrade item however has a touchscreen with no physical queues as to where specific controls are located.

Lastly, the reason why I returned it... no wifi. My primary reason for investing in a dashcam was an incident that my cousin had. His dashcam had captured a traffic accident in which he was not at fault. The other driver of course dishonestly tried to establish fault by my cousin, who promptly downloaded the related video content to his phone, showed it to the responding traffic officer and sent copies to both the reporting officer and his insurance company. While the content can easily be obtained from the onboard storage, the ability to share and view that content on the fly allowed my cousin to establish non-fault and include it as part of the LEO's official incident report. Wifi is the feature that made this possible and because of my cousin's experience, it's one that I didn't want to miss. I do wish however that my new dashcam had the capacitor feature that the LEVIN has.

Aside from lacking the wifi feature, this dashcam is everything I would need it to be. It's also more affordable that most given its feature set. Even if you were to upgrade at a later point, I don't think you can go wrong with this one. Unless price is not an object, if so look to this model as a good pattern for the kinds of features you'll want in a more expensive model.

Bottom line: This is a lot of fun! It’s perfect for hobby work when you need to take a magnified photo that’s beyond what you could do with a macro lens. Setup and use is straightforward, but there are some limitations. Still, a great value for the price point.

Full review: This provides the ability to take magnified photos or videos in a self-contained, easy to use unit. The build quality is pretty good considering the price. There is some wobble in the support bar, and the focusing knobs are not high-end in their operation, but overall, I found it delivered more than I expected at the price point it’s selling for.

It only took me a couple of minutes to assemble the hardware (no tools are needed). The software loaded quickly and easily from the included DVD. The software is very straightforward to use – there’s a limited set of options which are all pretty much self-explanatory. There’s also a decent user guide on the CD as a PDF file.

The camera plugs into a USB port to communicate with the software plus pull power for the LED lights. No external power is needed.

I had some problems running the software on an XP machine. Most of the time it worked fine, but it would occasionally crash, usually after snapping a series of photos. Clearing the crash required unplugging the camera from the USB port and plugging it in again.

I then loaded it on a Win 7 machine and had no problems. My XP machine is pretty old, so it may be a PC hardware issue rather than an actual problem with XP. In any case, it was smooth sailing on Win 7.

The first step that you need to do is to calibrate the unit using the included calibration scale. That was a bit challenging, and the instructions could have been a bit better. Calibration is not essential, however, unless you want to ensure your magnification settings are accurate. If you’re just looking to use this as an easy macro camera, then calibration is not as important.

I had no problems snapping photos, which can be done using a trigger on the USB cable or by selecting the photo icon on screen. You can also select from four resolution modes (ranging from 1.3M to 5M).

The software also has a pretty decent set of annotation tools. The menu comes up when you double click on a photo, and allows you to add text, lines, arrows, freehand drawing, etc. It’s very basic, but perfectly fine (and fast) for pointing out a feature in an photo without having to use something such as Photoshop.

There are some limitations. The LED lights are OK, but not great. I found I got far better photos using an auxiliary light in addition to (or in place of) the built-in LED lights. The built in lights are not as bright as they could be, have a limited light field, and have some hot spots that can impact photo quality.

There’s also some wobble in the frame. Not a lot, but enough that you need to be careful not to knock the unit out of focus at high magnifications. The focus controls (there’s a course and a fine focus control) are OK in terms of smoothness, but certainly not what I would call high-end.

While this would not serve the needs of highly exacting, precision work, it is a fantastic help for hobby work. I use it to take photos of various RBA builds, and it's worlds easier (and better) than using a macro lens. It delivers a lot of value for the price, and I would highly recommend it.

I've used this touchpad off and on at work over the last few weeks. I really tried to like it, but it just doesn't work well enough for it to be my main pointing device. Here are the things that are issues for me:

* Tracking speed is very different from my mouse, which is a standard Dell mouse. This wouldn't be an issue if the touchpad could replace my mouse, but it really can't. So I'm switching back and forth between the touchpad and the mouse for different tasks. And I have to visit the Mouse Control Panel in between to change the tracking speed. This just takes way too much time.
* It's not as precise as my mouse (my standard Dell mouse). So it just always feels a bit clumsy.
* As other reviewers have noted, there's a margin of dead space around the trackpad, but no tactile way to sense this area. So I'm always getting to the edge without knowing, except seeing that the mouse suddenly stops moving. This is a continual annoyance.
* Sometimes the responsiveness isn't quite there -- I think maybe this is because it's wireless. Not sure. But I've never had this problem at all with my wired mouse.
* The multitouch gesture for scrolling does work, but it doesn't work well. It works poorly enough for me to prefer the scroll bar. The track wheel on my standard wired mouse is much better.

There are some good points:
* On-off switch on the underside is easy to see and use.
* Stays put on my desk -- doesn't slide around.
* Buttons are pretty easy to operate, with just the right amount of resistance.
* USB dongle is tiny, and it can stay in my laptop all the time.
* Other reviewers have commented that the plastic surface doesn't "glide" as well as other trackpads. But that part works fine for me.

It's also very useful to get my iPad up off the counter in case I spill something too.

This is a very well made stand that useful and convenient for home, school, or office use though, so I'd gladly recommend it for those uses.

The images in the Marine model merged effortless. In the Commander XP, I have difficulty merging the images. They're obviously badly out of collimation. I don't care to fix this myself on binos in this price range.

I evaluated the real and apparent fields of view as well as the sharpness near the edge of the field.

In the Marine model, the real field of view is reasonably wide but apparent field is quite narrow. It's not bad but it's not a spectacular vista either. In the Commander XP, the real FOV is only barely perceptibly wider. Steiner's website lists the specifications. The apparent field is about the same. The almost indiscernable extra width of real FOV does not contribute much to the value for triple the price.

On the Marine model, I put Sirius and Jupiter in the center of the field. They look nice. Moving the binoculars so that the objects were farther from the center of the field I could see the image degraded about half-way to the edge of the field of view. Near the very edge, the image was appalling. Much more than half-way out of the center of the field of view, the star or planet turns from a bright point to just a smear. Near the very edge it's a dim smudge. I tried the same with the Commander XP. It was every bit as bad.

Are the XP's better on dim objects? The optics are supposed to transmit 96% light compared to the Commander V's 95% and the Marine's 90%. I saw very little difference on dim objects like the Orion nebula or the background of the Pleides or Jupiter's moons. Again, I can't see the justification for triple the price.

Both have generious eye-relief, 20mm for the Marine and 22mm for these XP's. They also have the same weight and dimensions. They're heavy but still reasonable if you're wearing a thick coat to pad your chest and a harness to keep them from swinging all over if you're moving. Also, at 7x they're reasonable for handholding. For me, 7x50 is about the limit for handholding. Heavier or higher power would be too shakey. 6x56 might be nicer if they were more common.

Where the XP is clearly better is with small details like the click-loc strap attachments (for use with Steiner straps and harnesses only), the better eyepiece covers, lens covers, focuser grips, shading eye-cups, and various doo-dads that come in the case. It comes with a flotation strap which the Marine doesn't, but I would still rather prefer a harness which neither comes with.

Nerd Alert - I am a nerd at heart and utilize geek speak way too often. I try to remember that the Amazon audience contains friends, family, and strangers that may or may not know IT.

PROS:
* Feature Rich -
The ZyXEL is 1/2 the price of the comparable Cisco device but it has a much more feature rich set of wireless capabilities. It supports WPS, allowing for easy setup. It supports WDS, allowing you to configure a network that allows you to carry your laptop from room to room in a large house without sacrificing much speed if setup correctly. It can access as a repeater if needed.

* Cabling -
The ZyXEL includes the power supply and a network cable (CAT-5). It supports a standard called MDI/MDIX, which means that you won't need a crossover cable if you connect it to a switch.
* Wireless Distribution Service -
You can make this part of your existing network using WDS, or Wireless Distribution Service, or simply configure it as an access point. I just removed two old Linksys routers from being WDS nodes since replacing my old Actiontec 802.11a/b/g with an Actiontec 802.11b/g/n wireless router. Eventually I will get around to using the ONI port and setting up a network with DD-WRT

CONS:
* LAN ports on the back are are 10/100 -
While the router notes that it supports connection speeds up to 300MbPS it only has two (2) 10MbPS/100MbPS RJ-45 (LAN) connections. Technically you may never truly realize the full throughput available with this device. This is not unlike other wireless access points, such as the Cisco WET610N (single 10/100) or the Cisco WES610N (quad port 10/100 for $10 more). I did what any good geek would do; used it as an excuse to purchase an 8-port Netgear 10/100/1000 switch to replace my 5-port 10/100 switch in my office/lab with the computers and Hyper-V lab systems. I am going to use the Cisco product downstairs with my home server and VMWare ESXi box.

* Setup may be difficult for the average home user -
I most certainly RTFM'd and reading the manual helped. It did take a quick configuration of my network card in order to even get to the point I could setup the device.
The Cisco devices use an APIPA address, which makes setup easier. Why? APIPA is that 169.254.#.# address that your computer gets when it connects to a network that doesn't give out addresses. This allows you to easily setup the Cisco WES610N.

I normally think of storage media and batteries when I think of Maxell. That said, this is my second pair of Maxell headphones. My first pair is an ANC set that isn’t perfect, but they’re far and away better than I would ever have expected. These phones are not ANC phones, they’re just wireless listening phones. I was hopeful that they would be as good as my ANC phones in terms of sound quality, and Maxell has not disappointed me. They’re not perfect but they’re better than you can reasonably expect from the asking price.

Up front, let me say that I am not a big fan of on-ear headphones, and these fall into that category. I prefer an over-the-ear phone which to me is more comfortable. These aren’t bad for on-ear phones. This comes down to preference. If you are cool with on-ear phones, these will work for you, but if you have to have over-ear phones then you should consider other options.

The pads are soft enough, though they aren’t super cushy like some others I have used.

Being Bluetooth phones I immediately connected them to my phone. The connection went off without a hitch, though the phone was slower to find these than I had hoped. Once connected, they have been stable and reconnecting is much faster.

The real test is the sound profile. On my ANC phones, Maxell worked a miracle and got the sound profile nearly perfect even when the noise canceling is turned on. With these phones, the sound profile is not precise but it’s very balanced and better than average. The bass is strong but not throbbing like most headphones made these days. I like bass, but I don’t appreciate the insistence on pumping it so heavily that it gives me a headache. The midrange is full and music sounds like it has some depth without sounding like it’s playing from the bottom of a well. The highs are bright and clear, though on specific frequency ranges there is the slightest hint of distortion if you really look for it (and since I’m reviewing these, I went looking for it).

I cranked up the music as high as I could, and there was only a hint of distortion in the highs. And I had a headache when I was done.

Build-wise, these are not too bad. I would not pack them in a gym bag or anything like that, but these should work fine for a long while as long as they’re cared for properly. There’s enough flex in them to make them durable enough to survive some rough handling, but at the end of the day they’re primarily plastic - a drop from the right height or being crushed in a book bag will break them.

These phones are under $50 as I write this. What’s really distressing is that I have phones that are north of $200 that do not sound as good as these. Maxell knows how to make a good headphone that competes well with more expensive phones - I have two very different pairs to prove it. It begs the question - why are they only making budget headphones?

I would rate these slightly lower if the asking price were above the $50 mark. But, at the asking price you’d be hard-pressed to find headphones that sound better.

NOTE: This review is written for the Small, Bluetooth edition.

I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

This thing is great! We already have a hard-wired security system in place including motion detectors. That said, if the power goes off for more than a couple of days or so our back-up battery is drained. So having these type of motion detectors that run off of 3 AAA batteries gives me a better feeling about security around the house. No, these do not automatically call the police when they are set off, but an ear-piercing shrill alarm is emitted that should cause most intruders (unless totally deaf), to change their minds and leave immediately.

These are very simple to install and set a 4 digit numeric password. I have ours set up facing the opposite direction of our other motion detector downstairs. The alarm will actually activate after 30 seconds upon detecting motion. I guess that's good or bad depending on how you look at it. 30 seconds is a long time to give someone access throughout your home and by the time the alarm goes off the intruder may have gone totally elsewhere in your home. But, it will give you a warning and let you get ready to do what might need to be done to protect yourself.

I had to write myself a note to remember to disable it when I go downstairs because I tend to forget it's there and it's scared the you-know-what out of me a couple of times. 30 seconds is more than enough time to disable it.

Installation is easy. It comes with all you need (except tools of course) and you can mount it at different angles as it has a swivel to let you adjust it wherever you think it needs to face. It works great in the dark so if you have pets that prowl around at night you might need to re-think your plans on how to use this alarm.

Overall, this is a pretty neat device for giving you a bit of piece of mind about your homestead and especially if you are on a budget. As I said earlier, I use these type of alarm systems as a supplement to our whole-house system that's hard wired to a monitoring company, but I l really like the extra monitoring in case of a prolonged power failure.

If there is one thing I love, it is a “transformer” type of gadget. Well, this little emergency radio is all that, and so much more. Please keep in mind that my review only reflects the use of the radio during non emergency situations. I spent just under two years living in the Great Smoky Mountains caring for a sick, elderly person. We were constantly losing our electric power, so this type of radio became a high priority item. The person for whom I was caring already had one, so that is the only one that I can compare this one to. The radio I am to review today came in a cardboard box titled, “Libovgogo Multifunctional Radio” Inside the box was a very tightly packed radio inside a thin plastic casing and cellophane bag. Within the plastic casing, there was the radio in its box, and extras hidden in little nooks in the flimsy plastic tray. Among the components out of the cardboard box were: a USB charging cable, a spring buckle, a special reset needle, and what appeared to be some sort of vice or clamp. There was also the owners manuel, and additional literature explaining what the additional items outside of the box were to be used for. I then read the manuel, and put this radio through it’s paces. The owner’s manuel identifies my new radio:”emergency radio DF-557/DF-580” According to the enclosed literature, this is the only radio offered with WB/NOAA capacity. The radio itself is made with a hard red plastic casing and black speakers. It features a hand crank, a USB cable, and a solar panel as ways to charge the radio. I tried all three methods, and I can tell you: try to charge vis a vis cable or solar if you can! In the literature, it states that charging with the hand crank will take several more HOURS than the other options! You must have the radio turned off to charge. A little red light goes on when it needs more of a charge, and the light turns green when it is done charging. For the most part, everything worked more or less the way the manuel said it would, with one exception being the SOS siren, which is LOUD. Despite what the literature stated, my radio SOS siren was turned off by quickly pressing the SOS button and releasing very quickly as well. To turn on the siren, press and hold the SOS button. I was amazed at how powerful the reading light was; which can be accessed by raising the solar panel. Equally impressive is the sound quality and volume! This dainty little radio can really belt out loud and succinct sound, especially when you raise the antenna. The sound is so good, in my opinion, that I opt to play this radio instead of my smart devices for enjoyment, and can’t help but notice it sounds just as good as my husband and my son’s speakers. Other added features include a built in flashlight, AM/FM radio, Blue tooth cell phone/device emergency charging, and TF capabilities. It also includes a clamp to attach to a tripod or bike, and a part to attach the radio to your purse or murse.

Heat is the main killer of computers and computer equipment so keeping a system cool and ventilated is a big deal, especially when involving systems that see heavy use. Laptops are just as vulnerable as larger servers and require the same precautions. One of the main solutions for heat dissipation and ventilation for laptops is a chill pad (a fan-based platform that moves air under the system) and this one by AMNIE has been outstanding. I have been using it for about two weeks on my personal system and likely will swap it over to the system in the house that sees the heaviest use.

This is a good-sized pad, able to comfortably handle laptops up to 17”. It has a total of 4 larger fans that move some serious amounts of air, and fans are paired two and two between a pair of switches. The frame is painted metal mesh and offers good support to the laptop it holds.

The switches that control the fans are dial controls and they provide variable fan speeds for each pair of fans they control. There are no graduations so you can set the speed anywhere within the range to suit you, though having that much control is probably not all that necessary. The fans run very quiet but on the highest speed setting really move the air. When maxed out and all four fans running at top speed the fans blew cooler air from between the frame and the laptop, telling me I had the speed up much higher than needed. For my particular system under my typical use load, it seems I only need to turn them on about half way.

I have worked with some chill pads that have flaws in either the fans or the bearings and they make awful amounts of noise. So far, the only noise this pad makes is a low-frequency hum. It is quiet enough that even with lower-end noise canceling headphones I can cancel out the noise completely. This pad is not silent even on the low end of fan speed but it is very quiet all the way through the range of speeds. I have been able to leave the fans on full speed all night and sleep through the sound.

I have not measured the temperature difference between when the fans are on vs. when they are not, but I have noticed that the internal fan does not kick in as frequently when doing video rendering as when the fans are off. It does turn on and it still hits high speed on occasion but it is noticeably less frequently.

This is an excellent chill pad for laptops and so far it has worked out exceptionally well for me. It is quiet, it moves a lot of air and my laptop’s internal fan does not kick in as high as often. Because there is a system in the house that is much more frequently used for gaming, I will be moving this pad to that laptop instead and will use the other pad for myself.
