Summary: The Matchstick address what is for me the biggest shortfall of the Fire: sound quality. The docking system provides MUCH better sound than the built-in speakers, and bundles that with some useful features. However, these pluses are countered by a remote with limited functionality and a balky on/off switch.

Main review: I was getting really frustrated trying to find a docking system for my Fire. I'd see all these great systems but they were only for the iPod, iPhone or iPad. I have been using an Altec Lansing iM227 Orbit portable speaker, but that didn't provide the functionality I wanted So, I was really looking forward to trying out the Matchstick when I was offered a system by the manufacturer to review.

This is a docking station for the Fire that provides dual speakers. The dock rotates so you can use the Fire in portrait or landscape mode. It charges the Fire when it is docked.

There's a lot to like about this. The overall design is nice. Nothing fancy, with lines that blend well with the clean design of the Fire. Unfortunately, the speakers are covered in a rather cheap feeling fabric. I like that it's a simple black-on-black color scheme, but better quality cloth would have been nice.

The power cord has a manageable "wall wart" on the end that is not too bad to deal with. The power cord could have been a bit longer - it's about 4.5 feet, which can be a problem if you want to use this on a shelf.

The dock charges the Fire while it is in place, but you can also run the Matchstick off of a battery. Battery power is a nice touch since it allows for portability. The catch is that you have to buy the battery separately -- it is a proprietary design. While I don't begrudge anyone from making a profit, it would have been nice if you could use standard size rechargeable batteries such as Eneloops. A battery pack was not included in my review model, so I can't speak to the battery capabilities.

The Fire slides into the dock and connects with the Matchstick for power and audio. There is a button on the Matchstick that allows you to turn the Fire on and off. It's a simple plastic peg that presses against the Fire's power button. I like the simplicity of the approach, but the execution could have been better. The peg is a wee bit too short (or perhaps just misaligned) so that you have to press REALLY hard to get it to turn the Fire on or off. Most times I found it easier to pop the Fire out the doc and press the power button myself. VERY annoying!

I was really looking forward to the remote since I often use the Fire at my desk, and it would be great to be able to control the Fire without touching it since it's out of easy reach. But, I found that the remote was too basic to be of much help.

On the plus side the remote is small -- about 1/4 thick and about 1.5 by 3.5 inches. The buttons allow for bass up/down, treble up/down, volume, mute and power. You can also use it to reset the bass/treble to "normal" and change input source (more on that later).

What is sorely missing is a track skip and a pause. So, the remote turns out to have very little use since I have to touch the screen to pause, change tracks, etc. Since the remote does not take the place of those key needs, you end up wondering why it's there at all. After a short while I stopped using it and just touched the screen or used the volume controls on the docking station.

The speakers perform very well at "soft-normal" levels (such as watching a movie at your desk at work), and are quite respectable at "loud-normal" volume (e.g., loud enough to make it difficult to converse with someone next to you, but not so loud that you can't hear the phone ring). It's better suited to reproducing dialog than music.

Excellent bass considering that it uses two 3-inch full-range speakers, but it gets boomy quickly at loud volumes. The spec's say 16 watts but this guy does not like to get pushed much when it comes to volume. It will get real ugly real quick.

But that's OK. The speakers are not designed to be audiophile quality or provide for room-filling sound for a large party. They are meant to produce better sound than what you get out of the Fire, and it does that admirably. Will your 16 year old son call them "wimpy"? Probably.

Still, they are a VAST improvement over the internal speakers and are much better than any of the single-speaker options I've tried (such as the Altec Lansing, the iHome and others). They won't compare at all to the quality of sound from some of the better multimedia speakers in the $70+ range (such as the GigaWorks T20 or T40), but that's the price you pay to gain the convenience of a dock.

There is an aux port on the back of the Matchstick that you can use to plug in a MP3 player (or anything else that will work with a 3.5 inch plug). Very nice feature since I have some music on various devices that I have not moved to the Fire. They also include a M/M 3.5 inch cable. Works well, although the port is hard to access. You'll find it easier to leave the M/M cable attached.

In summary, there are some clear strengths to this. It would be a 5-star product if it were priced in the $60 range, but at the $100'ish point some of the misses (especially the power button) are not acceptable. 3.5 stars, rounded down to 3 since the power button is such an annoying flaw.

As an old, retired guy, I find technology still significantly impacting my daily life in two ways. The first is that I spend a lot of time every day online - either gaming in my favorite MMO or binge watching the various streaming services. The second way is that I keep in touch with my far-flung network of family and friends via social media. Now, my desktop pc handles the first of those two very nicely. The problem is that I can get immersed for hours in gaming or in a good streaming show. Social media notifications break that immersion, causing me to move away from whatever I was doing to see what the latest notice was about. If I don't, it could be quite a while before I get around to checking my social media and responding to the messages there.

This is where a tablet comes in. I figured it would be nice to have a tablet that quietly beeped new notifications and allowed me to just glance over at the latest notice to see if it needed a quick response or not. Little did I know how hard it would be to find a low end tablet capable of that simple task. This is the fourth tablet I've tried and the first one which could do that one simple thing for me. The other low end tablets quickly crashed and burned for a variety of reasons. This is the first that actually continued to work after the first few days, giving me the notifications I wanted and that I could check out at a glance.

There are some issues with this tablet that folks should be aware of. The sound is tinny enough that I wouldn't listen to music or audiobooks on this thing. The visual quality is sufficient for modern movies and tv shows but vintage ones do look a bit fuzzy. The charge doesn't last quite as long as I'd like it to. The tablet needs to be charged twice a day, even when it's just sitting there beeping when a text message or email comes in. Charging once a day would be nicer but it is what it is. Still, this is the first low end tablet of four I've tried that actually does the simple task I want it to do. So for that, I have to give it a solid 4 star rating.

These are telescopic glasses – basically a set of binoculars that you wear. Although they may look like the magnifying optics that help with close-up work, they are not. These are for distance vision. It’s a good product if you want to have distance vision but do not want to have to hold a pair of binoculars. However, that convenience comes at a cost: a narrow field of view.

The build quality is pretty good for the price point. The frame is sturdy and doesn’t twist or bend in use. The nose pads and arms are comfortable to wear. It has enough weight that you know you’re wearing it, but I can wear it for extended periods without anything cutting into my nose or face. That being said, I do wish it had spring-loaded hinges on the arms. That would provide for an additional measure of adjustability and comfort.

The optics are also very well done. I can’t tell for sure if the lenses are plastic or glass, but it performs at such a good level in terms of clarity that I would be surprised if it were not glass. The focal action of the lens is also very well done, with smooth, fluid operation to adjust the focus. Each lens can be adjusted independently.

The kit comes with a lot of extras. There’s a set of rubber eye cups to help block side light and aid in comfort, an extra set of nose pads, a cleaning cloth, a pretty nice case with foam cutouts for all the items, and a set of five magnifying lenses that screw on to the main lenses. The latter is where the first problem crops up. You get five different magnification (2,3,4,5, and 6) but only ONE of each. Thus, if you want to use them, you’re limited to using just one eye. It would have been more useful to have a smaller set of adapters and get TWO of each mag power. As it is, the mag attachments have very limited use. I tried them out, and then didn’t use them again.

One item it lacks is an instruction guide. It does have one, but it is all in Chinese. Not much help for me!

The other issue is the field of vision. It’s narrow – very narrow. You’re dealing with tunnel vision when wearing these. It gets way worse when using the mag attachments.

Lastly, you can’t wear these at the same time as regular glasses. I’m a glasses wearer, and it got tiresome having to switch between these and regular glasses. Regular binoculars, in contrast, can easily be used when wearing glasses.

It’s hard to come up with an overall rating for these. The build quality and optics are easily 5 star worthy given the price point. The ease of use (if you don’t wear glasses) and comfort are 4 to 5 star worthy. The mag attachments are 1 star, and the field of vision offered is 3 stars. I’ll average those together and give it 4 stars. It’s a good product if you want to have distance vision but not have to hold a pair of binoculars, but will be out-performed by even a low-end pair of binoculars.

One star until I get this thing running. I've provisioned multiple Raspberry Pis since the original model. This thing... so far no joy.

Part of the problem is the chaotic Libre Computer website, which is a marvel of broken links and broken promises. For example, the preferred SD card burner application is shown as available for Mac, Linux and Windows, but when you get to the actual download page it's Windows-only. Oh, there's a series of links that you can wade through (mislabeled Google Drive but actually leading to a Baidu page) that yields to a page in Chinese that suggests there's a macOS download, but clicking through that yields a download of a Baidu NetDisk, a Dropbox-wannabe that I would really not want to install on my computer! Meanwhile the "official" download button yields an error.

Fortunately there's a second application, Etcher, which works well on my Mac. It does, however, require that you download the firmware separately. No problem, there's a link for that, right? ...Except that Etcher won't recognize the download. Etcher requires certain file extensions and the download doesn't have any of them. Appending .img to the filename let Etcher proceed, but attempting to boot the Renegade using the resulting SD card spits a "Error -110 whilst initializing" issue and freezes the Renegade. Most typically with small ARM-based computers like this, that seems to indicate a card incompatibility due to timing or something. But I've tried this with known-good 8GB and 32GB cards originally used in Raspberry Pis and the failure is consistent. Perhaps the .img extension I appended is not the correct one? Who knows. I asked on the "support" forum and it's been a couple days with no replies.

I really hope I can get this working, because I need the higher Ethernet I/O throughput that it promises vs. the sadly bottlenecked Ethernet-over-USB2 architecture of the Raspberry Pi. But first the thing needs to boot!

UPDATE:

I finally got the preferred "SDCard Installer" utility downloaded, after extracting the link from the inscrutable Chinese website's source HTML code (!). This allowed the utility to download and install directly without attempting to install the Baidu NetDisk thing, which I would not trust. It took a really long time to download, though... close to an hour for 58MB.

So, the SDCard Installer utility incorporates an automatic download feature. Unfortunately the Debian option does not appear. So, I tried the Ubuntu option. Suspiciously, the download is shown as 100% complete in a couple of seconds. Can't be right. And sure enough, the flash process fails, with a nonsensical error message. I tried with all the other download options with identical results. Unimpressive.

So I went back to the downloads page and downloaded the Ubuntu image directly. This download failed midway about a dozen times but could be re-started. Once complete, I then checked the MD5 checksum... and it didn't match. Either the repeated broken downloads resulted in a corrupt file, or the published checksum is incorrect. Nevertheless, I tried installing using the SDCard Installer utility, and the flash completed without error (using the known-good 8GB SD card from a Raspberry Pi). ...But the card still won't boot, still reports that "-110 whilst initializing" error and freezes in the boot process.

In order to try the over burn feature, I would need the appropriate disks that can normally hold 8.5 GB (DVD+R).  These disks are not too difficult to find online, but the office supply stores only seem to stock 4.7 GB disks.  I guess you either have to special order or buy online.  Most everything that I need to burn can either fit on a 4.7 GB DVD or can be compressed (without much loss of quality) to fit.  It may be false economy to buy the higher capacity disks, as they are nearly double the price of lower capacity.  With burnable media prices being so low anyway, you don't gain much by squeezing as much as you can on a particular disk.  So why did I get this drive?  I like to have a drive on the shelf if one goes bad (and they do sometimes), and then I don't have to wait for one to arrive.  I assumed it was probably good to have one that can burn to maximum capacity as this isn't much more expensive than a regular DVD burner.  Since I haven't actually installed or used the drive yet (waiting for disks), one should not pay as much attention to my review as some other reviewers.  I just wanted people to be aware that you can't insert a 4.7 GB disk and expect to over burn to 8.7 GB.  You need to understand the differences in available media and get the appropriate blank media. Update:  I finally received the appropriate media to test the drive.  It seemed to work good for the first 6 or 8 disks, but then 3 disks in a row had burn errors.  Bad media?  I don't think so; it appears the drive is failing already.  I'll test on another computer and see if it is the media or the drive and update the review again, but right now I can't recommend this drive at all.  UPDATE 2:  I tried this again after rebooting my computer and it now seems to work fine and does indeed overburn, so you can squeeze a lot on one disk.  When I had 3 bad burns in a row, I thought it was the burner, but it may have been bad media.  On the other hand, I suspect something flaky on my PC, as I have had bad burns before occasionally (not recently) and then after a reboot everything was fine again.  I may have too many programs loaded when I try to burn.  That's not the fault of the DVD drive.  Most likely the fault of the burning program (and I am using a major well-know program.)

I received one of these as a review sample and it works wonderfully when used to expand ports for low draw peripherals. You can charge a phone with it, but it's going to take forever. Also, it you are planning to use it to connect high-speed storage, you may be able to squeeze two of those, leaving two ports empty because the max output is 900mA. And if your high speed storage is using USB 3.0, just one device may max out this hub.

For me I use this to synch my phone and sometimes a tablet to an ancient laptop, as well as hang a mouse and occasionally a camera for also synching to my photo album on the laptop. For those tasks this is sufficiently powered.

What I love is this will work on my old ThinkPad T61 without additional drivers of any other hassle. More importantly it allows me to synch my finicky Galaxy Note 3. That phone balks at a lot of third party cables and even some USB hubs, so the fact that it works with this one is a major plus. Of course the synching rate is only at USB 2.0 speeds because the T61 does not have 3.0 ports. It's still fast enough for me, though.

Another feature that I love is the heavy-duty cable that is attached to this hub. Some hubs that I own have flimsy cables that actually wear out if you are constantly moving your hub, but this one will probably outlast me. Indeed, since I am 65 that is sadly possible.

Overall, as long as you are not plugging in high current draw devices like external drives, gaming keyboards (which can take up to 500mA of current), this is a great hub. Just bear in mind that this is designed with low power devices when making a purchase decision.

A good switch should require no real thought to install. You plug in, connect cat5e cables, and you're done. After that, it should work invisibly, giving you good throughput and no concerns whatsoever.

This one does that. If you need a modest-cost 5-port gigabit switch, I can recommend this one without reservation.

Notes: (1) If you don't need gigabit, you can get 100mb equipment pretty cheap right now. (2) Keep in mind that you use 1 port in a switch for the incoming cable, so a 5-port gives you connection to 4 devices, 8-port allows for 7 devices, etc. (Yeah, I know, it's dumb, but that's the way techies think.) (3) If you think you might need a couple more ports later, then definitely get the 8-port switch, since you don't pay that much more for the extra ports.

Since Ubuntu is a free Linux distribution based on the GNU/Linux Debian you can download it free at [...] You can also get the Wacom Bamboo Pen to work by copying and pasting the code below into a terminal within Ubuntu...

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:doctormo/wacom-plus
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install wacom-dkms

Reboot your system and your Wacom Bamboo Pen will be fully functional. Now, to install "MyPaint"...

sudo apt-get install mypaint

No need to reboot after that you will find the application under Applications>Graphics>MyPaint

Enjoy! your Wacom Bamboo Pen. One very important thing to know is that if you turn recording off manually (by hitting the OK button) for any reason, you must turn recording on again manually when you’re done with Settings or whatever made you turn recording off. The camera has a built in battery for holding the settings and powering the camera while the vehicle is parked. There are several instances where this item is not what was advertised. Here is the list:
Starting with the 26 melodies, this is false. There are likely a possibility of 26 different melodies available in the manufacture of this device, but a random four (4) will be chosen for your receiver. Each receiver mode will have a single melody selection within the sensor that will create a different ring depning on which if he four sensors is activated. Inside the sensor, there are two switches, one for sensitivity, the other which identifies the sensor as number 1, 2, 3, or 4. You can stand in the house (pre-installation) and move this switch, for the single detector package, and select ONE of the FOUR melodies provided, which will then become permanent once your screw the back panel on the sensor, and then screw the sensor to its permanent location. Sure, if you get sick of the melody, you can take it down, and apart, and then move the switch to a different number if you only have one sensor, however, if you order four sensors, each will have their own separate melody for location indication, and these melodies cannot be changed. It comes with four only.

The next problem, is that on the incuded pamphlet, it states that the sensor can be set up in two ways. One way is a straight angle, and from 3.5' to 4.5 feet. This will catch ANY motion, even the wind blowing, becaue this is a HEAT sensitive device. If the sensor has a heat image deviation, it will sound. The wind can do this during any evening or morning where there is a temperature difference between low and high air. The second set up is not higher, still from 3.5' to 4.5', but the sensor is angled diagonally across an area, and tilted downward. This is supposed to make a difference in only showing heat signatures and motion for larger objects.
Now, on the web page, it states that this second setting should be 4.5' to 6' high to achieve the best angle. It also states that the lense of the sensor should not be exposed to direct sunlight during the day as this can ruin the sensor leading to false detetions. It also says on the web page that a solid, non-moving mount is essential for accurate sensor monitoring. Nowhere in the instructions are these two critical pieces of information given.

My father, and octogenarian, was extremely firm in his belief that only the piece of paper in the box with its limited instructions should be believed, not some nonsense on the internet. The company needs to get a native English speaker to update the assembly and information pamphlet included with the device. It is not in agreement with the sales page, and it does not give pertinent information. I explained the differences to dad, and then remarked how his two receivers from a different brand, but also manufactured in the same country were non functional within a short time period when 1. He had them set up straight across at 3 feet high, and 2. They were positioned facing south where the sun shinned on the sensor all day. I got him to conceded that I had a point. These two factors give false alarms to the devices.

After measuring the distances, which was 15' - 20 feet of coverage distance needed, we chose the low medium setting, for 20 feet. We picked sensor melody for sensor 2. We placed the sensor at 5' high, and angled it slightly to the left, not straight across the driveway to the barn. Then we tested. A golfball rolled will not be picked up, so mice and chipmunks will not be picked up. I walked by(I am 5' tall) and it picked me up 15 feet ahead of the mounted position, coming from its distant angled side( its blind side). Dad, 6' tall, walked past it and back. It sounded at the same location as it did for me going by, and coming back, it picked him up twice as far out. Perfect. Driving a car by in either direction gives one sound, not repeated. Some models will sound forever for a vehicle, this one does not if set properly.

As far as it being waterproof, it has only drizzled, not hard rained yet. However, the shield on the top, shaped like a wide horseshoe, both covers the top seams, and covers the sensor well from side sunshine. The four screws on the back panel have rubber plugs in them. The seam for the panel is completely hidden when it is mounted.

With the mounting being so permanent for internal settings, no one is going to get inside easily and remove your battery, or try to turn down the sensor range to sneak by. It has a mini plug charger plug hole and a rechargeable battery. It can be charged in place or you can take it indoors to charge by dismounting it from its location.

I do recommend this unit for simple motion detection, especially since it is easy to install. The receiver has an on/off button, two volume buttons, and AC adapter plug, a low battery warning light from which you will know to go get your sensor and charge it.

If this product has any problems in the next 12 months, I will update this review.

First a caveat: I am not of the generation who grew up carrying backpacks to school and I do not have a lot of shoulder/upper arm strength; in addition I have arthritis in my neck, so to me any backpack seems a bit strange, stiff, and awkward. Frankly, I think if I'd had to carry around all the books I did in junior high school in a backpack (none of my classes were near my homeroom locker, so there was none of this dropping books off routine--we only had three minutes to get between classes), I'd have severe back problems right now, remembering the thick English, math, science, Italian, and history textbooks, plus a full size ring binder. Oy.

Now to our backpack: I like this. We have less expensive backpacks in our home, to use as a "bug out" bag in case of emergency. This is much nicer: padding, quality of material, and lots of nice pockets (I am a pockets-type person). I particularly like the "hidden pocket" that faces your back, which would be useful for money or any other valuables if you were backpacking or traveling. I have preliminarily tested this by putting my laptop and my 10-inch tablet in the space provided and walking around for a bit. My laptop is six years old and weighs a ton. However, the padded shoulder straps and the sternum strap were helpful in keeping this balanced well on my back. I went up and down stairs a few times and did not feel unbalanced or "top heavy." (I do now, however, understand why people like Airbooks.)

In addition to the laptop pocket with the inner sleeve for the tablet, this has a central compartment with two pockets, one zipped, and an outside compartment with all sorts of slots for pens, memory cards, CDs, whatever. A small pocket on the top of the back could hold a cell phone or perhaps your printout of a boarding pass, parking ticket receipt, whatever, and there are two small pockets, one on each side, one with an opening so you could put an .mp3 player in the pocket and have your earbuds come out through it. This is all in addition to the "hidden pocket." There is a strong handle at either end of the backpack as well as a handle.

My goal is to give this a better workout at Dragoncon, where I can carry lunch and snacks and juice boxes in the central compartment, carry my tablet in the laptop compartment, and also carry my camera, instead of slinging a lunchbox and my camera case over my shoulder. It seems like a much better option. I also see it being useful on the occasional weekend trip. If it works out for me, it's possible my husband might enjoy one as well.

[September: This was really, really good at Dragoncon; I will be using a backpack again next year. Much better than carrying the lunchbox and the camera separately and wearing a pouch. I put my tablet in the laptop pocket, my lunch things (juice boxes, sandwiches, snacks, fruit) in the middle pocket, and the camera in the outermost pocket. The little pocket at the top held my spare cell phone batteries, and my wallet was in the hidden pocket. This backpack needs a strap at the bottom, and, instead of an iPod holder, a water bottle holder. That's the only thing I can see wrong with it. Yeah, I could have put a water bottle inside with my lunch.]

The build quality is better than I was expecting, in all honesty, and for once I applaud the use of plastic over something like aluminum because the battery pack is already a bit on the heavy side and for something portable like this, every ounce counts.

I marked it down a star for a couple reasons:
1) The documentation that accompanied it was minimal and suffered from some translation issues (though I've come to expect that for products such as this). If not for reviews/questions here on Amazon, I wouldn't have known that the Red/Green LED indicator for charging is on the charger and not the battery pack. The battery pack LED is always Blue.
2) The Li Ion Charging/Protection Circuit is contained in the "wall wart" charger that comes with it. While I understand that this saves space in the battery pack itself (and I did just make the comment about every ounce counting), it also means that if I should lose the charger, I have to get another one to continue using the battery pack (the 18650 batteries used here are unprotected, I believe). For convenience, it would be nice to be able to plug the pack into any 12 volt power supply of sufficient amperage and have it charge without exploding.

These are truly minor gripes, though, and I am overall quite happy with this battery pack and its performance. I imagine I'll find another use for it when I no longer need it to provide life-saving warmth.

They sent it immediately, and I got it a few days later with plans to complete installation the following weekend from my original effort. I had been anxiously waiting to try out the NETGEAR Nighthawk. I’d read over the impressive specs long before it was released, I’ve read glowing reviews touting it as the fastest, most powerful router Netgear had yet to produce... Specially made for the high demands of Smart Homes. All the hype made it sound like it was going to be AMAZING.

Now that I’ve set it up and run a full battery of tests - honestly the best thing I can say about it is it looks cool. 😕

I have been working with NETGEAR products for 25+ years so setup was not a big deal. As with most of NETGEAR’s new products don’t expect much printed material - that’s OK with me... I downloaded the Nighthawk app and followed the directions - they are fairly straightforward.

Restart your modem, plug in your Nighthawk Router, plug Ethernet Cable from modem to router, connect cell to router’s network using the ID and password provided on the sticker on top of the routers plastic cover, return to app. Here is where things began making less sense.

When I return to the Nighthawk app it goes through the process of connecting to my router and I receive an error message: ROUTER NOT SUPPORTED. Odd, but I’ve learned when installing a new router anything can happen. I exit the app and return, same message. I exit the app, restart the router, wait and restart the app and it recognizes. Great - I’m in... no big deal.

I update the Firmware, change the network name and password and start checking through the settings. I notice right away there are very few settings within the app - no security settings tab, no parental controls tab - odd, but I’ve learned NETGEAR tends to move these types of things around when they redesign their apps, so I put that concern to the side.

I plug my Ethernet cables into the 1G ports (there are 4 of them) in the back and watch the lights on front illuminate.

One of these runs to my computer and once it initialized the internet connection I ran a speed test - I’d tested with my previous router just prior to switch and was consistently benching at 210Mb/s download and 15Mb/s upload. With the Nighthawk I speed tested at 130Mb/s and 9Mb/s - definitely not what I’d hoped to see but I knew all my smart devices were working on rejoining the network so that could be slowing it down.

I decided to give it some time to let everything register on the network. In the Nighthawk app I had 42 devices and about half were still listed as unknown.

I let it work for about an hour and it recognized the majority of them... I ran another speed test - again through my laptop connected via Ethernet through the Nighthawk and this time received 154Mb/s and 11Mb/s. Still not great.

Then I went into my Nighthawk app as it has a speed test feature in there - I try that and receive an error that I must be on the network to run a speed test. I was on the network. I exit the app and go back in and receive the message ROUTER NOT SUPPORTED again. Ugh - really???

I reboot the router again and then the app recognizes it. While I’m able to control the router the speed test function does not want to work. Not a huge issue. I went through the browser on my phone and ran a speed test. The results were absolutely pathetic. This is the NIGHTHAWK - the router that is supposed to provide blazing fast speeds to WiFi devices and I received results of 5.4Mb/s download and 2.1Mb/s upload - and similar on 3 consecutive tests. At this point I’m starting to be less than impressed.

I decided to log in to the more advanced router settings via my computer. I had no problem getting in there but to my surprise there are ABSOLUTELY NO PARENTAL CONTROLS. This is the same company that has sold itself as allowing you to have complete control over every aspect of your home internet. NETGEAR Genie is no longer available and the NETGEAR Nighthawk panel doesn’t even have a section for parental controls - let alone work with Disney Circle.

While there are some advanced security features available within the NETGEAR Nighthawk Router controls on the computer they are anything but user friendly - they are hard to find, hard to set, and less than optimal.

As I was discovering all of this and researching these issues in the NETGEAR Community Forums I started receiving notifications from my smart devices that they were losing WiFi signal and then after a minute or two they would reconnect. This happened with my security cameras, LIFX lights, Wemo switches, and August door locks. After this went on for about an hour I decided my experiment with the NETGEAR NIGHTHAWK had reached its conclusion.

Unfortunately I can’t recommend this router at this time. While the hardware inside should have this out performing most any other router on the market I found it to be slow and glitchy.

I've been testing this Epson ProSense watch for the past week. I also have a 2-year-old Garmin Vivoactive HR watch that has most of the same features, but costs half as much. To the compare the two, I've been wearing one watch on each wrist and going on runs and bike rides to see how their readings compare. Both watches have daily step counters that give similar results (today, Garmin says 12044 steps while Epson says 12790 steps). 5% difference is close enough for me.

When I use the GPS exercise mode, the results start showing big differences. On today's run, Garmin recorded 4.02 miles while Epson says 3.9 miles. That's a 3% difference which is close enough for me. Garmin says 529 calories and Epson says 955 calories. Garmin says 535 feet of elevation gain and Epson says 1142 feet. I know Garmin has a barometric altimeter, while Epson is using GPS elevation, which is notoriously inaccurate. Does Epson's terrible elevation data cause a wildly inaccurate calorie count? I could not find any information on Epson's calorie calculation in their documentation, so I really cannot trust it.

Both devices give me heart rate readings with graphs by time or broken out by training zones. The numbers look close enough for my purposes. Both devices also give me maps of my route, which is is nice to have for reviewing later, especially if it is a new route to me.

The Epson is a much larger device (both width and thickness), as shown in the photo. While the Garmin is not especially attractive, at least it is relatively unobtrusive. Epson is big enough to feel clunky on my wrist, especially if I am wearing it all day (to take advantage of the step counter).

Both devices have a smartphone app that syncs your data and also sends notifications to the watch. I'm using this watch with a Google Pixel Android phone. The Garmin app by default uploads your data to the Garmin website. With Epson, you have to upload to a 3rd party website like Strava, which may not be compatible with all the data that your device is collecting.

Notifications work much better with Garmin than Epson. For incoming phone calls, both Garmin and Epson will display the caller ID or contact name so I don't have to pull out my phone to see who is calling. For incoming emails, Garmin displays the sender name and subject line, while Epson just says "you have mail". For text messages, Garmin shows the contact name and message. Epson shows no notification for text messages.

The only advantage (for my use case) that I can find with this Epson watch is the much longer battery life. Garmin claims 1 week of battery life with the GPS off or 13 hours with the GPS on. Epson claims 46 hours of battery life with the GPS on, which I suppose is great for some ultra endurance sports. For me, I never exercise more than 8 hours in a day.

The Fujifilm FinePix Z90 is a great point and shoot camera. It comes in a variety of colors, but I like the bright red finish of the camera I have. The design is unique from other cameras - it resembles a wallet or envelope. To turn the camera on, you simply slide the lens cover down; this is the part of the camera that looks like an envelope flap. Some of the options are a little harder to use than other small cameras, but the available features are worth a little time to learn to use.

Besides the stylish design, I like the many innovative features of the camera. For example, it's very easy to switch from playback to camera mode with the buttons on the camera. Once in playback mode, I found the functionality to have many more options compared to other similar cameras. You can compare photos side-by-side or with the press of an on-screen button, you can display thumbnails of several photos at once.

There are too many features to describe each one in detail, but below is a summary of my favorites:
* Good picture quality for size and type of camera
* Many settings manageable by touching the screen
* Robust playback mode
* Includes lithium ion battery and charger
* Ability to take one photo without flash and immediately take same picture with flash and compare results side-by-side (Great for taking an initial photo to test lighting conditions)
* Can load photos to PC even without the included software using standard windows functionality
* In Playback mode, can go to Menu and select specific photo. Then when photos are loaded to the PC, only those selected photos will be uploaded to Facebook.
* Zoom in/out easily by touching a round button on top of the camera - easier to get to and use than the bars on other cameras that must be tapped on one end or the other to zoom in and out
* Can select a mode that allows a photo to be taken by touching the screen instead of the shutter button
* When turning the camera vertically to take a picture, the menu options are automatically displayed in a portrait mode so they are easy to read

Overall, this camera has several unique, up-to-date features that are surprising, especially for a camera at this price point. The stylish design makes it a great choice for adults or teens. Facebook and YouTube users will appreciate the technology making is easier than ever to post photos and video clips. If you're looking for a small camera with a fun design and new features, the FinePix is worth a second look.

I recently purchased one of these routers as a replacement for my Linksys WRT54GL, a stalwart in the realm of home networking. My Linksys router is healthy and it works but it does not allow me to set up DHCP reservations without a 3rd party firmware update, and it does not support Wireless-N. After searching for a good balance between functionality, quality and price I settled on this router by NetGear. So far I am very pleased with this unit, though I had some minor issues when setting it up.

Setup of NetGear routers (including this one) is simple and easy. There are two methods of setting it up, using the Wizard CD or going in manually. For users not too familiar with setting up wireless networks or routers, using the CD to get started is a good option. More seasoned users may prefer to work without the CD and work directly with the router. I chose the latter of the two. Even so, tapping in and finding any given setting is relatively easy, everything broken down into several pages. Because the router configuration is accessed through a browser, manipulating the router configuration is very much like accessing a web page and should feel familiar.

The factory-default username, password, and access address are printed right on the router itself so there is no risk of losing this information at any point.

I connected 3 laptops, one at a time, to the wireless network and encountered my only difficulty with moving to this router. Because I retained the network name and key I expected the swap to be seamless and mostly invisible, but my systems each complained when tried to connect, stating that the network configuration had changed even though I retained the settings, the type, key and everything else. To get each system working I had to delete the connection completely, then I allowed each to redetect wireless networks available. Two of them came up without any further incident, but one of the laptops required a reboot before it would properly connect.

Signal strength is important when it comes to wireless networks. My Linksys router gives me very strong signal strength, and I was fearful that this new NetGear router would lack the same power to broadcast. Happily, it broadcasts brightly enough that I have had no problems with connectivity due to losing signals. It is *at least* on par but seems to be stronger. My router lives on the second story of the house, while my personal laptop is in the basement.

As soon as the router was configured and provided a connection to the internet, I logged in ang got a surprise - it is configured by factory default to look for firmware updates every time I log in. This is fine as logging into the router becomes an infrequent activity after a while, though up front it can be annoying to have to wait for it to download and then update itself.

I have had no connectivity issues or drops since setting this router up.

The DHCP reservation and MAC filtering work well, which are the two advanced features about which I care most.

Something I have not seen in any other router up to this point is a USB port. According to the documentation, the router can be set up to provide persistent storage through the network by simply connecting a USB hard drive (or even a thumb drive) to it. I have not tried this but I absolutely plan to put this to work, which will make sharing files between the different computers simple without having to make several copies. It should be noted, though, that this could be a risky practice if using to access the same file frequently from multiple points.

Looking through the options that can be set up, I found a keyword-based page filter, QoS settings and a lot of other features I have not previously seen. For a mid-range wireless router this one has a generous set of features. Of course, the standard features are there - firewall, MAC filtering as mentioned above, different encryption key types and a lot more too.

This is a very nice router with a nice feature set. It is very easy to set up, easy to configure once it's running, and so far has proven to be stable. If you need more than a basic wireless router, consider this one as a good candidate.

Traveling with electronics is inevitable and when traveling abroad, it's necessary to understand a few things about the places you will be traveling to. Language, currency, electrical standards, and cell phone bands being a few of them. Traveling to the UK or Europe, 220v is the electrical standards. To deal with this, you must understand the electronics that you will be bringing with you. Most modern electronics such as cell phone and laptop chargers will work fine at 220v with a plug adapter (make sure you check the power adapter regarding input voltage), but personal electric devices such as hair dryers and maybe electric shavers might not. There are two choices here. Look for hair dryers that have a switch to allow 220v or 110v. Otherwise, purchase a voltage converter.

The BESTEK 2000W Travel Voltage Converter power strip is one of the more powerful voltage converters that I've seen. Most voltage converters will not support hair dryers because they don't output enough amps for the devices to work. At 2000W, this voltage converter power strip is powerful enough to power most dryers out there (many work at 1800w). This device is well labeled to reduce any confusion. There are two output sockets. One rated at 200w for less intensive devices such as the electric toothbrush and my camera's battery charger. The other socket outputs the full 2000w. This is good for the hair dryer.

I was disappointed that this device doesn't work in the UK and since their standards are a little different from the EU, I didn't want to even try using a plug converter to try it. There's no guarantee as to what wattage the plug converter can handle so it's better to play it safe. Use this device only in the European countries and the others that are listed on this web page.

For me, I didn't take any chances with it. Since the USB ports are fairly standard at 2.4a output but no quick charge or type-c PD, I charged my phones using a different, more robust phone charger. I used this power strip only for the hair dryer with nothing else plugged in. Even then, I don't know that this thing can handle running the thing for too long.

In the end, I think the better strategy is to purchase devices that are rated for both 110v and 220v to save yourself some headache. I was able to find a third-party oral-b electric toothbrush charger rated for 220v and a travel hair dryer with the 220v switch. I'll still have this power strip with me for my camera until I can find a third-party charger for it.

An air mouse is not something you would normally use with a PC-based system unless you are trying to save space or are giving a presentation in which case it is a convenient accessory. Such a mouse is a lot more useful for things like Smart TVs, though it is also useful for embedded systems like a Raspberry Pi. I have used several air mice and I was curious to see how well this one would compare to others I have used. So far it has worked well, under both Linux as well as Windows. I will state up front that I have not used it with a Smart TV.

At a glance, this little device looks like a TV remote and little more, but it is quite a bit more than that. It does work as a remote, of course, but it also works as a mouse with a full-up keyboard. On one side of this device there are all of the controls you would expect to find on a remote for a Smart TV remote – volume control, channel settings, mode buttons, play, search and more. Flip the unit over and there is a keyboard, with 38 keys and most regular keyboard functions accessible through function key settings.

The unit requires two AAA batteries, not included.

I decided to try it with my Linux workstation, running CentOS 7 with a 64-bit 3.10.0-series kernel. I did not have to load special drivers and I did not need to do any special configuration at all, it was just plug and play. I was able to move the mouse just by waving the device in front of the screen and several of the buttons on the remote side worked as I would have hoped – Home took me to the browser home page, volume controls worked, Search worked, the menu button brought up the menu for the current application with focus and more. The keyboard portion worked as it should and I was able to type, though I found it a little awkward after being used to a full-sized keyboard for so long.

I also tried it with my Windows 10 system and I got nearly identical results. It required no drivers, no special configuration, no extra set-up – it just works as expected. The buttons works the same under Windows as they did under Linux for me and I was able to navigate as desired.

This is a good air mouse that works well under Linux and Windows. It should work fine with smaller systems like the Raspberry Pi (which uses a derivative of the Linux kernel). As an added bonus, it is relatively inexpensive. If you need an air mouse, this one is worth some consideration.

I have always favored Verbatim products, particularly their CD-R Audio platters, so I was excited to try the Clip-It as a storage device. It does indeed work as advertised, but it is not a particularly remarkable product.

As a 4GB storage device, it does well enough but I noticed that the copy rate is somewhat slow. I did a side-by-side comparison with a SanDisk Cruzer stick and found that the SanDisk outperformed the Verbatim by an average of 2 meg/sec. That's an appreciable speed difference! When copying larger files, it means longer waits while the copy completes. For the impatient, this is bad.

I do not like the fact that the contact points are exposed and there is no cover for them. This equates to more opportunities for dirt and oil to contaminate the contacts which may eventually affect reliability.

As a paper clip (this product's other touted function) it performs well for a small number of pages but quickly is outdone when trying to clip together more pages or pages made with thicker paper.

I'm sorry, but I cannot recommend this product. There are other storage solutions that are comparable in price that perform better, have more storage space and are of better design.

The WEWATCH Video Projector with WiFi and Bluetooth is a basic projector that has all of the necessary features that one needs.

The description of this product may lead you to think otherwise, but this projector is not really a "smart" projector. It does not run on Android and the built-in user interface is quite basic. Yes, it will play videos and show photos from USB drives and it has WIFI... for whatever reason (I didn't really look into it because I simply plugged in a FireTV). The bluetooth, on the other hand, does have a function. I'll get into that in a bit.

So for video input, you have two full sized HDMI ports, a VGA (for those ancient laptops that your office may have lying around?) and a USB port which outputs enough amperage to run a fireTV, so no additional power adapter necessary.

There is no automatic keystone adjustment, but what is there works well. You can adjust the four corners up and down, although I found that it still seems to have some bloating in the middle no matter how I adjust it (could be a problem with my projection screen and projector positioning). A tip for doing the adjustment: If you aren't able to move the corners in the direction that you need, try adjusting the zoom first. By zooming out, it allows the corners to be pulled up or down more.

Audio is as expected in that it is not winning any awards. It can get pretty loud, but it still sounds empty. This is where bluetooth or the 3.5 mm headphone jack comes in. For wireless audio, you can either pair a bluetooth speaker/soundbar to the projector itself or you can pair the speakers directly to the FireTV or whatever dongle you're using. The advantage of pairing the speakers to the projector is that they will work for both HDMI inputs. If you really wanted to get full surround, you'll have to extract the audio out of the HDMI wire. Basically plug the HDMI into an audio receiver, then the audio receiver to the projector. The receiver can take care of decoding the surround depending on your setup.

For the brightness, the 1100LM beats out many other projectors of this price and resolution. You can really tell that the picture just pops. It will work well enough in a dimly lit room, but you can only truly appreciate it when the lights are completely off.

Overall, this is a low-priced projector that will work well for outdoor, temporary use, or even a permanent setup inside the home.

Originally review follows:
Before I go into what I don't like, let me tell you what this product is:

If you are the only driver of your car, you'll likely never know or care about this, but all of Atoto's Android powered units (S8 included) will only pair automatically with the last phone used. That means if you share the car with other family members, and they drove the car last, your phone won't auto-connect next time you drive. It does not make any sense to me and is a complete user experience failure, to the point that my wife has told me she might want us to go back to our old OEM head unit- at least that one would auto-connect to whoever is driving the car, regardless of who drove it last!

I don' t have a way to test the claims of an 1800-foot line-of-sight range for this driveway sensor, but it does work on a heavily wooded lot at 200-plus feet, right through the trees. It will be months before I'll know if the sensor's rechargeable battery actually works for nearly a year on a single charge, but for now, it's working.

The receiver accepts up to eight separate sensors. Each sensor has an individual sensitivity setting (you have to remove the back of the sensor to adjust it), and a group of switches to set the channel for each. Once paired to the receiver, a simple process, each sensor can be assigned its own alert tone.

And there are a lot of alert tones. Some of them I thought were quite funny.

The receiver can be powered via the included power supply, which also recharges the sensor, or it can run on three AA batteries (not included). With batteries installed, the detector system will still work during power outages.

Some things I think could be improved:

- In just the first couple of nights the receiver sounded three false alerts on three separate channels that have no sensor paired to them. I checked the manual to see if the unused channels could be switched off, but there was no option for that. So I checked to see if there was a silent alert tone to assign to unused channels, but their isn't. So alerts on unused channels can't be silenced or stopped.

- There's a volume control for the alert tone, but no brightness control for the display, and it's pretty bright.

- There's no memory feature for reviewing previous alerts and when they occurred.

- There's no slot on the back of the receiver for wall mounting.

- The sensor mounting plate holes are spaced almost 3-1/2 inches apart, which puts them right on the edges of a standard US 2 X 4, making it difficult to mount on one. I got around this by rotating the mounting plate to diagonal, cutting off the side corners, and using the top and bottom holes to mount the sensor.

- The back of the sensor must be removed to make some adjustments. (The included screwdriver works fine for that.) I noticed there was no weather proofing gasket when I removed it. That's not a problem for me since I mounted the sensor in a three-sided, roofed box I built some years ago for a driveway sensor. - When batteries are installed, the receiver apparently runs on the batteries even if the power supply is plugged in. The low battery alert started going off---in the middle of the night---after two weeks of running with the receiver plugged into the adapter. This probably means the batteries aren't really working as a backup power source but the primary one when batteries are installed. So it's an either/or situation---install batteries and run the receiver off of them, or remove the batteries to run on the external power supply.

Other than that, setup is easy. The included sensor is already paired with the receiver, and a quick start guide is printed directly on the back of the box. A more thorough manual, which includes instructions for adding receivers and setting alert tones, is included in the box. Mounting screws and a screwdriver are included too.

So I got this thinking it's the deal of the year, until I had issues the first time using it on a job. One of the motors appears to be faulty and would vibrate like crazy at certain angles. I'm attaching the video I sent to DJI's tech support team to help troubleshoot the issue.

I realize that this is sort of a niche use product, but I did not let that affect my review either. This does what it is meant to do and does it well. It's a fairly simple product, but I can't think of any features they missed. I mean, you have two types of dial tone and you can call from the cell service even if the land line is up, and it has automatic failover and a battery backup. The LEDs tell you what you need to know and even the SIM holder is easier to use than most cell phones.

Their most legitimate stated use is to back up your security system's auto-dial feature in the event the phone line is cut, and I think that is an excellent use because a smart thief would know what your advertised security plan is comprised of, but they wouldn't know about your backup.

I don't like the idea of paying any monthly fees unless they are absolutely necessary, but one could conceivably use a pre-paid SIM card for such a service. I don't have much experience with those plans in the States, but some foreign providers have a prepaid "higher end" plan that allows you to keep your service alive indefinitely (and supposedly get higher end features) for a $ or two each month. Alternatively, you could just be sure to make a cheap call every month or two to keep the service from expiring.

But then I thought of an excellent use myself:

I have just a cell phone and no land line, but I often wonder what I will do to provide my future children with phone service since I'm not about to give them their own cell phones at a young age so they can be little entitled brats. Just put this down in the telecom closet, before phone line split (or just next to a single phone if that's all you have) and it will power all your phones just like a home phone, and the kids can share it when they need to make a call. Ordered one from Amazon, $35. Like that camera can sit inside on window sill, flush to the glass of the window, and perfect video picture, night vision is spectacular (have read some ambient light outside is required). No need to worry about batteries or wiring, it plugs into the wall. You also do not need a subscription for just basic usage, but it will only film an event and notify you once every 5 minutes if you opt for no subscription. For $15/year, it is unlimited with no 5 minute pause between even detections. Has a micro SD slot (micro SD card not included), we just used one we had, but not necessary for camera operation. It can also be paired with other appliances through an IFTT app like a garage door.
The MAJOR ISSUE is that even though you may set your detection area, the detection is via a change in pixels (where Ring, Blink, etc. are infrared and detect a heat source) and we receive an EXCESSIVE DETECTION NOTIFICATIONS when the sun sets and shines through the leaves or at night when car headlights flash across the detection area. We have also read where people receive excessive detection notifications when it rains or bugs attracted to light, but we have not had an opportunity to put it to the test with these. The only solution to minimize these notifications for these non-events is to move the camera or to set up rules to silence events during certain times of the day. For the cost, we decided we can live with this. Our walk around for now, is to just have one family member's phone receive alerts. And the other family members must block the alerts for this specific app in the settings of their phone (not within the app, or it blocks everyone's notifications).
Only the initial person who sets up the camera on the app, can make a lot of the changes to the camera within the app. And other family members are just shared access to the camera and can set up their own rules. The initial person who did the set up will receive notifications a split second before the people it is shared with.

Wow, before saying anything, the screen on this laptop is stunning; bright and sharp. It is not the first nice thing I noticed about the laptop. Out of the box, it has a solid, perhaps a little heavy feel. It has a matte crosshatched finish which is not my favorite, but looks classy enough. The basic shape is elegant, it is thin and sleek and satisfying in the hand.

Keyboard/Touchpad

The keys are backlit, crisp to the touch and typing is easy. It has a slightly compressed full keyboard with a squeezed 10 key which is nice, and at least for my uses fine that the keys are 2/3rds their normal width. Keypad is sensitive but clicking works better than most and I have no problems with fine control of the cursor. The fingerprint reader is on the touchpad but does not affect usage and is a nice touch in general. All in all, inputs through keyboard, touchpad and touchscreen are perfect.

Screen

Like I said, once this one on, the screen is what stuck out for me. Wonderfully bright and crisp. Touch screen controls seem to work fine. Screen size is great. We watched a number of HD nature films on it and felt comfortable. The screen hinges completely around to create a tablet which I far prefer to swivel options. I also liked the way that it tents for movie and presentation viewing. Could not be happier with the screen.

CPU/Performance

This is a nice quick machine. SSD, i7 and plenty of RAM out of the box had it booting quick and I see no problems with performance. I would be amazed and happy to see it approach the 9 hours of battery life that it promises, we'll see about that over time. My son wanted to put it through the paces with STEAM games but I'm passing - It's mine, but it should handle most reasonable games although it is obviously not optimized for hard core gaming.

Summary

This is a well built, solid laptop. It has the makings for a great Netflix platform with it's screen and flexibility of viewing positions of the screen as well as crisp, bright HD. This is hands down the best laptop I have owned as a complete package.

Pros
+ Super Bright, HD screen
+ Nice crisp feel to the keyboard
+ Well powered for standard uses, SSD, i7 and RAM gives it enough muscle

Cons
-The design of the power cord and jack are disappointing, It looks spindly and its design encourages lateral pressures. I really wish more thought went into that.
-The pattern on the outside is not my favorite, but looks nice enough

Beside myself with joy. Backing up 775,000+ files with Time Machine could not have been easier.

This external drive was recommended by an Apple technician whom I hired to come tidy up the many issues that had developed over several years of working with my several Apple devices. While he was here, we called up Amazon and found the drive he recommended -- this one. It was promptly delivered. Connecting and running it could not have been easier. Feeling much more confident about continuing to work on my ancient MacBook.

UPDATE: This little guy has fallen on the tile flooring more times than I can count now. Amazingly, it hasn't broken yet. You should be aware that the connection to the cord that leads to your USB port is kind of loose -- especially where it plugs into the external drive. IO've had to use Scotch tape to secure it. Inelegant, but useful, BECAUSE...

Yesterday the client's gigantic file, replete with uncompressed images, crashed not only the file but my entire MS Wyrd program. Thanks to this little hard drive and Time Machine, Word was backed up -- although I didn't need to use the back-up to recover Word, the back-up could have been a life-saver. Time Machine failed to back up an uncorrupted version of the file recent enough to contain the six or eight hours' worth of edits I'd entered during that session. Ohhhh well... Not a function of the drive: a function of Apple's Time Machine.

I plan to buy another of these drives and manually back up current files, so as to have more than one copy of key data, one of which will always be unplugged from the machine.
///////

ADDENDUM: Made in Thailand, this little guy is tougher than one would expect. Because of a back problem, I can't sit at a desk; so, the external drive has been attached to a MacBook that allows me to work in pain-free seating. This entails my hauling the computer array around with me to more than one seating arrangement, and lifting the junk on and off of various nearby tables. I've dropped it several times and each time expected it would be dead. No: it survived a half-dozen drops on tile floor before I figured out that I could tape the cable into the Passport connection. Last night, though, a fairly mild tap (not a drop!) did it in. I'm ordering two more, so that I can switch them out every other day; that way, the next time I break one, I'll have a backup to the backup.

The connection between the USB cable and the Passport comes apart readily. You can remedy that -- not aesthetically but effectively -- with a piece of Scotch tape.

I love mini PCs and I've collected a few of them for different projects. The Celeron chip isn't a speed demon, but combined with Intel's GPU it is fast enough to drive 2 HDMI displays quite well, and like most other mini PCs out there, it has enough RAM and storage for light media consumption and internet tasks.
But there are few things that stand out with this model:
- This one is FANLESS. Without moving parts whirring, this actually manages to stay completely quiet while running.
- Also since the body is the heat sink, it doesn't need space for airflow and is therefore more compact as well.
However, not all of those changes are positive:
- There is no upgrade option for the storage like other mini PCs. Some of the popular boxes out there have an access door to add your own sata SSD drive for additional storage. This does not.
- The fanless design also sometimes means that in hot environments (such as attached to the back of a large TV display sign), there is no way to cool itself off other than throttling the processor. Most of the time this doesn't mean anything, but like all fanless computer designs it is extremely possible the unit will need to slow itself down to prevent overheating if used for extended periods of time. A fan unit has alternative ways to cool itself off at least.

But the biggest disappointment to me personally, is the lack of USB type C ports. It looks like this has one, but that look is deceiving. The port is just a PD input to run the unit. I actually like that it is using a standard instead of the circular DC ports that other mini PCs use, the PD power port is plentiful these days and you can use most laptop and other standard PD chargers to run this device. However, it still does not work as a standard USB-C for peripherals that are compatible with one. To be fair, most of these mini PCs I've tried oddly lack a type C port as well. I can't really detract any stars for that, but I got excited for a moment that this would have one only to see it is the power port.

I have gotten so many pair of earbuds that have disappeared in the house, that I finally decided to get a pair I could use for me. I got these and was very excited to test them out. The problem is, they were stolen, like A BAZILLION TIMES.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These ear buds are easy to wear. There is a wire band that you wear around the neck and make sure that they controls are on the right side. The ear buds are marked R and L but it can be hard to see. HOW DO THESE COME?
These come in a great box that is perfect for gift giving.

CONTROLS
The controls for these are very easy to use. They work well, are simple, and pretty easy to catch on to.

PHONE QUALITY
My daughter talks to me all of the time with these on, and they are almost impossible to know that she is using. Otherwise I would have known that she STOLE MY EARBUDS AGAIN AND WOULD HOLLER AT HER. MUSIC QUALITY

CUSHIONS
The rubberized cushions fit okay, but we have had to use different ones for the best fit- well the fifteen seconds at a time I get to use them before the earbud thief strikes again.

ANY PROBLEMS?
The only problem that happens is that if we are using these long enough and are moving around cleaning or doing things, your ears can get sweaty and they will start to slip out a bit. Wiping them off helps though. Other than that, they are really nice.

I'm a huge Lensbaby fan. I've been using them with my Canon SLRs almost since they first came out, and have assembled a pretty extensive collection of them over the past few years. Yes, I am a lover of blur. It's one of those creative effects that you either love or don't (although I certainly will admit it can be overused with some horrible results). I've recently been playing around with Micro Four Thirds cameras and was thrilled to see that Lensbaby came out with a model specifically designed for the MFT format.

Quick primer for those not familiar with a Lensbaby: it's a very simple device that allows you to tilt the focal plane of the lens to shift focus to any area of the frame and produce a smooth blur effect. It can be in a small or large part of your photo depending on which of the several aperture rings you choose from (all supplied with this Lensbaby) and how much tilt you apply.

This particular version of the lens, called the "Composer" is part of Lensbaby's new Optic Swap System, which allows you to use any one of several optics (plastic, glass, double glass, pinhole/zoneplate) that you can easily swap out of the main body. This comes with the double glass optic - the other optics have to be purchased separately.

The new Composer design allows you to lock the tilt into place for some level of repeatability in your shots. A lot more convenient than earlier versions of Lensbabies, which required you hold the tilt with your fingers. Now it's just pick your aperture and your optic, tilt, and snap away!

This lens comes with an extra you can't get with other Lensbabies for other camera formats - the "tilt transformer." This is an attachment that will allow you to use any Nikon-mount lens as a close approximation of a tilt/shift lens (only close, since you really only get the benefit of tilt and not shift). With this attachment and a "regular" lens, you get a movable sliver, a line of focus, as opposed to the movable point of focus you get with a Lensbaby Optic. Same basic principle, but it produces a slightly different look.

Build quality is good. There's a lot of plastic in it, but my other Lensbabies have performed very well over the years with zero problems. The product comes nicely packaged, but only has minimal instructions. That's not really a problem since the company website has a lot of resources on how to use Lensbabies, plus has photo galleries, forums, instructional videos, and a lot more. Very nice resource if you own one. If you're not sure if a Lensbaby is for you, that should be your first stop to see what type of effects their products can produce. I've spent a lot of time there, and it has been time well spent. The company itself is excellent when it comes to customer service. I've contacted them a couple of times with questions, and they answer emails promptly.

This lens is versatile, and is more convenient to carry (both the Lensbaby as well as a MFT camera itself). I've found with all my gear that convenience of toting it means I'll carry it more often, and thus have more opportunity for taking great shots. The tilt transformer is a wonderful addition - you can play around with a tilt lens at a fraction it would cost you to buy a real tilt/shift lens.

While pricy for a Lensbaby, when you add up all the features it brings to the table, I find it to be a real winner. Highly recommend if you have a MFT camera.

I was going to wait until I actually had truly tested and used this before I wrote a review.  I got this free as a review unit.  The problem is that I can't use it without spending some money for cables, as it does not come with cables.  StarTech says that's on purpose since people have different cable needs, especially different lengths. The cables that StarTech has available for it are over $21 each, which comes up to well over $60 for my 3 computers, almost the price of the switch.  With 4 computers connected, the price would be even more.  Okay, so they don't provide cables, but for the price of the switch, maybe they should at least give you a coupon or a voucher for one or two cables or a discount on the cables.  Interestingly the 2-port version does include cables; the 4-port does not.  StarTech's cables are nice, as they combine the needed USB with the VGA cable; otherwise you have to run two completely separate cables (one VGA cable for monitor and a USB cable for keyboard and mouse).  If you have USB cables as most people do, you can easily purchase the needed VGA cables inexpensively.  This brings me to the first real issue I have with this switch.  The master monitor connection is a female connector, which is standard.  Unfortunately the 4 computer monitor connectors are all male connections, so you can't use a standard male to male VGA cable that you would normally use from a computer to a monitor.  You have to get male to female VGA cables (which are typically called extension cables).  Why they would use this non-standard method of connecting monitors is puzzling.  A couple of reviewers were also concerned that this switch does not come with a power supply.  That's usually not a big deal as I found out that a power supply is not necessary, as the switch gets it's power from the USB connections.  There is no explanation as to why it has a place to plug in a power supply, although in some cases if you have a lot of USB devices connected to your PC, you might need additional power that a power supply would provide, so I assume it is for supplemental power.  It's good that they provide a way to add additional power, if you need it, even if not the actual power supply.  The next issue I encountered was trying to determine whether or not you could switch between computers with a hotkey sequence on your keyboard or whether you actually had to reach over to the switch and press the button for the computer you wanted.  Apparently there is no keyboard switching or if there is, no one seems to know what keys are used.  I read the manual for the setup and was concerned that it states that for PC to get the switch to work properly, a couple of BIOS settings for PC need to be changed.  I am not even sure that my computers have those particular settings, especially my older computers that sometimes have more limited BIOS settings available.  I have had 3 other KVM switches and none of them needed a change to BIOS settings.  Given the problems that others have had with this switch in that it doesn't always work flawlessly, I am not sure that I want to take time to test it right, since I already have a nicely working KVM switch.  I still have to buy cables.  On the plus side, this switch appears to be well built with a metal case; not cheap plastic.  It appears to be nice and solid and just heavy enough.  If the issues I mentioned are not a deal-breaker for you, I think this is worth trying.  I will update my review and add or subtract stars once I have a chance to test this in actual operation.

It's MUCH easier to see and use the onscreen keyboard than on the original Fire. I had no problems typing without a stylus; on the original Fire a stylus is a must.

We recently got these privacy screens where I work. The first problem was with fit: I have a Dell 17" flat screen, and although this product is supposed to fit a 16-18" monitor, it is an awkward match at best. The little tabs on the side of the screen that hang over your monitor are placed a bit too far apart to comfortably work with my monitor, so as a result, they wind up half on, half off. Furthermore, the tabs are supposed to move up and down to position the privacy screen at different heights, but they won't lock into the highest height position (which is where I need mine placed). In general, the screen just seems unstable and ill-fitting.

Then there is the privacy issue itself. If I place myself just to the left or the right of my monitor (ie, so my right shoulder lines up with the left edge or vice versa), I can still see about 2/3 of the screen; I have to move another foot or so away before the entire screen goes black. Similarly, when I stand up and look down on the monitor, I can still read it clearly as long as I am standing directly in front of it (even though I am above eye level). Therefore, someone walking up behind me and standing over my shoulder can easily see my screen--not ideal for privacy issues.

Overall, this expensive privacy filter offers some improvement in privacy, but it certainly does not solve the problem, and the design could definitely stand some improvement.
