(WARNING- This is an IN DEPTH review of this stereo to help anyone interested in making an informed buying decision. If you prefer a more brief summary, see section marked THE BOTTOM LINE)
------------
In my house there is a variety of quality of audio items. There are those who really don’t seem to care what kind of quality, as long as it is not too bad. Then there are those who really want to hear definition of sound but they can tolerate lower quality. Then there are those who are so sensitive to audio that they will go on in great depth to analyze and evaluate anything related to stereos whether it is the CD player, bluetooth player, headphones, speakers, and fine tuning of sound.

This stereo system was picked to replace a very old Onkyo which is hanging on, but not for long. Let’s see how this measures up.

WHAT IS THIS STEREO LIKE?
First of all, the write up when I had the opportunity to get this stereo said it was a mini stereo system (different than it is now). I expected it to fit where my other stereo system is which was also a condensed system. Boy was I surprised. This system is a LOT bigger than I expected it to be, but still will fit where I wanted to put it although much tighter than I thought it would.

This system has a CD/bluetooth base to it. There is a dial which is rather large on the front that deals with volume. The CD player has the usual controls on it and there is only an FM radio, no AM. There is an infrared remote which has all of the controls you would need to run the stereo.

LIST OF CONNECTORS
FM Antenna terminal
Line 1 and 2 terminals
Speaker light terminal
Speaker out terminal
USB input on front
Headphone jack on front

MEASUREMENTS
Receiver: 11 x 11 13/16 x 5 5/8
Speakers: 12 x 10 3/4 x 16 5/16
Speaker cords approx 2 ft

HOW DOES THIS UNIT PERFORM?
The CD drawer in the bottom right corner operates about average as far as loading and reading. When playing a CD there were not any problems. As far as the equalizer goes, there are only five functions (one is flat- ewww). For this price there should have been more or customizable options.

The equalizer options sound okay, but the two that we choose most often for a variety of music is jazz and rock. Pop, flat, classic seem lack luster for all of the CDs we tried including classical, rock, country, jazz, hip hop, etc.

Despite limitations, the sound did separate well on one of our CDs which has very muffled and quiet background noise at the beginning of a song that we have never heard clearly before.

SOUND QUALITY
The highs come through pretty well, due to the two tweeters per speaker. The mids and lows depend on the music. They tend to suffer more. It booms but not overly clearly. This is more of a mediocre sound that is designed to pump at very high volumes such as for a party. This is not high fidelity sound if that is what you are looking for.

SPEAKER LIGHTS
Although they are interesting at first, the lights seem kind of odd. For the price, it should have had better options. You can choose colors that stay on and do not blink or change out of seven choices. You can choose to have it flash and change color continuously, or you can choose to have the lights flash fast and change continuously, or you can flash the light in white. None of the settings go in time with the music.

You can also opt for no lights on as well. The lights do connect to the speakers by a second wire- it is not in with the speaker connector.

BLUETOOTH
The bluetooth took a while to recognize on the phone. We used android. Once it was paired, many types of music from old to new tracks, and older songs were not as clear or loud as newer tracks. As far as decoding from the bluetooth, it sounded pretty good and did not drop once.

RADIO
The FM sound on this was good and no complaints. Reception was pretty standard, nothing remarkable, but not horrible either.

REMOTE
Remote has to be pointed directly at the receiver. There were a few times where we had to press buttons twice because it would not pick up the signals. The remote itself is black and very small, which makes it easy to misplace. Marking it with neon paint is something we are going to do to make it harder to lose.

PROS
Nice and loud
Picks up highs very well
Bluetooth and CD player in one both work well
Two tweeters per speaker is nice

CONS
Remote very small
Lights sometimes are annoying
Wires are way too short- speakers can not be separated to put in corners of room
Speaker wires are proprietary to the receiver with special attachment (can not use other speakers)

THE BOTTOM LINE
If you want to have a good middle of the road stereo with nice separation of highs and decent sound, you might like this one. The lights and loud capacity also make this a great party unit if you like to fill up a large room or house with sound. Remote works okay , but speakers can not be separated very far. Due to proprietary speaker connections, the only way to change that would be to splice the wires if you are good at electronics.

RATING
This stereo is rather high priced for what you get. It does not have any bass boost, or customizing options for the equalizer. The sound is loud, but not overly high quality. Although this is not a bad unit, it really is not jaw dropping either. I want to give this THREE AND A HALF STARS due to the price and what you get for it. Unfortunately there is only a choice between four and three stars.

I was ecstatic to receive these headphones because, while I like to do some gaming before I go to bed, my wife gets shuteye earlier as her workday begins at the "buttcrack of dawn" (her expression); but while the TV is located next to the bedroom, the volume has to be kept at a reasonable volume so as not to disturb her beauty rest, which leaves me, then, with little to no volume.
Therefore, these headphones seemed like a lifesaver for the PS3, but when I first received them, I could not for the life of me get them properly connected. Like everyone else, it took me a while (days, unfortunately) to realize that I would need to use the RCA cables from the PS3 to use these to their fullest potential.

To start off, and due to the fact that I couldn't get them hooked up the PS3 first, I'll explain testing them on the Mac. They work terrifically. I tested out a bunch of music and some videos, and the sound was supreme. The software is a digital download from their site, and necessary to fully utilize the headphones' capabilities. At times it sounds a little overwhelming, but tweaking it to your standards with the software helps to alleviate that. It even lets you save profiles in case someone wants to set the settings to their own preferences.

After one charge, I've yet to recharge the headphones and been using them for days. Once I was able to wrap my head around the fact that I'd have to dig for my RCA cables from the PS3 box, I plugged them in, followed the slightly confusing instructions that came with the headset, and played away. True, the sound isn't the greatest in terms of clarity, but it suits basically nonetheless. For the price, you're probably better off getting other headphones that are specific to consoles. While these headphones advertise as being cross-platform, the Mac/PC audio leaves much to be desired from console hearing.

With that, the customer service is marvelous. I placed a comment on another's review before posting mine about the console frustration I was having, and I received an email a few hours later from a customer service rep from the company, asking me to get in touch with them about the issues I was having. With some patience and instruction, I finally realized that the HDMI cable just isn't enough to use these.

If you want some good cross-platform headphones and don't mind sacrificing quality for consoles, these are excellent; if you do more computer gaming than console, then go ahead. However, if you want some headphones that are superb for PS3 and/or 360, I'd suggest other ones. I didn't get to test these on the Xbox 360 as I don't have one, but from what I've heard don't even bother.

I am always on the lookout for radios to use in an emergency. Having lived through an extended outage during severe weather emergency for several weeks, not having any way to find out what was going on was difficult.

SIZE
This radio is a nice small size. Picture two juice boxes standing next to each other side by side. It fits just about anywhere. If you want to take it on a trip or camping, it has a very small footprint for packing.

CHARGING
Charging this is either micro USB, crank, or solar. I would say solar is more of a way to keep the radio trickle charged. I would not use that as my primary source as it takes a long time.

SOUND
The sound is really really nice. I am shocked at how nice this little unit sounds. It has great bass and midtones without sounding tinny or far away.

FLASHLIGHT
In an emergency having this as a flashlight is handy, although I would not use it unless no other options were there.

CHARGING PHONES?
I have not used it for charging phones. I keep power banks for that.

ALARM CLOCK/CLOCK
This is a great feature if you are camping or if you have to be up at a certain time during a power outage due to expected weather, checking on sump pumps, etc. It works well if you follow the instructions.

SD CARD
This plays music from an SD card and I have to say the sound is great.

CHARGING TIME
This took a few hours to charge up for us. Between 3 and 4.

PERFORMANCE
When running the radio, we got several days. We did not have it full volume, and we only played it a few hours at a time, not continually.

LOW BATTERY LIGHT
This has a low battery light which is a great feature. It helps you not let it run dry in power.

RECEPTION
The reception is excellent for FM, Very good for AM (some stations don't come in as well), and WB is also hit and miss, but still way nicer than most radios of this type that I have had.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a fantastic little radio. The sound is way nicer than expected and performance is great. Lots of great features make this handy to have.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. This is one of my favorite radios so far. It is really nice to work with and all of the power sources work well.

I received this as a free review sample. I subtracted a star because in small quarters the fan can get irritating, and also the picture area is a little skewed. The latter is not enough to ruin a video, but combined with the fan noise I felt that this falls into the four star category. To be fair, this is about on par with other portable projectors in this price range and sharing the general form factor.

On the plus side, this is an inexpensive way to get a large screen TV (assuming that your wall is the screen), that does a credible job of projecting movies, TV and presentations. I tested it using a Chromecast and streaming video from YouTube to my phone, then casting from my phone to the Chromecast dongle connected to one of the HDMI ports in the rear. No issues and it was actually a treat. I also tested it with an old Roku in an HDMI port streaming a movie from Netflix. To be sure, neither experience compares to my HD TV screen and surround sound system, but this does not come close to the price tags of those. Bang for the buck this is excellent if you are in a budget.

Frankly, I did not test the other ports, but do want to point out that the 'SD' card port is really USB A that will take a flash drive or an SD card using an adapter. Actually, I think that is a plus as well because flash drives are cheap and a 32GB one can hold a respectable amount of movies, home videos or presentations.

Sound quality is not spectacular, but is definitely adequate. Overall, this is as good as any projector among the four that I have either owned or tested, and is better than some. It would easily be a five star projector if it had a quieter fan. If you can live with that you will probably love it.

As the product description does not list or show the size of this MP3 player I list them here:

Length: 2 3/4 inches Width: 2 inches Thickness: 3/8 inch

Yes, small, but a powerhouse in functionality. I really miss the days when an MP3 player just played music. After a near fatal fall of my phone (luckily just the screen protector cracked!) it became important that an expensive phone might not be the best thing to lug around while performing yardwork. This excellent device solves that issue, and solves it well.

Songs and MP3 audio books were loaded easily onto the player. It is not made by Apple nor is part of their line, so the iTunes program does not work with this. However, it is a easy fix - just go to your Music folder on your computer, and drop the files you wish into this device's memory. Easy peasy and quick. It comes with an included 32 GB of memory, but can easily be upgraded if you install your own micro SD card, up to 128 GB.

It comes with wired earphones, which I did not use or test. With the invention of easy to pair Bluetooth earphones, I have no desire to be ever tethered with a headphone cord again. The player pairs easily with all 3 of my Bluetooth devices - earphones, headphones, and speakers. The sound from each device is flawless, which might be a function of the device, but is also determined by the source.

There are just 3 buttons on the side of this MP3 player - on/off button, volume up, and volume down. All other functions are controlled by the small but well designed touch screen. It is very comparable with the touch capability of modern phones, the programs are opened with ease and operate in an intuitive logical manner. There are other functions built into this device, but since I really got it as an MP3 player, that is what I am focused upon.

With this player comes a handy removable back clip, letting you clip it on/in a pocket, armband, belt, anywhere. Without the clip, it is small enough to easily slip into any pocked of your cloths, even the tiny change pockets in most jeans. Besides the wired earphones & clip, there is a 3mm audio cable for attaching it manually to another device, and a Micro USB cable for charging. There is a plastic protective film on the front face - it can be removed, but the touch screen operates just fine if it is left on.

This is my new favorite toy, It it not cheap or flimsy, but in all honesty, looks and feels like a tiny cell phone in how its constructed. It does not happen often, but this wonderful MP3 player exceeded my expectations.

The things that bothered me, however are:
a) It has USB-C, but does not allow itself to be charged with it. Unlike modern tablets and laptops that use PD chargers to juice up over the USBC, this actually uses a tiny proprietary plug that is almost certainly going to get lost eventually. It's not like it will be easy to find replacements or backups unlike major brands like HP and Lenovo, if I ever lose this plug I'm probably out of luck. I don't understand why it couldn't have used PD over the USB-c like every other modern device.
b) This one is a little bit more serious, but it complains that Windows is not activated. If you try to activate it, you are told that the server won't allow activation and to contact the vendor. I'm not entirely sure how to do that, and instead I'm left with a suspiciously inactivated version of Windows. Feels almost like for this price the software isn't licensed, which concerns me. I'm going to try and found out what it will take to activate, but it is definitely something you should know before plunking down money on a tablet that might not be using legitimate software.
Otherwise it is pretty useful for the price.

I've had the Harmony One remote since the day it came out, and now "upgraded" to the Harmony Ultimate Remote.

Build and Setup:
This is a very solid remote. It is heavy for its size with clean lines and elegant design. Inside the box is the powered hub with two remote blasters, remote, base, and power cords for the hub and the base. There does not appear to be a removable battery like with the Harmony One.

Set up was very simple. As I already had my settings in myremotesetup.com, I simply had to log into myharmony.com, transfer my settings to the new remote and the remote was setup. It was very easy.

The difference between this remote and other Harmony remotes is that this has a hub and blaster units that connects through your wireless network to allow you to connect and control your units with your smartphone.

You have to connect the hub and blaster units around the units you want to control. It has to be connected to your home wireless network, which was easy. You can either do it through myharmony.com or by pressing the setup button on the hub and your router (if it supports it) it was that easy.

I have my hub on the shelf with my Blu Ray, Dish Box, and Xbox. The one blaster is near the television, and the other is on another shelf with my Wii and my surround sound box. When you go into advanced settings on your remote you tell the remote to control the devices with either just the remote, with the hub, blaster 1, blaster 2, or all of them. This allows flexibility where you setup and place your devices and blaster and hub units.

Using the Remote:
The remote is easy to use. Many of the major buttons; play, pause, fast forward, volume and such are hard buttons on the remote. The remote has a large touch screen that can do all the other device options you may seem fit to try. It scrolls across several pages: Home screen allows you to choose between actions such as watch tv or dvd, channel favorites (which you program), current action screen that controls actions related to what you are doing, and finally the number screen, here is where you can enter numbers to change channels. This last part is a bit of a pain as when I am channel surfing I like to be able to press number buttons to change channels and you really can't do this with this remote without looking.

To operate DVR like functions you can also swipe up from any screen to access a black screen where you can program gestures. By default you press to pause, swipe right to skip forward, swipe right to swipe back, etc.

Phone App:
The phone app for the android is a bit lacking as it is not quite as sophisticated as the remote itself, but can do most of the actions of the remote as long as you are connected to the same wireless network as your hub is.

Troubleshooting:
The remote is easy to use and troubleshoot, Simply rebooting or re-syncing the remote can resolve most problems I've found. It also prompts you for assistance the first time you add an action or new device.

Overall this is a great remote. This will demand, though, some knowledge on your part as it is a very sophisticated remote. Many problems that occur can easily be resolved by some knowledge of networks, remotes, or Harmony devices in general. If you have experience with this you will enjoy the functions and capacity of this remote.

The Skagen Men's Hybrid HR Jorn Smartwatch is an elegant watch first and smart watch second. It is considered a hybrid because it is a watch first. Even with almost no battery life left, it still serves as a traditional watch with a stylish, all metal body and actual watch hands with glow-in-the-dark inserts for visibility without a front-light. In terms of thickness, unfortunately, this watch isn't any thinner than other Android Wear watches I've used.

For the "smart" portion of the watch, the Skagen is equipped with an e-ink display, which means that once the watch face is drawn, no more power is drawn from the battery to keep that display. This means that the watch will last much longer than a regular, oled-display smart watch. It is easy to tell that this e-ink display is of high quality because it does not have the yellow hue that older e-ink displays had. It is quite similar in quality to the paper-white kindle.

Beyond the screen is the software. The Skagen watch pares down the smart functionalities to only what a user may actually need on a watch. No games, no maps, no speakerphone functionality. Instead, the watch will track your workouts, show you notifications, and control your music player. It really is everything I normally do on my Android Wear watch. There are many watch faces, and multiple complications for customization. One can even use a photo as the background for the watch face. I did find that any watch faces with numbers tend to crowd out the UI and there is very little room for complications.

For all of this, Skagen priced this watch about $100 less than other smart watches so it really is a good option for those who just want a wearable that gives them the essentials.

I hate to change the battery for the Ring Doorbell. It's one of the reasons that I didn't purchase those "stick up" cameras to put up around the house. I am not interested in having to change batteries every month. With that in mind, I set out to find a solar panel that works with my Ring Doorbell 2.

Looking at other listings, I saw that the ones that claim to work with Ring generate 5v, 3amps. I confirmed that this board also generates 5v, 3a (check my pictures) and took the chance to cut off the microusb connector that it came with.

What was exposed were two wires; red and black so there was no guess work necessary to figure out which wires would be positive and ground (usb usually has 4 wires). After stripping the wires, I screwed the wires to the back of the doorbell and crossed my fingers.

From my pictures, you'll see that the Ring app recognized the solar panel and also charged from 46% to 55% after one day in the sun.

Purchased this 4 year plan in November 2016 on a Dell Laser Printer. Thus the printer was a little over 2 years when it started doing weird things and I made a claim.

Basically ... the printer stopped printing black ... it just got lighter and lighter. I attempted to clean the heads and change the cartridges to no avail. The printer would also keep running and not stop after done doing a printer job.

I printed my receipt / invoice off Amazon to PDF. I then went to SquareTrade's website attached the receipt. I then made a claim. The claim process was pretty easy and they actually approved me for a full refund. I just needed to fill out an affidavit. I did this but a week later I still had no refund. Somehow my affidavit didn't get logged even though I got a confirmation email. I called them on the telephone and they fixed everything and were kind about it. Within 24 hours they emailed me an Amazon gift certificate (my choice) which gave me an additional 5% back. I this received a $121 refund on an $118 printer that died in its 3rd year.

I have no complaints and would purchase a square trade warranty again.

Bits of interest as I read other people's low reviews:

1) You purchase a 4 year warranty, but really, for example, it is just 3 extra years beyond the purchase's original 1 year warranty (or however long applies). If your item dies in a year, you have to go to the manufacturer for help.

2) You need to have your receipt. No biggie. Amazon is super amazing that way. I can see all my order back to when Amazon just sold books. Print the invoice / receipt to PDF and there you go. Receipt. Proof of purchase.

3) There is no paper copy of this plan. This is great. It saves trees. You would probably lose it anyway. But Amazon also kept a copy of the fact that I purchased this along with the printer. It was in my order history. There is your proof and all the telephone numbers are there. It is so easy. You don't need a stack of papers.

4) If you file a claim and get 100% of your purchase price back, you cannot file a claim for the same item again. No brainer.

5) This isn't accident insurance. If you do a dumb thing like leave your camera on top of your husband's big rig fender and it ends up in a million pieces 1/2 mile from your house ... it is NOT covered. If you think it should be ... well then ... Take out an insurance policy ... not a warranty. Those are two different things.

6) If you got a deal and paid $65 for your item, but the item now sells for $400 ... you still only paid $65 and $65 is all you are getting back. You don't make money off warranties.

Lets start by defining what this set is and is not: it is a set of devices that are designed to be aesthetically pleasing. It is designed to be minimalist. It is not designed to be ergonomic.

I liken the keyboard to the apple wireless keyboard; keys feel like a laptop and you can't adjust the angle of the keyboard unless you stack up stuff under the back of the keyboard.

I do like the design of these. They are good looking devices and have an interesting magnetic battery compartment. If sleek and minimalist is what you are going for in your work space, these fit the bill.

These devices are plastic. I don't find this to be a major drawback, but some might have issues with it.

I have already stated, this set is not ergonomic. The mouse is especially awkward to use (unless you like the generally flat styles mouses like the apple magic mouse). My everyday mouse is the Microsoft Arc mouse (the older hinged one, not the one that bends). If you like the programmable back button on your mouse, you will find that you miss it on the microsoft designer set.

Pairing is where most people seem to have the biggest problem with this set. I also had issues. I am running Win 7 64 bit and have bluetooth on the computer. I had the most current BT4.0 drivers, but still ended up having to check the manufacturer's driver site for an additional driver. Even after installing a new driver, I was only able to get the keyboard to work consistently. The keyboard seems to work well and even when I start up my computer. The mouse, on the other hand, was less forgiving. No matter what I did, I could only SOMETIMES get the mouse to correctly pair. The computer could see it, but it wouldn't save the device or even stay connected after the pairing was complete. I am sure with more noodling around, I could probably get it connected, but for me, it isn't really worth it (I like my old Arc Mouse better). I bought the set with the intent of using just the keyboard, so it was not really a huge issue for me.

It seems that this set is intended for devices that use with Windows 8 or above, so keep that in mind when purchasing. I am using 7 and it generally works, but it is going to be most dependent on the Bluetooth drivers you have installed.

Pro-Tip: Look for used sets. A lot of people buy this keyboard thinking it will be easy to set up, then return it when they realize that you need bluetooth on your computer or you will have to buy a dongle. Currently, there are sets that are like new at 30% the suggested retail (half what they are actually selling for). Buy from Warehouse deals and the purchase is guaranteed by amazon (just like any new item that is sold by amazon). I think the deals that can be had on this set make it worth while for someone who is looking to try out the set, but not sure if it will play nice or if they will even like it.

The vignetting (black corners) came out on about half the pictures; some of them came out without much vignetting at all, which was surprising. There haven't been any light leaks, which may disappoint some users, but I know there are some mods out there (involving drilling holes into the side of the body) to create that effect if you wish. Double exposures are quite easy to do. I recommend using ISO400 speed film for best effects, especially when you're just beginning. The aperture is pretty much set at something like f8 and the shutter speed is around 1/100 (though this can vary), so most indoor pictures and even outdoor pictures in overcast lighting came out dark and dismal. I kind of wish I had bought the one that comes with a flash unit (holga 15b) but I'm gonna purchase that separately. The ones I took in sunlight are great though, so i recommend taking your Holga outside on a pretty day for your first roll. As for loading and unloading the film, it's quite easy to do. Just remember to press the film release button on the bottom of the camera before you rewind your film to avoid stretching or ripping apart your exposed film.

Overall, i think that the Holga 135BC is a wonderful little camera, great for those of us trying out a plastic camera for the first time, and a great attention-getter in public. I would definitely recommend it!

If you expect things to look like daylight, you'll be disappointed. It is far better than an old Russian unit I have which was an early generation light amplification unit, (green glow type). What you have here is a lot like a B&W security camera with an IR illuminator built into a hand held portable unit.

As some of the other reviews indicate, in the beginning it will seem somewhat cumbersome and clunky getting used to the controls and finding the most pleasing contrast settings. Takes a while, but once you get used to it, it gets a lot easier to make it work like you want it too.

One problem is that if you are just moving around in very low light and want to take a better look at things, it takes time for your eyes to adjust from darkness to the brightness in the viewfinder and then going back. The best way to use it is looking through it for an extended time scanning the area of interest, keeping your eye on the eyepiece. Different types of scenes will take some adjustment to optimize the appearance. Some things reflect light better than others so the best scenario is watching a particular area for an extended period. Once your eyes adjust and you get the contrast dialed in, it works pretty well. The IR illuminators are surprisingly pretty powerful. At short distances the high powered one will "wash out" what you're looking at, but it does seem to reach out pretty good. The claimed 600 feet is a bit of a stretch except under the most ideal of conditions. If you have some ambient light, I think it is better without it. But in really dark country night where you can't see your hand in front of your face, it does a great job of lighting things up.

My feelings on it are mixed. The basic idea of a monocular fits that role of "occasional use" where you want a quick better look at something, but I think that is asking too much from such a device. Plan on spending some time to get a better look at things because your eyes need adjustment time. Once you get the unit dialed in for the scene your watching, it will work pretty well. It's not cheap by any means, but it does work and it's a nice compact package. If you want really high performance night optics, plan on spending a lot more. It will definitely allow you to see reasonable well in darkness, but you have to fiddle with it. A lot has to do with the application. The pros and cons have given me some ideas about building a special purpose device.

Overall, it's a big improvement on some of the early night vision technology. The more I use it, the more I like it and learn tricks about using it effectively. I am happy with it, but for the average person with little experience with night vision, your expectations may not be met and that's why I'm giving it 3 stars. You will need a little patience to go through the learning curve using it.

Projectors for home use are typically set up for home theater systems. I have seen a number of systems set up with projectors suspended from the ceiling, and I have seen a few that rely on being mounted on a table top. This is a table top model and it is a very good and easy-to-use projector.

This is a 300-lumen projector which is fine for home theater systems, though it would be a little underpowered to use in a larger room or something like a small church. It is good for small presentations too and is a good option if you want to take it with you for meetings instead of keeping it permanently placed somewhere.

There are several input sources for which the projector is configured. For testing and experimentation I found it easiest to work with HDMI though I was able to use some of the other sources as well. It accepts VGA (which is great for older computer systems and other hardware), it can read files from an SD card or even a USB drive. Using a USB drive or SD card, this projector becomes very compact and portable and doesn't even need an external source of input.

This projector even has a pair of speakers inside so you can use this projector for the entire A/V experience, though you will get better sound from a dedicated sound system. This projector is capable of receiving sound as well as outputting it.

I used the HDMI input to feed the image from my computer to the projector and it did a fine job of displaying my desktop on the wall for me. I was also able to configure Windows to use it as an extended display so I could then look at PowerPoint on the computer screen and use the projector to output the slide show. This is very, very convenient and makes this configuration ideal for presentations. I was able to adjust the focus manually and get the image as sharp as I wanted too.

The remote with this unit is great. It provides full access to the projector's functions, so if the projector is on a shelf out of reach the remote is sufficient for any adjustments you may want to make. If you prefer not to use the remote or have some reason you would rather directly interact with the projector there are several buttons on the top of the projector that give access to the different functions. You can change the input source, power on and off and get into the menu system which allows you to tweak all manner of settings: brightness, change the resolution, update the firmware from USB, set the date and time and more.

This projector does output a lot of heat – to be expected from a projector with a bright light in it. Make sure that you have decent ventilation in the room when using this projector unless you want the room to warm up. I did notice that when the projector is shut off, the fan stops too which is a minor disappointment – I would rather have had the fan continue for a few minutes afterward to cool down the LED.

This is a nice projector. It accepts a lot of different input types, it works well for small rooms and home theaters and it is easy to take with you due to the small size. It is especially useful if you want to run your video or presentation from either USB or from the SD card. If you're looking for a small-scale projector, this is a good choice.

A UPS is one of those products you don't give much thought to until you are in a situation where you REALLY need it to work. The display on the Cyberpower is a great feature - tells you all sorts of useful info such as your battery status, run time, load level and others so you always know what's going on.

Nice footprint, puts out very little heat (compared to a Tripplite that this replaces which threw off a huge amount of heat - nice in the winter time, but not so nice in the summer), simple setup. My only complaint, and the reason it lost one star, is the spacing of the outlets. You have to use outlet extenders if you have the "wall wart" transformers. I have three of them (modem, router and external hard drive) - they all fit on the Tripplite since it offers widely spaced outlets, but couldn't fit them into the Cyberpower without extenders.

The other nit is the location of the power button. It's right on the face of the unit, and you have to be careful not to hit it accidentally. A better design would be to either locate it somewhere else or, better yet, put a safety lock on it so you can ensure you don't power down unless you truly want to do so.

Both are minor issues and can be easily worked around. I'm very pleased with the unit so far, and recommend it to anyone looking for a good UPS and a nice price.

OK, take 2. My original review of this product got hijacked somehow. After writing it, I checked back a couple hours later and my screen name and original title were there, but my review got replaced with what seemed like some guy's journal entry. It had absoluterly nothing to do with this or any other product. Strange.

Anyway - as mentioned in my original posting, this review is more a condemnation or earbud headphones in general than the Sennheiser CX300-B, which I decided to try after my "over ear" style Sony noise canceling headphones went on the fritz. My past experience with earbuds was not good, although I had only ever tried the type that come with the iPod and not the "ear plug" type that go in the ear canal, like the Sennheiser CX300-B. However, having owned a pair of Sennheiser over the ear headphones back in the 70's, my impression of the company and their products was good. So, I decided to take the plunge. What a mistake.

After opening the package (no easy feat - damn sound welded plastic clamshells!), I popped on the medium-sized bud covers (appropriate for my size ears) and inserted them into my ears. I turned on my mp3 player and listened for a few minutes. The sound was adequate - nothing spectacular. I did notice they had decent bass and did block some external noise. I kept listening as I stepped outside to go to the store. I couldn't believe what I heard. Every step I took was amplified in my head - like a booming bass drum. Even the gentle bumping of the cord against my chest was amplified - a constant thump, thump, thump that was impossible to ignore. As it turns out, the very feature that blocks a modicum of external noise, also amplifies any sound that travels through the body. Even breathing is amplified! As I walked, it sounded as though I was listening to someone breathe over a PA system! I had hoped to use these while running, but there's no way that's going to happen. In fact, the problem with amplified sound is so bad, I won't use them at all.

I am very disappointed in this product and will never buy any ear plug style headphones again. I don't understand why anyone would sell them, let alone use them. They may have great sound reproduction, but the listening experience is totally ruined by the sounds that get amplified through the body. It amazes me that people buy similar style products that sell for hundreds of dollars. The only way you can enjoy the sound they produce is to sit perfectly still. I'm glad I only paid about $16 for these things. I won't return them because it'll be too much of a hassle - probably cost more to ship them back than I paid.

BTW - The photo of the product is misleading. The cord looks thicker than it actually is and there's no way it can be coiled as is shown in the photo. It gives the impression the cord is more supple and flexible that it really is. Also, one end of the cord is longer than the other. Not sure why this is, but the thinness of the cord makes it prone to kinking and tangling. In fact, since one side of the cord is longer than the other, it makes it even more prone to tangling.

Bottom line - steer clear of the Sennheiser CX300-B and all ear plug style earbuds.

I was in the market for a case for a thin mini itx system I was building and this one was the cheapest I came across that didn't make me fear for my components. I read all the reviews I could find and even watched a few YouTube videos and ultimately decided that this was the case for me. The build went fairly smoothly (no late night trips to find parts I found out I needed at the last minute or incompatibility issues), but I did encounter a few problems which other reviewers had also mentioned and I chose to ignore.

First Problem: Cannot use hdd mount with stock Intel heat sink installed
The product description claims this case can accommodate a stock heatsink, which is absolutely true, but if you do use one, a hard drive, even a thin ssd like I used, can't be mounted using the bracket they provided. I thought I was stuck at this point, and even tried mounting the ssd to the top of the case, but then I noticed some screw holes on the back of the case just above the I/O shield that seemed to be spaced just right for the holes on the side of the ssd. A few minutes and a little creative drill work later, and I had a place to mount my ssd, no bracket required.

Second Problem: The front panel connectors are way too short
My major problem with this case is the front panel connectors. For a case this small, it seems like it would be easy to include cables long enough to reach from the corner where they connect to the case to the opposite corner, just to be sure there was enough wire no matter what the motherboard setup was. Minibox did not take this approach, leaving me to splice the wires for the power button with and led with doorbell wire and plug the front two usb connector into a single auxiliary usb header, which only allows one port to work. It's mainly for this reason that I knocked off a star.

In conclusion, this is a really nice, well-made case if you're willing to deal with the few problems that it has. View the attached pictures for a better idea of how I ended up mounting the ssd and a general view of what this case looks like with a system in it.

Basically these phones have a distinct bias towards the higher frequencies, with a crossover to bass in my right ear and flat mid range response. I was prepared to give this a poor rating. As other reviewers stated there is an issue with the fm transmitter strength leading to static.

I found there is stronger FM signal if the device is installed away from electrical components. Since most people, including myself, installed it initially on the dash, the radio and other electrical system components caused interference. I moved the device to be on the corner of the rear view mirror and had noticeably stronger FM reception.

The device plugs into the cars cigarette lighter. There is a port on the plug to insert an additional USB charger, so you can continue to use your phone's charger while this is plugged in.

Synching is fairly straight forward. Press the button the back of the device, search USB devices on your phone, and it will pair. The readout is red when not connected, blue when connected.

FM transmitter will transmit on most every frequency from 88.1 to 107.9fm. There is a button on the top to search for the best signal, but I found it was unreliable. It also has two presets so you can set two signals you know to work.

The button on the front lets you switch between playing music from your phone to working phone controls. It also allows you to pause music playback and end calls by pressing the music or phone button respectively.

Since it plays through your car stereo, music and calls play through your car speakers. When you are connected to a clear channel, the sound is clear and distortion free. Phone calls sound clear. There is a small microphone on the front that picks up your voice and I was pleased at the quality of my voice. Every person I called with the device were surprised to hear I was on a hands free speakerphone. They said it sounded better than my USB headset, and almost as good as using the phone's internal microphone.

Overall the base features were very good; music playback and phone features worked very well. There was an issue with the FM signal; there was often static, but found that it was improved by placing it where there was less electrical interference. Once I found the correct place, it was acceptable in that regard. Though I am only giving 3 1/2-4 starts as I am not fully comfortable with recommending it based on that alone.

There are 5 card slots. I only used the CF and SD slots since those are the cards that I use. No problems with card insertion or removal. There's a visual indicator of read/write activity.

In addition to moving items to your hard drive, you can also do card-to-card data transfers.

The reader is compact, measuring just under 3.5 inches long and about 1.75 inches wide. It's very low profile, standing about ½ inch tall. The card slots are on the front, and the USB connection is on the back.

Simple, straightforward and works well. That's pretty much all I need in a card reader. Hopefully it will last longer than my previous one - I'll update the review should this not perform well over time.

This is a great, mobile, easy HotSpot device that works just like any Wi-Fi on any device with a great connection. Mobile supposedly for 10 hours, less than hour recharge.

There's only one caveat: AT&T will tell you the pre-installed SIM card it comes with, sealed in new packaging, is INVALID. AT&T will give you a good one for FREE. This according to AT&T themselves. They will send you a new, free one you can use; tell them what device you have and setup a data plan.

All you need then is to add a Data plan. This device, according to AT&T, *only* works with a postpaid plan ($50.00/month for 5 G's minimum), however there's no contract. There is a credit check. It will not work with prepaid, it will not work with a lesser plan, no matter what the packaging or Amazon description says. I just spent like 20 minutes on the phone with a very helpful, patient, and knowledgeable AT&T customer service representative who also consulted another department for verification.

The one exception is if you already have an AT&T cellphone plan (I do), you can "share" your data package you already have for only $20/month. So that's what I did. It still is postpaid, and there still is no contract on that part of the plan with your new HotSpot device. You'll be given a new number that's only for the HotSpot without a cellphone (Voice) plan component.

I'm really glad I bought this great device, I was a little apprehensive because I'm not techie and I've never tried a mobile HotSpot device before. To make it simple, get AT&T to install (instore) or send you a new SIM card that they say works with this device, and then you can set up the device (supposedly) online with ease. I paired this sound bar with our Sony XBR-65X850E 65” TV and it could not have been easier.

While my TV would allow me to connect to the sound bar via Bluetooth I opted to connect via the HDMI ARC connection to avoid any sound lag. In addition to these 2 connection options you can connect via optical cable.

I followed the instructions - plugged the HDMI cable (included) into the ARC HDMI port, plugged the sound bar and subwoofer into the surge protector and turned everything on. The TV automatically recognized the soundbar and changed my output.

The sound bar automatically connected to the subwoofer without me doing anything at all. I decided to move the subwoofer to another area of the room - I unplugged it, moved it, plugged it back in and it again reconnected without any problem.

I was able to pair the system with my iPhone without any issue and the sound is stunning. From the rich bass of the subwoofer, the vibrant midtones, to the crisp highs - every note is clear and distinct.

While I have a true 5.1 surround system most of the TV broadcasts are not going to utilize that type of system and the sound is actually richer through this sound bar with a subwoofer.

This soundbar can be easily wall mounted using the included template. Since I have my TV on an entertainment center base I’ve used the “AmazonBasics Universal Sound Bar TV Bracket - Adjustable Arm for Mounting Above or Under TV, Black” to mount the sound bar below the TV where it hangs perfectly level. Since this is a universal bracket it requires a bit of figuring out the best configuration but it comes with everything you’ll need and it works great.

The entire system is intuitive and user friendly. While many sound systems require hours to hook up and figure out how to use correctly this one is so straightforward. The remote doesn’t have a bunch of excess buttons that you’ll never need or use.

The new sound technologies Sony employs with this sound system are incredible. The “Immersive AE” function changes the directionality on the sound and is remarkable.

In my instance my TV remote was able to control it immediately with no issues.

I have always been impressed with the quality of Sony’s audio and video products - they are constantly innovating and improving on their products and in my experience they hold up far better than other brands.

I highly recommend this soundbar for anyone looking for an easy way to improve the quality of the sound from your TV - and you’ll be pleasantly surprised by the rich sound it will deliver regardless of what you play through it.

While I'm quite comfortable using an SLR, I've not been all that handy with a camcorder in the past. It's been a few years since I used one, so I was curious to see if user-friendliness has kept pace with technological advancements.

With this model it has. I found it very easy to use right out of the box with just some minor trial and error. I did end up reading the manual (which is pretty decent) but the main functions were pretty self apparent by just fiddling around with it a bit. The menu structure is logical and well presented; the screen is clear and easy to view.

The overall build quality is excellent. It feels more substantial in hand than I expected at this price point while retaining a very lightweight and easy to carry profile. I like the button placement - feels very natural in hand.

I love having the internal memory for storage as well as the little touches, such as a built-in USB connector. These features help make this a grab-and-go type of device, which increases the likelihood and ease of bringing it along and capturing video. (Note: you can also use a plug-in memory card should you want to.)

The video quality in good light/outdoors is excellent - very sharp and clear. Low-light performance is a somewhat grainy but quite decent. Stills are pretty decent. It won't put an SLR to shame, but it's more than good enough for casual snapshots. The internal mic works well and is more immune to wind noise than I expected.

My only significant disappointment with the cam is the projector. Wonderful idea, but the actual performance is lackluster. The projected video is hard to see clearly if there's any appreciable amount of light in the room. The 100 inch projection spec is wildly optimistic if you expect to actually see what is being projected.

Given that this cam does everything else so well, is so easy to use, and a breeze to tote along, I won't detract any stars due to the shortcomings of the projector feature. This is a great cam for the novice cam user (such as myself) or even an intermediate user. However, if the projection feature is a primary need, this may not be a good cam for your needs.

If it makes a beeping noise:
One beep - for low pressure alarm (di - di - di - di)
Two beeps - for high pressure alarm (Didi - Didi - Didi - Didi)
Three beeps - for overload protection (Dididi - Dididi - Dididi - Dididi)
Four beeps - for short circuit protection
Five beeps - for overheat protection

The solution for each problem:
Undervoltage alarm: Replace the battery or fully charge the battery before using it.
Low voltage shutdown: Change the battery or fully charge the battery before restarting
Over voltage alarm: Change the battery with a voltage lower than 15V higher than 10.5V
High voltage machine shutdown alarm: Change the battery with a voltage lower than 15V higher than 10.5V
Overload protection: Unplug the load, restart the inverter, and the inverter will work normally.
Short circuit protection: Remove the electrical appliance that caused the short circuit
Overheating protection: Shut down and cool down

I wouldn't run epic settings on anything short of a NASA computer, and even still I'd be worried it would crash the space station or accidentally launch missiles.

Bottomline; this computer will make most games playable, they will not be "epic". It's a decent entry level gaming computer. I am not going to tell you to build your own if you want to save money and get a better set up for the same amount. I have built my own computer, I have also wanted to throw it on the lawn and light it on fire, because when something goes wrong I have no one to blame but myself, and no one to fix it either. So... ignore the "build it yourself" shamers. You do you. If you want to buy an entry level gaming computer go for it. Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.

This was my first telescope.  I have read a lot about telescopes and plan on buying a much more expensive one but then I read that you can take a scope like this and upgrade the eye piece and the finder scope and have something very usable for a basic telescope.  It is below zero here so rather than go outside I did all my reviewing inside looking out my window at the mountain.  The listing provides a great overview of what you get with the scope so I won't detail it here.  I will say that it does comes with everything you need to get ab great intro into having a telescope of this type.  The trip is very shaky  and when you look out at such a great distance any movement of the tripod makes focusing difficult. Using a remote for your camera or phone would work best.  It comes with a phone adapter so I attached an older phone to it and took a couple of nice shots of a portion of the top of the mountain.  Given I didn't have to do much I thought they turned out pretty good.  The focus needs improvement but I guess I wasn't expecting a lot from this lens.  The finder scope is used to first find the object you want to see in the telescope.  It worked fine.  Then you go to the telescope lens and the object should be there and all you need to do is focus, which I did.  Because the tripod is shaky it is hard to get a good focus as just touching the eye piece cause it to shake.  This is a very inexpensive tripod and most good scopes would require a tripod 3 times the cost of this entire product.  For this price you are getting an intro to using a telescope.  With some experience with this I should be able to get better at focusing.  I took these mountain pix with the 25mm eye piece.  It comes with a nice carrying case for the scope and tripod.  There is also a nice small case for the lenses.  The instructions and well done with a nice bird watching book included also.  I will enjoy taking this with me when I go camping where maybe I will see some birds.  I highly recommend this scope as a good start for getting into this hobby.

This BOSE SOUNDLINK COLOR BLUETOOTH SPEAKER may not be the ideal portable speaker for serious audiophiles--because it has no treble/base buttons, only volume buttons--but I love mine. The sound is rich and full, whether it's paired with my old Sony Bravia TV, iPad2, or Kindle Fire, or connected by AV stereo cable (3.5mm M/M) to my MP3 player's headphone jack. The volume is controlled by the device the speaker is connected to, or by the plus/minus volume buttons on the speaker itself. The speaker also has an Aux button for the direct cable connection, and a Skip button that lets you go forward or backward in your music selections.

This Bose portable speaker can support two Bluetooth-connected devices at once, so you can switch between two devices (e.g., an iPad and a Kindle Fire) without repeating the pairing process every time. A great feature! The speaker automatically connects with the last-connected Bluetooth device, and switches devices when you press the Bluetooth button. The speaker's voice prompts help you with pairing, and tell you which two devices are currently paired. The voice prompts can be disabled, if you wish.

This Bose speaker is definitely an improvement over the speakers built into my old Sony Bravia TV. Voices are much clearer--including the dialogue from British TV shows--and the sound is far richer. Of course, using this speaker instead of a TV sound bar is only a temporary solution, because the speaker needs regular recharging. When fully charged, it delivers sound for many hours (up to 8) and outlasts the charge on the [[ASIN:B004B8GF7Y TaoTronics® Bluetooth Transmitter]] that I added to my non-Bluetooth-enabled TV.

Whether the TaoTronics transmitter was connected to the TV's headphone jack or to the TV's AV ouputs, this speaker paired instantly. However, when the TV transmitter was connected to the AV outputs, the speaker produced some static unless it was positioned close to the TV. When the TV transmitter was connected to the headphone jack, the speaker produced no static at all, no matter where it was positioned (within the Bluetooth range).

This Bose speaker charges quickly with the included AC adapter and USB cable. Pressing the speaker's power button produces a battery indicator that glows red, amber, or green to indicate the current level of charge. The speaker is lightweight enough to carry around in a backpack or tote bag. There is a case available (see [[ASIN:B00NJGRKG4 Bose SoundLink Color carry case]]), but I don't think a case is needed, because the speaker seems to be sturdily constructed.

Several of my family have been into taking photos for a long time. We have been through quite a few cameras, although not top of the line, still not inexpensive by any means. $500 is usually the price range of cameras we have purchased.

The Fujifilm FinePix S1 is a contradiction of sorts. You might say there is a love-hate relationship with it.

WHAT WE LIKE
Camera lightweight for what is in it
Easy grip- to hang on to and hold
Great neck strap
Macro and Supermacro capabilities are good
Durable
WiFi feature works great with tablet (android OS)
50X zoom works great (have to have very steady hand for that)
Great movies for what it is
Mini HDMI port works for TV or monitor
Photos with flash turn out well consistently
Left and right zoom buttons come in VERY handy
Takes decent self portraits, although a bit clumsy at times to hold
Timer worked well

WHAT WE DON'T LIKE
Navigation can be frustrating
Directional pad can be frustrating
Light sensor is unstable
Automatic settings very unstable and inconsistent
Photos look better on LCD pad than they actually are
Sometimes photos look flat and/or grainy (not 3D looking or clear)

THE BOTTOM LINE

THE LIGHT PROBLEM
We tested this camera extensively inside, outside, at night, in indirect light and with sunlight and found that the light sensor in this camera is way too inconsistent for satisfying picture taking. Sometimes the colors captured were exquisite and better than any other camera I have ever used. I didn't have to do any adjusting at all. Other times they were abyssmal.

For instance, in taking 10 pictures in a row, changing absolutely nothing, it was virtually impossible to have two pictures turn out alike. They were all vastly different. Sometimes they were dark, sometimes way too light, sometimes perfect. That is a lot of effort to capture the perfect picture.

On the flip side, one night in absolute frustration not being able to capture anything decent at all, I turned out all of the lights so that the room was pitch black. I held my camera up to my fish tanks and snapped a few pictures. Besides traumatizing my fish from the sudden light, I was shocked to see some of the most beautiful photos I had taken all evening. Perfect colors, clarity and definition consistently.

It appears that when you use the flash, that the color calibration kicks into high gear and you get pretty darned good photos.

You can not live your life taking flash photos unfortunately.

PHOTO QUALITY
I found that by using various settings and experimenting, I could get pretty nice photos- but I had to use a lot of effort. The menu is not easy to navigate, nor is it forgiving if you take too long to decipher it- it shuts off on you and you have to go through it again.

I did find that sometimes I was taking what I thought were fantastic photos (from the LCD screen) only to upload them to my photo editing program and seeing that they were grainy or blurry or just plain flat and un-dimensional. On the LCD screen they looked amazing. On the other hand, sometimes they turned out blah on my LCD screen, but great on the SD card.

Once in a while, I have problems with my Canon with color. I love bright colors and my photography focus is often color oriented. Canon often understates color way too much for me and I have to spend some time to get it to look accurate in photo editing. With the FinePix S1, however, once in a while, I could capture color that was so gorgeous and realistic that I would gasp and be very excited.

The problem is that it is not always predictable and that was frustrating. Like the proverbial carrot on the string in front of the horse, I find myself reaching for this camera when frustrated with my others to capture colors that don't seem to do well on any other camera. Once in a while the effort is worth it so I come back for more frustration.

FINAL COMMENTS
As I said at the beginning, I have a bit of a love hate relationship with this camera. On the one hand it is a lot of work to get decent photos, but on the other hand, when you do manage to get one, it is amazing. Rare, but amazing.

If Fujifilm would fix the issues with depth in photos, consistency in the light sensor, and quality issues on automatic settings, this camera would be a MUST buy. As it is now, however, I can only give it three stars because of the inconsistency in quality of photos and the effort I have to go through to get a good one. I gave it three stars because once in a while it does capture photos with brilliant colors that none of my other cameras will capture, despite the slightly lower quality at times. The videos are great- sound excellent and clarity nice. The flash is great. Out of the way when you don't want it- and nice photos. It has potential to be a fantastic camera.

As it is now, until they correct a few things, it is only average.

The A7000 has cloth speaker covers on top, while this A5000 has plastic. I have smaller ear canals than normal (as told by my audiologist), so I always opt for a size down when trying on tips. I followed the instructions to insert these Technics buds into my ear holes with the smaller tips, and they fit great. Sony actually sucks out the volume outside; these Technics add a white noise filter, which to me obstructs the audio I'm listening to. There's an app you can download to your phone which turns off the white-noise filter, so I did that, and turned of equalizer settings. On my phone I use Poweramp v3, AntennaPod, and Amazon Prime HD. They all sound great, but, because the Technics don't slide all the way into my ear, some of the bass gets lost. Higher volumes help, but then you run into ear damage.

Overall, I'm pleased with my first set of wireless ear buds. While they won't take over my Shure IEMs, they're super convenient to have during my work commutes.

I got my mother the Lifeproof FRE case for her iPhone 6. For the last year, she’s been using a cheap case I bought on Amazon, the Diztronic Voyeur Case. I didn’t feel it was protective enough, so I hoped the Lifeproof FRE would work for her.

Unfortunately, she didn’t like the case at all, and wanted it off her phone minutes after I put it on. I made her use it for a few weeks, and while she didn’t experience any sound problems, there were several quality of life things that sealed the dislike for the Lifeproof FRE case.

PRO:
—The built-in screen protector is pretty good. I liked that I didn’t have to install it myself, as it’s part of the case.

CONS:
—Within minutes of putting the Lifeproof FRE case on her phone, I dropped it. The back of the case is slick, some kind of hard plastic instead of the grippier TPU case. The Lifeproof case just didn’t feel nice to hold in my hand, and with the slicker plastic, I worried that my mom would drop her phone as well.

—The little “door” that protects the charger port was super hard for her to open. Every time my mom wanted to charge her phone, I had to come do it for her, since she couldn’t get the door open. I understand needing a tight seal for the waterproof protection, but there has to be an easier way to access the charger port.

—The small oval cut out for charging cords was too small for my non Apple Lightning cables. I have two that are Apple certified, AmazonBasics and Zerolemon, and neither fit.

—My mom found it impossible to manipulate any of the buttons. I assume the buttons will loosen up over months, but boy, they are super hard to press when the case is new.

My mom’s not quite the intended audience for the case, but as she plans to keep her iPhone for a few years, we want it to stay in nice shape. And you never know when you’re going to drop your phone into a snowbank or puddle, so having a waterproof case adds peace of mind. But I’ll have to keep looking for her, because the Lifeproof FRE had a couple of little problems that added up to big annoyances.

The UPRIGHT SMART WEARABLE POSTURE TRAINER is an "anti-slouch" posture trainer that really works! I discarded my [[ASIN:B00N9P8GMW Lumo Lift]] after a week or so, because my sitting posture is pretty good, and I rarely slouched badly enough to trigger the Lumo Lift. In contrast, the Upright buzzes me whenever I start to relax my posture even partway to a full slouch.

The Upright needs to be pasted to your back with gentle adhesive pads (60 included), rather than pinned to your clothing (like the Lumo Lift), but the greater sensitivity makes the extra effort worthwhile. Packets of one-time-use adhesive pads are available from the Upright web site for about $15.

You can wear the Upright between your shoulder blades if you're going to be standing, walking, and sitting; or at the small of your back if you're an Upright novice or generally sitting. As long as it's turned on, the Upright works even without the accompanying app (Android or iOS) that tracks your training progress. The Upright app uses Bluetooth to connect with the wearable Upright.

The app walks you through the simple setup, which mostly involves (1) finding the proper spot for placement on your back, and (2) calibrating the device so that it can detect a slouch. Once it's calibrated, the device will gently buzz you whenever you sink into a slouch--which inevitably happens as your muscles tire from holding a single position--so that you can straighten up. (There is no sound. The product page video that demonstrates the buzz is kind of amusing.)

When you create an account (free), the app collects information about your height, weight, and age, and then generates a daily posture training program that is personalized for you. The training program begins with your wearing the device for a few minutes, and then for longer and longer sessions. At the end of a session, the app gives you a score, based on how long you held your upright posture. (Mine was only 86%, because I intentionally slouched to test the buzz.)

The Upright arrives fully charged. The app tells you how much charge is remaining in your Upright. When you're charging the device in the supplied charging dock, a solid red light tells you that it's properly connected and charging.

My work bought each person in my branch a pair of QC25’s from Amazon. I also own a set of QC2’s.

I have to say, whether I’m wearing my QC25’s or QC2’s, I love my Bose QC headsets and will not travel without them. I also use them for work, not just at work.

Since I have both a pair of the old and new, I thought I’d do my own comparison:

1. Equally comfortable

2. In a quiet environment, where noise cancelling isn’t really a factor, I think the sound quality (even of the older QC2’s) is pretty comparable. If I were thinking about upgrading just for sound quality, I don’t think I would.

3. Noise cancelling has definitely improved in the QC25’s over the older QC2’s. In a noisey environment where noise cancelling matters, the difference is noticeable. The QC2’s are good, the QC25’s are clearly better.

4. The QC25’s will work w/o a battery. If the battery dies in the QC25, you will have music, just not NC. In the older QC2’s, the headphones would not work at all w/a dead or no battery.

5. QC25’s have a mic for taking or making phone calls. The QC2’s did not.

6. The case is smaller, but just as protective for the QC25’s. The QC2’s do not fold up as small.

7. They both look good.

8. The prices really haven’t changed over the years.

The bottom line, I love my Bose headsets, both of them. I would absolutely recommend buying a set, particularly if you have a need for a set of quality headphones at work or for travel.

For me, after reviewing the older and newer QC headsets, I don’t think I’d upgrade until the older QC2’s stopped working. I think that Bose headsets are built so well, that time doesn’t diminish the quality and utility of Bose’s older products.

Okay, I am not an audiophile. In fact, I have cookie-bite hearing loss, which makes it very difficult to listen to anything without either the voice range being too hard to hear or all the frequencies outside of my bitten-off range being way too loud. But I'm starting to exercise indoors more (just moving around, "dancing," is my favorite activity) and have purchased several sets of Bluetooth headphones to try to find something that would work for me for that. This review will briefly compare (to the extent of my ability to describe the experience without audiophile-type knowledge, and also in view of my planned use) three sets of Bluetooth cans, in descending order of quality and expensiveness:

Parrot Zik 2.0
Phillips SHB9100
Alpatronix HX110

I tested each of these by playing two songs ("Money For Nothing" by Dire Straits and "Love and Affection" by Joan Armatrading), both of which have a decent range of complexity but not so much that my ears would get too fatigued too quickly. Also, please note that I have a small head and small ears; the fit of each of these is good on my head. All but the Parrot Zik are on-ear; the Zik is over-ear. Only the Zik requires an Android or iOS app to get the best sound, although all can be used no-frills. I think the Zik is the only one with noise cancellation.

First, the Alpatronix. If you're going to ruin a pair of headphones during a workout, these are the ones to do it with. The overall effect of these is a kind of "wall of sound" that gives you the illusion of a large, expansive sound. After comparing them to the high-end Parrot Zik, however, it soon became clear to me that little details and nuances of the music are lost. If you're sweating to dance tunes, however—especially if you're going to a gym or anywhere else that losing an expensive pair of cans would be a disaster—these are the ones I'd go with. And they are small enough, I believe, for a middle-school child. The range of the Bluetooth is not great. It cuts out badly when I'm in the kitchen or bathroom, where there are appliances in the path of the signal. And of the three, this is the only one that cannot be used wired.

The Phillips headphones are a discontinued model that I've had a while. They used to be my favorite, but that was more because of how comfortably they fit, not how discriminating I am musically. The cup covers feel buttery. The sound is okay. They don't feel as boosted as the Alpatronix ones, which can be a good or a bad thing, depending on what you're after. The on-ear cups fit snugly but don't press to the point of headache, and the headband is sufficiently adjustable that people with larger heads would have no trouble with them. The Bluetooth range is just a tiny bit better than the Alpatronix. If I had to pick a word to describe the sound of these, it would be "smudged." Again, depends on what you're listening to and what you like.

And now we get to the Parrot Zik 2.0s, which are the real point of this review. At first I had a very maddening time with these, so much so that I started to just write them off as impossible. You must have an Android or iOS phone or tablet to be able to install the app that allows you to do all the fancy Concert Hall, Equalizer, Noise Reduction, and Tuned By stuff, and that's a challenge for me because I don't really use any of those. (I have a MacBook Pro, which I tried first without the app, both plugged in charging and via Bluetooth. It was okay but not hundreds-of-dollars okay.) But I do have an up-to-now little-used Android Jelly Bean tablet that I downloaded the app(s) to for testing.

CRITICALLY IMPORTANT: Don't do what I did, which was follow the directions to download the Parrot Audio Suite; the only one in the Google Play Store did not end in a "2" but maybe the Apple Store has the "2" version mentioned. The Audio Suite app did not work at all with my headphones, so I went back and got the Parrot Zik 2.0 app. I had both apps on my tablet, and they were apparently conflicting badly, because all I got was constant cut-outs and garbage. I called Technical Support to find out what I was supposed to do, thinking maybe the headphones were defective, and they said to completely uninstall the Parrot Audio Studio, remove the pairing, and just use the Parrot Zik 2.0 app. When I did that, BEAUTIFUL!

Those little details and subtle nuances I mentioned before? I can hear them. I can manipulate the speaker placement through the Concert Hall effect (my sweet spot is actually closer to 60%, not the wider placements many of the Tuned By presets favor) and also the equalizer settings. If I knew what I was doing, I could tune everything to help compensate for my cookie-bite hearing loss. (I'm thinking a visit to an audiologist to get a current printout of my range of loss is in order.) I love that I can just tap the right ear cup to pause the music without taking off the headphones (why would I bother with that if I don't have to?), and the directions make sense; up to up the volume, down to reduce the volume, swipe back toward the back of my head to go back, swipe forward toward my face to move forward to the next track.

Okay, though, here's what I don't like. The controls are very sensitive, so every time my little dog (who sits above my head on my recliner as I work) moves his tail, the music is paused. It would be nice if this could be better controlled to a degree with an app or firmware update. I've got everything disabled in the app and it's still a problem. Also, I started out trying to use just a finger to swipe, and this requires starting right in the center of the cup or it doesn't work reliably. (You have to look in the mirror to locate the center of the cup, and that's not going to happen.) I finally figured out that a flipper-like movement with all my fingers works better, but it's going to take some getting used to. And the app really needs work. My main request is that I'd like to be able to adjust speaker placement and room size (Silent Room, Living Room, Jazz Club, or Concert Hall) without losing the other Tuned By preset settings that I've selected/downloaded. If nothing else, at least don't block out the preset's visual information in the equalizer window so I can see roughly how to duplicate the setting as a starting point. A "duplicate/revise settings from Tuned By X" in Producer Mode would be a marvelous enhancement. Also, I wish the app would auto-rotate like all my other apps do. Because now I'm going to have to use this tablet more often. I'm going to have to start listening to music every day, and not just while I'm exercising either. The Ziks sound that good.
