I love the look and feel of this VERSO "DARWIN" CROCCO standing cover for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" tablet. Red is my favorite color, and the faux crocodile texture is really fun.

This cover holds the tablet firmly with silicone-enhanced elastic corner bands (patent pending). The bands have a rubbery material on the underside of the elastic that grips the surface beneath it, so the tablet does not slide around inside the cover or want to fall out. (I have screen protector film on my tablet, which seems like a good idea when a tablet is held in place by elastic bands rather than a hard plastic shell. This [[ASIN:B009NHU556 3-Pack Ultra-Clear Screen Protector)]] is easy to apply, and you get three chances to get it on right.)

The cover's built-in stands are quite intriguing. There are two of them attached to the inside of the front cover. One stand supports the tablet at a low angle for typing; the other supports it more or less upright for watching movies. Both provide comfortable viewing angles. The stands themselves are flat, microfiber-covered pieces that match the rest of the cover's interior. You pick the stand angle you want, and open out the appropriate stand. The stand is connected to the cover on top and also with a ribbon underneath, so that the stand converts into a triangular support for your tablet. This design is very clever, and I would consider it perfect if I hadn't already tried the [[ASIN:B009X0167Y Marware Vibe Standing Case]], which is a little easier to set up and offers more viewing angles.

This Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover has an elastic band that holds it tightly closed inside a book or tote bag, as well as an automatic magnetic wake/sleep feature. For the wake/sleep feature to work, you must insert your tablet with the camera at the left and the charging port at the right. This I don't like, because the charging port ends up at the tablet's bottom edge when you use the stands. This means you are limited to using the low-angle stand whenever your tablet is plugged in, because the plug contacts the table top. (With the Marware Vibe cover, the charging port ends up at the tablet's top edge, so you can use the tablet at any angle when it's plugged in.)

According to the accompanying retail literature, this Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover is "compatible" with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9", the Nook HD+, "and more". Because the cover holds the tablet with elastic bands, it should fit any tablet near in size to the large Fire or the large Nook. However, it is definitely too small for an iPad 2.

For me, it's difficult to choose between the Marware Vibe cover and the Verso "Darwin" cover. But in the end, as usually happens, good looks win out. My 8.9" Kindle Fire HD tablet is going to stay in the red faux-crocodile-skin cover, which is eye-catching, looks and feels luxurious, and is extremely well made.

Turning off auto-sleep/auto-lock may get you through thousands of pictures in one shot. This is what I mean... I'm no stranger to trying out different back-up programs. The current program we use is from Plex. When the iphone is backing up to my plex server, the iphone doesn't know that plex is working, so it goes to sleep after about 50 pictures. When it goes to sleep, plex stops backing up. So I always turn off auto-sleep prior to backing up. With the Qubii, the iphone KNEW that it was working, so it "almost" never went to sleep. I said almost because after 4000 files, for some reason, the phone went to sleep. Still, this is much, much, better than the plex app. When I started Qubii again, it picked up where it left off and backed the remaining 1000+ files. But I did the test one more time to make sure! I cleared the micro sd card, and I reset the Qubii count. This time I turned off auto-sleep/auto-sleep on the iphone, and it backed-up the entire camera roll of over 5000 photos and videos in one shot! More trials need to be done to conclusively say this thing can't get through 5000 files without the auto-sleep disabled.

After backing up everything, you should remove your SD card from the Qubii and transfer them to a larger permanent hard drive where you store your collection. The next time you charge your phone, the Qubii will remember the photos it already backed-up even if those photos are no longer on the SD card. So you can always clear your SD card. For whatever reason, if you need the Qubii to back-up the same photos again, like I did when I was testing things out, all you have to do is RESET the Qubii count, which you can do in the Back Up Settings in the app.

Below are the two pictures showing you the scenarios in which I tested this Qubii. Both scenarios used third party charging hubs, but I believe I had the original apple cable. As with all products dependent on apps.. one Apple update can ruin everything. LOL! So these types of app products depend on the company to stick around, so that if Apple breaks anything, they can fix it with a new firmware update. Qubii was on Kickstarter, but only time will tell. As is, this is an amazing product.

1. Understand this will only extend the coverage you already have. If you are not satisfied with your current speed when located close to your current router this type of device will not help. In this instance you will need to improve your internet service, modem or router.
2. An extender / repeater must be placed close enough to receive an optimal signal that it then repeats - if it is too far away, it can only transmit what it picks up - if this signal is weakened due to distance from your primary router the end result will be a reduced signal. It can only work with the signal it is receiving.
3. When placing any extender / repeater pay attention to what is between it and your primary router - keep in mind interior walls tend to not have insulation and are thus easier to penetrate than exterior walls, metal objects deflect signals more than other materials as do especially dense materials.
4. Optimally a primary router should be placed in a centralized location within a home and where the bulk of the time is spent. Extenders / repeaters can then be utilized between that and where you have found weak signal points.
5. In some instances, such as within Mesh WiFi networks extenders / repeaters can slow down the entire network and are thus not advised. A lot of this depends on advanced settings.

The HP Sprocket! Print pictures anywhere!!! Great for journaling and scrapbooking!

Yes & no.

The Pros of this little printer are: size (iPhone-sized), lightweight, quick printing, decent photo quality for a small, portable, Zink-paper printer, easy to set up, charges quickly

Cons: Comes with no instructions. You have to download the user guide from the app; the app is difficult to manage when you have to keep checking back to the user guide to adjust something on the app; once an item is in your printing queue, that baby isn’t coming off your queue until it’s printed. If you’ve accidentally uploaded multiple images of something, those items will print until you shut off the printer. Any new pics you add are loaded behind the old images, so if you think you’re going to quickly print a picture you’ve just taken, guess again. You’re getting the duplicate photo that might be days old. There is no way to delete these duplicates—and I’ve tried customer service MULTIPLE times. The “Virtual chat” with a Robo-tech tells you to cancel the print. This stops the printing of the image, but doesn’t delete it. The next time you flip your Sprocket on, guess which picture from your queue is headed your way? Exactly. This brings me to customer service, which is pretty shabby. You’re directed to chat with a virtual assistant, and, if you’re lucky and your question goes through (it often says “cannot send message”), you’ll get a generic answer that helps with bandaid fixes. HP has also added an “App Doctor” app that helps you do your own troubleshooting and performance tweaking on your sprocket. With the somewhat difficult maneuvering on the plain sprocket app, I’m praying for all I’m worth I never have to go to “the Doctor.”
Also somewhat annoying—there are different sizes of Zink paper for the Sprockets. Be sure you look carefully at which Sprocket model you have before ordering more paper, or you’ll end up doing the exchange dance. Just because the product headline says a package of paper is “For the HP Sprocket,” you’ll need to look much closer to see if it will fit in your model.

Boiling it down, I’d have to say the product is awesome in itself. It accomplishes exactly what a journaler on the go wants. But the app that drives this little printer? If I had ten thumbs, they’d all be down.

UPDATE: Everytime the app “adds improvements,” it decreases productivity. I now have to turn the printer off between prints, wait a few minutes, then turn it back on. Then I have to go to the printing queue and reactivate the process. The device freezes frequently when in use. I liked my original brand-new Sprocket Plus; the “improved by app” model less so.

But for just 329 (+ tax from Sony direct) I can't complain. The wireless internet access is the key feature that sold me, and it works fine.

PROS: Wireless internet works well w/Netflix, Pandora, Youtube, etc. and was easy to set up (using a wireless-G router two rooms away and no problems); very diverse selection of online content (more than Samsung); 720p is no problem; sound is very good; doesn't get hot; energy efficient; no dead or stuck pixels; no noise or buzz; very good HD and SD picture quality which did not require a ton of calibration out of the box -- just set it to Theater mode and it works.

CONS: Usual LCD problems (as mentioned above) but not worse than any other LCD; base doesn't swivel; remote is kind of clunky to use and doesn't light up; only one USB port and that's occupied by the wireless internet device; not a lot of picture controls compared to the Samsung; not great when there's lots of motion on screen (only having a 60hz refresh rate doesn't help); the black plastic frame around the screen is very soft and scratches easily.

Overall I'm satisfied. It does what I need it to do and for not a lot of money, and some channels look better than my Samsung that cost more than twice as much. Those people complaining that it's slow to start up have to remember that any device using wi-fi takes a few seconds to start up and connect to the network.

Had a 45 inch Sharp Aquos in the living room for over three years, and always thought it delivered wonderful HD output. On my PC, I own a Nvidia 3D Vision Set for the past two years for my PC gaming. The 3D Vision uses shutter technology, and definitely works beautifully with a 120HZ Monitor. Being a huge fan of all things tech, I've been watching the 3DTV market for the past few years, and finally it happened: Passive 3D! An affordable option which can feed 3D to a group of four+ without making you bankrupt.

I transferred the Sharp to the bedroom, and plugged all peripherals (PS3, 360, HDDVR and Roku) into the LG. Fired it up and immediately noticed how the colors popped. It actually ran rings around my Sharp Aquos! I transferred some 3D tech demos I saved on my PC to a USB drive, then ran them on the LG and was blown away by the 3D quality. Clean, bright and wonderful depth! Next, I popped in a BluRay movie (Monsters vs. Aliens) and again, my jaw dropped. I understood that the passive tech on the LG is suppose to have one drawback: horizontal resolution is decreased in 3D mode, but I'll be damned if I can see any difference. The TV arrived the day after Thanksgiving, so we still had the Thanksgiving Day Parade saved on our DVR. We used this to test the 2D to 3D on the fly conversation and it worked out pretty nicely. It definitely adds depth to any 2D broadcast, but nothing compared to true 3D.

As for gaming, the PS3 recognized I had a 3D TV from the start, and the few games I quickly tried (Wipeout, Uncharted 3 & Super Stardust) were mind-numbinlgy gorgeous. I didn't get a chance to try any 3D gaming on my 360 yet, but that's next!

Overall, I couldn't be happier with my decision to go for this LG!

Some quick notes:
- Unlike my 3D Vision PC shutter set up, the LG Passive does not darken the screen; colors remain bright and vibrant!

- My eyes were able to handle much longer periods of 3D viewing with the passive glasses. The 3D vision shutter would screw me up for the night if I played a long gaming session wearing them.

- The LG uses the same glasses they give out in theaters; go see Hugo and keep the glasses! :-)

- Get access to YouTube on your TV, and search YT3D! The LG Passive supports a number of different 3D formats which work brilliantly with most of YouTube's 3D showings'; there's TONS to see on there!

- The only ghosting I noticed was when you were not watching the TV from a normal viewing angle. For instance, if you stand up and move a bit close, you'll see overlapping images, but who watches TV like that?

- The two negatives: LG supplies a set of two orange and two white glasses. Orange and White? Really? What happened to the black glasses shown on the box and in a zillion ads? No big deal though, glasses are cheap. I found an eBay vendor selling a lot of 10 Movie glasses for $15.00! Try doing that with shutter technology. The USB input does not support DTS sound, so if you have a movie stored on a USB drive, it has to be converted or you will have no sound.

Years ago I bought a little 2MP 3X Zoom digital camera. It was a Kodak and it took great pictures. Several years after that I won a Kodak Z650 in an online contest and flat out loved the pictures it took. So when the stars aligned and Amazon had the Kodak Z990 on sale and my gift card balance was enough to afford it I jumped at the opportunity.

I really LIKE the Kodak Z990 and I'm sad that it will probably be the last Kodak camera I ever buy...

I LIKE this camera... I almost love this camera. While my Z650 almost never came out of Auto mode I find myself accessing the PASM controls and bracketing the exposure compensation when I use this camera.

It isn't that the Z990 doesn't take great pictures. It does. It just takes a little work to get them.

The camera is hefty, weighing in at 1 LB. 5 OZ. (593g) and feels substantial. To me it feels like what a camera should. The gripping areas on the front handgrip and rear thumb rest are lightly rubberized and the non-movable ring on the lens has a sturdy ribbed rubber covering.

The controls are reasonably easy to access and use. I like that you can use either the 5-way controller (similar to a Kindle's) or the clickable toggle wheel next to the thumb rest to access and control many of the camera settings. I like having the zoom controls on a ring around the shutter button. It feels easier to use than those cameras that have this control on the back. It also requires a very light touch as with 30x total optical zoom the lens and controls are very sensitive. At first you will find yourself zooming or going wide-angle past the point you wanted but with a little practice it becomes much easier to control.

The Z990 uses AA batteries (4) which, personally, I think is great. You can, in a pinch, get replacements at any convenience store, gas station or mega-mart in the US. It also comes with a serviceable if feature free slow battery charger and four Kodak brand rechargeable NiMH batteries. I've since replaced these with a smart charger and better batteries but out of the box they're enough to get you started.

Another great addition is the Optical View Finder. This is incredibly handy when shooting outdoors in bright sunlight. The 3" LCD screen is great but in direct sun it, like all LCD screens, becomes almost impossible to see.

I've, as of the time of this review, taken a bit over a thousand images and a handful of videos with my Z990 and I've barely scratched the surface of experiencing all the features and functions it has to offer.

Some notable features are:
Two panoramic image modes. One has the camera stitching two or three images together to produce the image and the other allows you to hold the shutter button and 'sweep' the camera to produce the panoramic image.
Multiple Kodak film time emulations - Kodacolor, Kodachrome, Ektachrome, T-MAX, TRI-X as well as standard B&W and Sepia modes.
In camera HDR mode.
Multiple burst modes.
Full 1080p video in stereo.
The camera can even emulates a Photo Booth taking four images in quick succession and stitching them together.

Nothing being perfect the Z990 has a few cons I feel need to be mentioned:
The memory card is stored in the battery compartment and the battery door is one of the few things I worry about breaking on this camera. It is light plastic and not easy to close with batteries installed.
To use a USB cable to transfer images from the camera to a computer the camera needs to be powered up requiring removal of the lens cap (because the cap mounts on the body not the lens). I don't like that it needs to sit with the lens exposed for no reason.
The lens isn't threaded so you cannot use any filters with this camera.
Preview mode, where the camera shows you the last image taken, cannot be disabled on this model, you can bypass it somewhat by 1/2 pressing the shutter once the preview displays but it would have been nice to be able to turn off this feature.

In conclusion:
While the Kodak Z990 Max isn't perfect it is an affordable bridge camera that takes excellent pictures day or night with an extremely powerful zoom lens, a host of useful features and controls that can only be topped by DSLR cameras. As Kodak's last hurrah, it's a pretty good note to go out on.

I can't provide any definitive conclusions on whether this particular aspect of my "treatment" really does anything. My ultimate conclusion is that while treating with other things (e.g. braces, compression, cold or hot), using an alternate device sometimes to change the stress points probably doesn't hurt. Sometimes when going back to use my normal mouse, just putting my hand into position seems to cause some strain, so I think this upright position is helping some. But my experience is that if I use anything for too long, I'll find some joint and/or muscle getting stressed. I'm concerned that this upright mouse position may not be as good for my elbow. I got this (and the [[ASIN:B004NBL9WK Amped Wireless High Power Wireless-300N Smart Repeater (SR300)]]) to extend my wireless network to my workshop, at the back of the yard, about 250 feet from the house. This is far enough away that I don't get even the smallest amount of the WiFi signal from the house. I wanted to watch TV while I work, and I also needed to be able to use a phone there. I could run Cat-5e wiring underground, but that would require digging a trench across the yard, and also running the Ethernet cable from the router inside the house to a demarcation point at the exterior of the house, which would be quite a bit of work. Using this antenna--two of them, actually, one at the house and one in the workshop--I'm able to get a very strong and fast network link in the workshop.

It's incredibly easy to set up. The antenna is designed to be mounted outdoors, and they recommend using 25 feet of [[ASIN:B004WW5WAA Amped Wireless Premium Outdoor 25ft Antenna Extension Cable (APC25EX)]] to connect the antenna to the Smart Repeater. Instead, I connected the Smart Repeater directly to the antenna with the short cable that comes with the antenna, and both are sitting in a closet at the edge of the house. I would probably get an even better signal if I mounted the antennas outside, but it works just fine for me with the antennas inside. In the workshop, I aimed the second antenna in the general direction of the one in the house, and it works great. There are a few trees between the buildings, and the signal still gets through.

Without doing anything to really optimize things, I'm getting 2.5 Mbps downlink, and about half that uplink. This is slower than my router's upstream connection, but it works just fine. I'm really enjoying having the network and phone in the workshop.

After flashing the SSD firmware from a bootable CD, putting a 120gb SanDisk Extreme in a (Dell GX620 sff/3ghz Pentium Dual Core w/2gb of RAM) was a walk in the park and so was installing Linux Mint 13 Cinnamon on the SSD. Enabling the Trim function as described on various Mint/Ubuntu websites went without a hitch. I've enabled a few other basic tweaks and they also have worked without any problems. Be sure to use the the EXT4 file system when partitioning, Linux Mint 13 uses it by default. Do not use the Linux Mint 13 KDE release, not even Orkin could kill all the bugs on that turkey.

At this point I am using the swap partition and browser caching on the SSD, but will be moving those to RAM as soon as Amazon gets my memory delivered to bump my computer up to 4gb. A note to other Dell GX620 owners. The Normal mode in the BIOS is in fact AHCI mode, as such it does fully support the Trim function. Linux can also emulate the Trim function using CRON if you do not have an AHCI capable box.

I'm telling you all this because getting the information to determine whether an SSD would work on my computer was like pulling teeth. User Name "SpeedStep" on the Dell forums was a lot of help.

Buy an SSD, you'll like it. Unless your Mac or an XP user, it isn't that big a deal.

I received one of these as a free review sample. Up front, the reason I subtracted a star is the set-up using the libratone app is maddening (to say the least.) On the other hand the sound quality is simply the best I have come across for a wireless speaker. That means I have to eat some recent words along the lines of there is no bluetooth speaker that is truly audiophile quality. This speaker disproves that.

Out of the box this quickly pairs and connects to bluetooth devices. I tested mine with a Note 4 phone and it took literally seconds to have it up and running. I was so blown away by the fact that this speaker reproduces music in a neutral manner by default that I was ready to sit down and give it a glowing review. Then I downloaded and installed the app.

The app is the Achilles heel. It had trouble finding the speaker, and the scant instructions were not very helpful either. Some how, some way it finally found the speaker, then was totally confusing when it came to setting up my personal profile (speaker location, bias and other features.) It also presented me with radio stations that were accessible via WiFi, and after connecting to my router I was able to access those. However, I am not personally interested in those offerings so did not explore them too deeply.

Basically, the app is good for linking multiple speakers, and some basic controls. Since I still cannot get the profiles set correctly I cannot speak about those. I will say that out of the box, without the libratone app and just connecting from my phone via bluetooth this speaker is spectacular. That is why I gave it the four stars that I did.

Bottom line: if you are looking for [possibly] the best bluetooth speaker on the market (and, yes, that includes Bose), this is it. If you want a speaker that can do everything this one is supposed to do, including fine tuning it for your room and musical tastes, you may be disappointed or frustrated. With a more intuitive app and more detailed instructions this would easily be a solid five star product that would keep Bose engineers and marketing up late at night. Until that happens, though, it's merely a superior bluetooth speaker that has crossed over into audiophile country.

This seems like a fairly average keyboard with nothing to make it stand out above the crowd. There are some issues involved with it though that you should be aware of before buying. The first issue is general one with all wireless keyboards, a matter of the trade-off involved in going wireless. The advantages of a wireless keyboard and mouse are that they reduces the clutter of wires on your desk and they are more portable than their wired kin. The main disadvantage is that they need either regular batteries or regular recharging, either of which is just extra maintenance that wired equipment doesn't need. Only you can decide if the trade-off is worth it or not to you.

There is a big issue specific to this keyboard though that you should be aware of. The keys on this board come in three colors - red, grey, and black. The lettering on the black keys is done in white which makes them easy to read. The lettering on the red and grey keys though is done in a grey tone that is hard to see. Even though the keyboard is done in a fairly standard layout, the difficulty in seeing the lettering really is a pain. So, all in all, this is not a terrible keyboard but it's not a great one either, and I have to give it an average 3 star rating.

With the head unlocked, I could center an object in the FOV.  Then I would attempt to move the object to the edge of the field.  I push on the scope or handle and the head resists this movement until I give enough pressure to overcome and it moves.  Once the object is on the edge of the field, I release the scope or handle and the object bounces out of the field -- because to overcome the stiction in the head, I was using enough force to bend (elastic deformation) the scope/mount combination so when I release it, it springs back.  This is annoying at high magnifications where even a slight amount of elasticity will mess up your field position.  It's totally worthless for video where fluid movement is critical but this head is not for video anyway.  It would be adaquate for low magnification (20-30x) wide-angle spotting of terrestrial subjects where framing does not need to be precise.  For my purposes, Gitzo's ball head worked far better. This is a review for the Baseus 5-in-1 USB C Hub. I have a few different hubs now because Apple decided I only needed USB-C ports on my laptop. Depending on what I’m doing and how many devices I need to plug in, I’ll either use a hub or adapters.

WiFi signal strength can be impacted by hubs or similar devices, there’s some interference with USB 3.0 and 2.4Ghz networks. It’s a known problem, there’s a lot about it online if you’ve also run into it. I’ve noticed this using other hubs, and I have about the same degree of interference with this one.

I don’t love the design of this hub. I wish the hub’s USB-C plug was straight, not an “L.” While I can still plug in other USB-C things next to the hub, the “L” shape of the plug dictates how the hub sits on my desk.

The hub is bigger than it needs to be. Maybe if the glassy front was repurposed, the USB 3.0 ports laid out in a square rather than a line, it wouldn’t take up as much room on my desk. The big display only has a tiny icon to show me when the hub is on … I just don’t like the wasted space.

Overall I can give this 4 out of 5 stars. I see at least two drawbacks. The first one is when you put it on the handle of a suitcase the zipper must be opened up wide at the top, leaving room for items in that pocket to fall out, possibly. #2 is the side compartment snap. Why a snap? It is not handy and does not allow the side pouch to open fully. I know this is being picky but hey, this is what cost it one star in my opinion. The padding is probably thick enough but feels less than what I am used too.

Overall this one will do just what I need. It is not quite as nice as my old one but it will be just fine for my needs.

A good laptop chiller pad becomes important when you run a lot of graphics-intensive games or if you are doing anything requiring the CPU to run a heavy load. Heat is the enemy of a computer system and the fastest way to a dead laptop is to not deal with heat issues when there’s a problem. I had a chill pad some time ago and it was sub-par. This one by LotFancy is much better and it does a good job.

First off, this is a big chill pad, the same basic dimensions as my laptop but much thicker. I have a 15.6" laptop and this pad is almost a perfect and exact fit, with only a narrow area in the back that extends past the end of the laptop. If you want a small and petite chill pad, this is not the one you want. It does incline too with a metal bar and slots in the case so that the laptop can be angled up. This actually is good for exposing it to even more air.

This chill pad connects to a USB port so it can either be plugged into a port on the computer or into a hub. There are two ports on it and both seem to be the same in terms of how the pad operates. That is, the pad operates at the same speed regardless of which port is used. There are also two buttons on the pad for turning it on. One turns on the larger fan in the middle, and the other turns on all the other fans. Two green LEDs next to those buttons indicate that the pad is powered on and working.

This pad moves a lot of air and it does a good job of cooling the laptop. But, it does so very quietly which is a huge plus. I have it set up in my home office and the pad makes about as much noise as a desktop computer, maybe a little less. The sound it makes is a gentle hum.

When powered on each fan has a bright blue LED in it. While they look cool when there’s no laptop on the pad, they’re all but invisible when the laptop is sitting on top. There isn’t even much of a glow coming from the pad. I turned on the pad, turned out all of the lights and the glow from the laptop screen was enough to overpower any light that might have come from the pad. Except for the low hum I wouldn’t know it was even turned on.

This is a good chill pad. It works quietly and it moves a lot of air. Compared to other chill pads I have used this one is very good and I am happy to recommend it.

I have a laptop that has (had) a 5400-RPM drive in it. It performed well enough but I wanted better performance from it and I was eager to see what difference the Crucial M550 SSD would have on it. It made a world of difference, even more than I anticipated.

If you’re not familiar with SSDs, they are essentially memory arrays that act like hard drives. Because the data is all contained in memory and not on platters, seek times drop to near-zero and the overall system performance is greatly enhanced. File system fragmentation goes away. Also, with the absence of the platters in an SSD, SSDs are generally more lightweight. Finally, with no moving parts an SSD consumes less power than a standard hard drive which is great for laptop users.

Installation of this SSD was easy. It fit my laptop without a hitch and within 15 minutes of starting the process the system was able to detect and identify the drive at the BIOS level.

I did not install Windows. Instead I chose to install Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6.5 on the drive, and I loaded up pretty much everything available in the distribution and turned on a lot of services. When finished I essentially configured a server system capable of running a small business. In the past this configuration would take 45-60 seconds to load as it iterated through the runlevel scripts and enabled all of the services I specified. With the SSD in place this dropped to about 20 seconds total, and much of that was waiting on services that take a while to initialize after being loaded in memory and started.

Load times aside, the whole system runs better and faster. Application launch times are appreciably shorter. The system is quieter too.

I can’t find anything about this SSD that I would consider a negative. It brings a new lease on life to a laptop. If you have a laptop that you wish would load faster and run quieter, this is a worthwhile upgrade that will bring noticeable results.

I had been looking at various GPS units for some time for my wonderful, but directionally challenged husband but was put off by the price and the monthly fees required by some. When I found this unit was offered by a local department store at a deeply discounted price I decided to check it out. I was very pleased because:

1. There is no monthly fee involved.

2. The screen is large enough to read.

3. The unit gives directions as you go along, both written and verbal, including updates 'in one mile turn....in 1/2 mile....in 500 ft etc'

4. When a turn has been missed the route is recalibrated, first prompting the driver to correct the error then ultimately selecting an alternate route.

5. There is a wealth of information, besides route ETA, speed (with the option to set a warning), altitude, local points of interest including restaurants, gas stations, etc.

We took this along on several trips since getting this, one of several hundred miles, others a bit closer, and were quite pleased for the most part. For the most part this was like having Mapquest in the car with you. It had some of the same problems as Mapquest (addresses might be slightly different, recent changes to route not noted etc) but had the advantage of being able to recalculate the route if you for any reason deviated from the plan, like to stop at a restaurant. There were a few minor problems some were caused by our reluctance to really read the manual, preferring to just push buttons and figure it out, others are inherent to this product.

First the on/off switch is in the back and must be operated with a pen/bent paperclip. Once started it did take a long time to locate the satellite and load. Another issue is that, like mapquest, local names are not always used and addresses may not appear exactly like they are used. In addition we discovered that a very small (pop 300) town we were looking for was not available on this unit. Most of these problems were minor inconveniences.

I highly recommend this product particularly for those who have not had a GPS before. It is quite user friendly and forgiving of operator error.

My son is very much into making stop-motion videos and he spends a great deal of time working with a camera on a tripod. Before we got this particular Vanguard Abeo tripod he used a very lightweight, no-frills tripod that eventually broke. This new tripod is a huge upgrade from what he was using.

The very first thing we noticed is that this is a heavy-duty tripod that is built to last. It is very well constructed and it has some heft to it - enough heft that it would not be the best choice for carrying any appreciable distance such as on a nature hike. For moving relatively short distances, though, this tripod is a winner.

This tripod has all manner of adjustments that can be made. Aside from the length of the legs, the angle of the legs is adjustable to the point that the camera can be lowered almost to ground level without ever removing it from the base. Of course the camera angle is easily adjustable, and unlike some other tripods we have used this particular tripod has tight settings that do not slip easily.

I especially like the bubble level, a feature lacking in some other tripods on the market. It makes getting the camera straight almost foolproof.

Not being a photography expert, I am no authority on cameras and tripods but from what experience I have I can say that this Vanguard Abeo tripod is a solid piece of equipment that works well. There are cheaper and lighter tripods on the market, and for snapping pictures from a camera that requires very little adjustment those may be fine. However, it's far better to have a heavier-duty tripod when the job requires some adjustment and movement, in which capacity this particular tripod will serve admirably.

Using this shutter release is so easy that even a beginner like me had it up and running in less than one minute. I've never used one before.

I'm using it on a Nikon D7000 to shoot long exposures, and hope one day to capture a heavenly lightning show without getting electrocuted in the process.

This product has only four components - shutter release button, shutter release button lock, cord and plug. You simply make sure that the camera is turned off, insert the plug end into your camera's accessory terminal and turn on the camera. Remember to turn off the camera when you're done before disconnecting the plug.

Pressing the button (there's only one) is just like pressing the shutter button on your camera, except that you can slide the button to the locked position, go have a cup of tea, and come back and release it to complete the photo. (I exaggerate, but I guess you COULD have a cup of tea if you were doing an extra-long exposure.) The D7000 offers exposures up to 30 seconds, but if you use this handy gizmo, you can scroll past that to "bulb" mode and keep that sucker open to your heart's content.

You can also use it for portraits, self-portraits and for those times when you really want to minimize camera shake. The only problem with the self-portraits is that the cord isn't that long, so you'll probably only get extreme close-ups. If self-portraits are your thing, better get a wireless remote. The one made by Amazon is pretty darned good.

So, camera, tripod, LED flashlight and this wired remote, and I'm all set for some light painting. This is definitely an essential part of any camera gear collection.

Amanda Richards, December 8, 2011

I have to say that I love this little guy almost as much as I loved my Withings Activite--which was a lot. But, my husband bought me a gold watch, and you can't wear two watches, so I switched to the GO on my coin pocket. It seems to accurately capture my steps and the e-ink screen is awesome: totally visible from any angle, which is really nice when you just want to glance down and see how you're doing (which, for me, is what I want most of the times I'm looking at it at all). I also vastly prefer Withing's "percent reached of your set goal" indicator (as also on the Withings Activite and their lesser watches) rather than a numerical display of steps, and I loathe numerical digital watch/clock displays, so the e-ink analog timeface is a wonderful touch. I've never actually looked at the thing to learn the time (cf. "I'm wearing a wristwatch," earlier) but it's classy--IMHO--that Withings has maintained the analog style and not just cheaped it with numbers.

The only thing it doesn't have that I might have added is a second indicator when you sweep your step goal twice (or more times) within the day. I'm very fond of how the central icon turns into a star after the first 100%; changing to a "2" or "3" or something other would have been nice for multiple sweeps.

Finally, the only constructive feedback I'll give is that the recent software update to the Activite made it sync almost imstantaneously with my iPhone SE, while the software in the GO (or, perhaps, the Bluetooth energy level in the GO) syncs as slowly as the Activite did before the recent update. My iPhone is set to auto-lock after 30 seconds; there's no good reason why the device can't sync with the phone app in that time, when the two (GO and iPhone) are sitting next to each other, with the GO near the iPhone's "silencing" switch for maximum pickup. Sync speed was always my only constructive feedback about the Activite (other than that it doesn't come in a 14k gold case option) and sync speed is the only thing I'd suggest that Nokia and Withings continue to perfect.

Enough complaints. I'll close by saying that Withings' customer support is among the fastest and best I've experienced. Can't go wrong.

I own the [[ASIN:B00MVXUACM Koss SP330 On Ear Dynamic Headphones Black with Silver Accents]] (current price $105.52) and I love them because of their comfort, good sound, and overall quality. I selected these headphones because I wanted to have a spare set and also to see how these would compare to my Koss.

I tried these headphones on the iPhone 5, iPad 3, and a Dell Latitude E6430 laptop and on all of these devices the sound was fabulous. It was actually more stereo sounding than my Koss.

PROS:

- The stereo sound is crisp and slightly better than my Koss.

- I LOVE, LOVE, LOVE the electric blue color which is called "candy blueberry."

- A headphone port on each earpiece provides the user with the ability to share the headphones by plugging in a music share cable which is NOT PROVIDED. A music share cable is not really needed in my opinion because all headphones come with one cable. While my boyfriend was listening to music on his iPad, I just plugged in my Koss cable to the side of the headset he was not using, and listened to the same music through my Koss headphones while he was using these.

- I like that the provided headphone cable can be used in the left or right earpiece which enables me to switch sides when I want.

- The headphone cable has an in-line MIC control for Android, tablets and other devices. Based on my research, an in-line MIC means there's a built in microphone that is built into the cable which should enable the wearer to answer calls without removing the headphones. I was able to get this to work on my boyfriend's iPad and iPhone and he was able to talk and hear through the headphones. There is a one button control on the in-line MIC which lowered the volume.

- The headphone band is adjustable.

CONS:

- The only CON I see is that they are not as comfortable for me as I would have liked. I used these a few times for a period of several hours. Even though they can be adjusted, I wound up getting a headache with extended use (more than 2 hours). So in this sense they were not as comfortable as they initially feel when just putting them on. The Koss headphones I own are the only ones I've ever tried that have been comfortable on me.

OTHER THINGS TO NOTE:

- The Amazon product page says that a music share cable is included; this is not correct nor is it really needed because if you are sharing just plug in a cable from another pair of headphones to the extra port on these.

- According to the manual, it takes 20 hours for the headphones to break in. It says the sound mellows out over time.

In summary, these headphones are great. They have fantastic stereo sound (at least to my ears), the ability to share by plugging in another set of headphones, and an in-line MIC. They are adjustable and relatively comfortable but not as comfortable as my Koss. The color is also attractive.

I purchased one of these 9th generation Kindle Oasis. The first unit I received would freeze during the configuration process. You could reset it, but if you try to configure, it would freeze again. At this point, I made the mistake of asking for a replacement instead of just returning the faulty Kindle Oasis for a refund. A replacement unit arrived in three days. Unfortunately, the replacement unit was DoA. There was a fixed image on screen, and I wasn't able to get a response from this Kindle after charging it for a long time and multiple reset attempts. I had already shipped the first unit back using a UPS shipping label created by Amazon at this point. I went to my Amazon Orders page to return the second unit for a credit. But Amazon web interface wouldn't allow a self service return for refund. I had contact customer service and deal with several customer service representatives. They consistently asked me to try some simple trouble shooting steps ( most of which are not even applicable if you have a completely dead kindle). They wouldn't listen to me when I said I just wanted to return it, and try to pressure me into another replacement. At this point, I had spent several hours troubleshooting, talking to Amazon Customer service, taking packages to UPS, etc. so I insisted on a return for refund. This time, the customer service representative said he was having problems generating the return label, and then disappeared. After several minutes of wait, another customer rep took over and worked on this case for another 10 minutes or so. At that point, I ended up with two sets of return labels in my email. The customer service rep told me to use the labels from the second email (in chronological order). So the next day, I shipped the replacement Kindle Oasis back. A few days later, I saw on UPS tracking that the package was delivered to Amazon and three days after this I received an email confirmation from Amazon that my first return was received. A few days later, I saw on UPS tracking that the second Kindle Oasis (replacement) was also received by Amazon. I waited a few days for return confirmation and refund from Amazon, but nothing happened. When I contacted Amazon Customer service, they kept telling me that I shouldn't worry about getting charged as my replacement is complete. But they could see no record of my return of the replacement. I spent probably a good half an hour chatting with a customer service rep but they couldn't help me at all since they could only see the record for on return request. That chat ended with no resolution because I ran out of time and had to get to an appointment. Later, I got in touch with yet another service rep, and explained everything from scratch. Luckily, that person was able to find records of both returns being received by Amazon and finally issued me a refund.

So lessons from this story:
1. Don't buy a 9th gen Kindle Oasis. There seems to be serious quality control issues. The probability of one customer receiving two faulty Kindles in a row would be infinitesimal unless fault rates are in the 20% range.
2. If you receive a faulty Kindle from Amazon, return it for a refund. Don't ask for a replacement. Amazon's automated return process cannot handle the return of a replacement unit, and you will sink a lot of time dealing with customer service representatives

I got thermal paste because I do some circuit board work and have added heat sinks in the past.  When adding a heat sink it usually comes with a sticky material but nothing to aid getting the heat from the processor to the heat sink.  Thermal paste aids conductivity so always use thermal paste when using a heat sink.  To do otherwise you may overheat your circuit and make it worse.  This kit comes with gloves, cleaning wipes and applicator to spread the silicone material once poured from the tube.  This is a must have for the electronics workshop bench.

Definitely recommend the watch, especially for beginner and intermediate runners.
